notes: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is the dry, waterproof epidermis of the skin. Pick it if the question asked about the outer surface of the body rather than a moist internal tube.
Correct. The esophagus is lined by moist, many-layered nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium that withstands abrasion.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract, such as the trachea, where cilia sweep mucus. Choose it for an airway question, not for the food tube.
Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells built for secretion and absorption. It lines the stomach and the intestines, so it would be the answer for those organs, not the esophagus.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the hard palate and the soft palate?
options: The hard palate is cartilage and forms the anterior roof; the soft palate is muscular and forms the posterior roof
The hard palate is bony and forms the posterior roof; the soft palate is muscular and forms the anterior roof
The hard palate is muscular and forms the anterior roof; the soft palate is bony and forms the posterior roof
The hard palate is bony and forms the anterior roof; the soft palate is muscular and forms the posterior roof
questions.why: Together the two palates form the roof of the mouth. The hard palate is the bony anterior part, formed by the maxillae and palatine bones and covered by mucous membrane. The soft palate is the muscular posterior part, and its finger-like uvula closes off the nasopharynx during swallowing. You can feel this with your tongue: the front of the roof is firm and the back is soft.
notes: The hard palate is bone, formed by the maxillae and palatine bones, not cartilage. Cartilage would fit a question about the framework of the larynx or the external nose, not the roof of the mouth.
This swaps the positions. The hard palate is in front, right behind the upper teeth, and the soft palate lies behind it, ending in the uvula.
This swaps the tissues. The hard palate is the one built on bone, which is why it feels firm, and the soft palate is the muscular one that can move during swallowing.
Correct. The bony hard palate forms the front of the roof of the mouth and the muscular soft palate forms the back.
questions.answerText: The hard palate is bony and forms the anterior roof; the soft palate is muscular and forms the posterior roof

questions.q: What is the lingual frenulum?
options: The finger-like projection of the soft palate at the back of the mouth
The midline fold of mucous membrane that anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth
The projections on the tongue surface that carry taste buds
The opening from the mouth into the oropharynx
questions.why: The tongue is skeletal muscle covered with mucous membrane, and it needs to move freely while staying attached. The lingual frenulum is the thin midline fold of mucous membrane on the underside of the tongue that anchors it to the floor of the mouth. You can see it by lifting the tip of your tongue in a mirror.
notes: The finger-like projection of the soft palate is the uvula, which closes off the nasopharynx during swallowing. Pick it if the question asked what hangs from the back of the soft palate.
Correct. The lingual frenulum is the midline fold under the tongue that anchors it to the floor of the mouth.
The projections on the tongue surface that carry taste buds and help grip food are the papillae. Choose papillae for a question about the rough upper surface of the tongue.
The opening from the mouth into the oropharynx is the fauces. It would be the answer if the question asked where food passes from the mouth into the throat.
questions.answerText: The midline fold of mucous membrane that anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth

questions.q: Which structure is the muscular tube that carries food from the laryngopharynx down to the stomach?
options: The pharynx
The trachea
The esophagus
The duodenum
questions.why: The esophagus is a collapsible muscular tube, about 25 cm (10 inches) long, that carries food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach. It runs posterior to the trachea through the thorax and passes through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus. It is collapsed when empty and opens as a bolus passes.
notes: The pharynx is the funnel-shaped throat passage that food passes through before reaching the esophagus. Choose it if the question asked where swallowed food goes right after the mouth.
The trachea is the airway that lies directly anterior to the esophagus and carries air to the lungs. Pick it if the question asked which tube is held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
Correct. The esophagus carries food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach.
The duodenum is the first region of the small intestine, just past the stomach. It would be the answer if the question asked where food goes after the stomach.

questions.q: The hard palate and the soft palate together form which part of the oral cavity?
options: The opening into the oropharynx
The lateral walls of the mouth
The floor of the mouth
The roof of the mouth
questions.why: The palate is the roof of the mouth. The hard palate forms the bony anterior part, and the soft palate forms the muscular posterior part, ending in the uvula. Together they separate the oral cavity below from the nasal cavity above, and the soft palate rises during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx.
notes: The fauces is the opening between the mouth and the oropharynx, framed by the palatal arches. It is a passage at the back of the mouth, not the roof, so choose it if the question asked where food passes from the mouth into the throat.
The lateral walls of the mouth are the cheeks. They would be the answer if the question asked what bounds the oral cavity on each side.
The floor of the mouth is the mylohyoid muscle, and the tongue rests on it. The palates lie above the tongue, so they cannot form the floor.
Correct. The hard and soft palates together form the roof of the mouth.

questions.q: Which two regions of the pharynx carry swallowed food toward the esophagus?
options: The laryngopharynx and larynx
The nasopharynx and oropharynx
The oropharynx and laryngopharynx
The nasopharynx and laryngopharynx
questions.why: The pharynx is a funnel-shaped passage with three regions stacked top to bottom: the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx. Food passes from the mouth through the fauces into the oropharynx, then down into the laryngopharynx, which leads into the esophagus. The nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity, carries only air and is closed off by the soft palate and uvula during swallowing.
notes: The larynx is the voice box, part of the airway that leads to the trachea, not a region of the pharynx. Food entering the larynx is choking. The larynx would be the answer for a question about where air goes after the laryngopharynx.
The oropharynx does carry food, but the nasopharynx carries only air and is sealed off during swallowing. Pick this pair for the path of air from the nose into the throat.
Correct. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry swallowed food toward the esophagus.
The laryngopharynx carries food, but the nasopharynx does not, and this pair skips the oropharynx that food enters first from the mouth.

questions.q: Which ring of muscle at the bottom of the esophagus closes to keep stomach contents from rising into the esophagus?
options: The pyloric sphincter
The upper esophageal sphincter
The lower esophageal sphincter
The ileocecal sphincter
questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter, also called the cardiac sphincter, is the ring of muscle at the bottom of the esophagus where it meets the stomach. It opens to let a bolus into the stomach and closes to keep acidic stomach contents out of the esophagus. When it is weak, reflux occurs, as in GERD.
notes: The pyloric sphincter is at the exit of the stomach into the duodenum, not the entrance. Pick it if the question asked which sphincter controls food leaving the stomach.
The upper esophageal sphincter guards the top of the esophagus, where it meets the laryngopharynx. It would be the answer if the question asked which sphincter a bolus passes right after the pharynx.
Correct. The lower esophageal sphincter closes to keep stomach contents from rising into the esophagus.
The ileocecal sphincter sits where the ileum meets the large intestine. Choose it if the question asked about the junction of the small and large intestines.

questions.q: Which sphincter is also called the cardiac sphincter?
options: The upper esophageal sphincter
The lower esophageal sphincter
The ileocecal sphincter
The pyloric sphincter
questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter guards the bottom of the esophagus, where it opens into the cardia of the stomach. Because it sits at the cardia, it is also called the cardiac sphincter. The name has nothing to do with the heart's own muscle, even though the cardia lies just below the heart.
notes: The upper esophageal sphincter guards the top of the esophagus, where it meets the laryngopharynx. Pick it if the question asked which sphincter lies at the start of the esophagus.
Correct. The lower esophageal sphincter is also called the cardiac sphincter.
The ileocecal sphincter sits where the ileum meets the large intestine. Choose it for a question about the junction of the small and large intestines.

The pyloric sphincter guards the exit of the stomach into the duodenum, at the opposite end from the cardia. It would be the answer if the question asked which sphincter controls food leaving the stomach.

questions.q: A swallowed bolus has just passed through the lower esophageal sphincter. Which region does it enter?
options: The laryngopharynx
The oropharynx
The duodenum
The stomach
questions.why: Food travels from the mouth through the oropharynx and laryngopharynx into the esophagus. The lower esophageal sphincter sits at the bottom of the esophagus and opens into the cardia of the stomach. So once the bolus passes this sphincter, it is in the stomach.
notes: The laryngopharynx is the lowest part of the pharynx, just above the esophagus, so the bolus passes it before entering the esophagus. Choose it if the question asked which region leads into the esophagus.
The oropharynx is passed early in swallowing, right after the mouth. It would be the answer if the question asked where food goes after the fauces.
The duodenum comes after the stomach, past the pyloric sphincter. Pick it if the question said the food had just passed the pyloric sphincter.
Correct. The lower esophageal sphincter opens into the stomach.

questions.q: The esophagus is a simple muscular tube with no villi or absorptive folds, while the small intestine is covered in them. Which statement best explains this difference?
options: The esophagus must stay permanently open, and folds would block its lumen
The esophagus only transports food to the stomach, so it needs muscle to push food, not surface area to absorb it
The esophagus absorbs water from swallowed food, a job that needs no folds
The esophagus stores food between meals, so it needs a smooth wall that stretches
questions.why: Structure matches function along the canal. The esophagus simply carries swallowed food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach, so it needs a strong muscular wall to push each bolus down and a tough, abrasion-resistant lining. It does no absorbing, so it has no use for the villi and folds that give the small intestine its huge absorptive surface.
notes: The esophagus is actually collapsible, flattened when empty and opening only as a bolus passes. A tube held permanently open by rings would be the trachea, which is the answer for a question about the airway.
Correct. The esophagus is built for transport, not absorption.
Absorbing water from waste is the main job of the large intestine, not the esophagus. Choose the large intestine for a question about where water is reclaimed and feces form.
Storing food between meals is the job of the stomach, whose rugae flatten so it can stretch. Pick the stomach for a question about holding a meal.
questions.answerText: The esophagus only transports food to the stomach, so it needs muscle to push food, not surface area to absorb it

questions.q: Which finger-like projection of the soft palate closes off the nasopharynx during swallowing?
options: The lingual frenulum
The uvula
The palatine tonsil
The epiglottis
questions.why: The uvula hangs from the back edge of the soft palate. During swallowing, the soft palate and uvula rise to close off the nasopharynx so that food and liquid head down toward the esophagus instead of up into the nasal cavity. You can see it at the back of your mouth in a mirror.
notes: The lingual frenulum is the midline fold of mucous membrane that anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth. Pick it if the question asked what holds the tongue down.
Correct. The uvula closes off the nasopharynx during swallowing.

The palatine tonsil is lymphatic tissue between the palatal arches at the sides of the back of the mouth, not a projection of the soft palate. It would be the answer for lymphatic tissue guarding the oropharynx.

The epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage on the larynx that covers the airway below during swallowing, not the nasopharynx above. Choose it if the question asked what keeps food out of the larynx.

questions.q: What is the opening from the mouth into the oropharynx called?
options: The uvula
The esophageal hiatus
The fauces
The pyloric canal
questions.why: The fauces is the opening at the back of the oral cavity that leads into the oropharynx. Swallowed food passes through it on the way from the mouth to the throat. The palatine tonsils sit on either side of the fauces, between the palatal arches, where they guard this entrance.
notes: The uvula is the finger-like projection of the soft palate, hanging just above the fauces rather than being the opening itself. It would be the answer for what closes off the nasopharynx during swallowing.
The esophageal hiatus is the opening in the diaphragm that the esophagus passes through, much farther down. Pick it if the question asked where the esophagus passes from the thorax into the abdomen.
Correct. The fauces is the opening from the mouth into the oropharynx.
The pyloric canal is part of the pyloric region of the stomach, leading toward the pylorus. Choose it for a question about the exit end of the stomach.

questions.q: What is the opening in the diaphragm that the esophagus passes through called?
options: The fauces
The cardia
The lower esophageal sphincter
The esophageal hiatus
questions.why: The esophagus runs down through the thorax behind the trachea and must cross the diaphragm to reach the stomach in the abdomen. It passes through an opening in the diaphragm called the esophageal hiatus. Just below the hiatus, the lower esophageal sphincter opens into the cardia of the stomach. If part of the stomach pushes up through this opening, the result is a hiatal hernia.
notes: The fauces is the opening from the mouth into the oropharynx, at the top of the swallowing path. Pick it if the question asked where food leaves the mouth.
The cardia is the region of the stomach that surrounds the opening from the esophagus, below the diaphragm. Choose it if the question asked which stomach region the esophagus opens into.
The lower esophageal sphincter is a ring of muscle at the bottom of the esophagus, not an opening in the diaphragm. It would be the answer for what keeps stomach contents out of the esophagus.
Correct. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus.

questions.q: What anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth?
options: The uvula
The lingual frenulum
The fauces
The papillae
questions.why: The lingual frenulum is the thin midline fold of mucous membrane under the tongue that anchors it to the floor of the mouth. You can see it by lifting the tip of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. The submandibular ducts open on either side of it.
notes: The uvula is the small fleshy projection that hangs from the back of the soft palate. It would be the answer for the structure dangling at the back of the mouth.
Correct. The lingual frenulum anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth.
The fauces is the opening from the mouth into the oropharynx. Pick it for the passage at the back of the oral cavity.
Papillae are the small projections on the upper surface of the tongue that carry taste buds and help grip food. Pick them for the structures that hold taste buds.

questions.q: Which muscles originate outside the tongue and move it side to side and in and out?
options: The intrinsic tongue muscles
The buccinator muscles
The extrinsic tongue muscles
The masseter muscles
questions.why: Extrinsic means outside, so the extrinsic tongue muscles start on bone or on the soft palate outside the tongue and end inside it. Because they anchor elsewhere, they can move the whole tongue side to side and in and out. The intrinsic muscles, which start and end inside the tongue, change its shape for speech and swallowing.
notes: The intrinsic tongue muscles lie entirely within the tongue and change its shape and size for speech and swallowing. Pick them for reshaping the tongue rather than moving it as a whole.
The buccinator muscles form the wall of the cheeks and press food back between the teeth while chewing. Pick them for the cheek muscle, not a tongue muscle.
Correct. The extrinsic tongue muscles move the tongue as a whole.
The masseter muscles are chewing muscles that run from the zygomatic arch to the mandible and close the jaw. They would be the answer for a question about the muscle that elevates the mandible.

questions.q: Incisors at the front of the mouth have a flat, chisel-like edge, while molars at the back have a broad surface with several cusps. What does this difference allow?
options: Incisors grind food and molars cut it
Incisors and molars secrete different digestive enzymes
Incisors cut food and molars grind it
Only molars chew, while incisors serve only for speech
questions.why: Tooth shape matches tooth job. The chisel-like edge of the incisors cuts and bites off pieces of food, while the broad, cusped surface of the molars crushes and grinds those pieces. Molars do the heaviest grinding in the mouth, which turns food into a soft mass the tongue can shape into a bolus.
notes: This reverses the jobs. A thin chisel edge is suited to cutting, and a broad surface with several cusps is suited to grinding.
Teeth do not secrete enzymes; digestive enzymes in the mouth come from the salivary glands. Pick the salivary glands for the source of salivary amylase.
Correct. Incisors cut and molars grind.
Incisors do help shape some speech sounds, but their main digestive job is biting and cutting food. Students pick this when they think only the back teeth take part in chewing.
questions.answerText: Incisors cut food and molars grind it

questions.q: The hard palate is the bony front part of the roof of the mouth. Which bones form it?
options: The maxillae and the vomer
The palatine bones and sphenoid
The maxillae and palatine bones
The mandible and palatine bones
questions.why: The hard palate is the bony anterior roof of the mouth and the floor of the nasal cavity. The palatine processes of the two maxillae form its front portion, and the horizontal plates of the two palatine bones form its back portion. Behind it, the soft palate continues as a muscular flap that ends in the uvula.
notes: The vomer is the thin bone that forms the lower part of the nasal septum. It sits on top of the hard palate rather than forming it, and it is the answer for a question about the bony nasal septum.

The sphenoid is the bat-shaped bone in the middle of the cranial floor, behind the nasal cavity. Only the palatine half of this pair is correct, and the sphenoid would be the answer for a question about the sella turcica.
Correct. The maxillae in front and the palatine bones behind form the hard palate.

The mandible is the lower jaw and forms no part of the roof of the mouth. Students pick it because it is the most familiar bone of the mouth, but it would be the answer for the bone holding the lower teeth.

questions.q: During swallowing, the uvula and soft palate rise. Which space do they close off?
options: The larynx
The laryngopharynx
The nasopharynx
The oropharynx
questions.why: The uvula is the finger-like projection hanging from the back of the soft palate. When you swallow, the soft palate and uvula move upward and close off the nasopharynx, the part of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity. This keeps food and liquid from being pushed up into the nose.
notes: The larynx is protected during swallowing by the epiglottis, which folds over its opening. Choose the larynx if the question asks what the epiglottis covers, not what the uvula closes.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest part of the pharynx, which leads into the esophagus. Food passes through it on the way down, so it stays open during swallowing.
Correct. The soft palate and uvula seal off the nasopharynx so food does not enter the nose.

The oropharynx is the part of the pharynx behind the mouth, and food has to pass through it to be swallowed. It would be the answer for the region you see at the back of the throat when you open your mouth.

questions.q: The esophagus is a collapsible muscular tube. Between which two structures does it carry food?
options: From the nasopharynx to the stomach
From the laryngopharynx to the stomach
From the oral cavity to the oropharynx
From the stomach to the duodenum
questions.why: The esophagus is about 25 cm (10 inches) long. It begins where the laryngopharynx ends, runs down through the thorax behind the trachea, passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm, and opens into the stomach. Muscular contractions of its wall carry swallowed food down this path.
notes: The nasopharynx lies above the soft palate and carries air, not food, so the esophagus does not start there. Students pick this when they forget that the pharynx has three regions and only the lower two carry food.
Correct. The esophagus runs from the laryngopharynx to the stomach.
Food moves from the oral cavity into the oropharynx through the fauces, an opening rather than a tube. This would describe the first step of swallowing, not the esophagus.
The passage from the stomach to the duodenum is guarded by the pyloric sphincter and leads into the small intestine. It would be the answer for where food goes after the stomach.
questions.answerText: From the laryngopharynx to the stomach

questions.q: What opening does the lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter guard?
options: The opening from the esophagus into the stomach
The opening from the pharynx into the esophagus
The opening from the ileum into the cecum
The opening from the stomach into the duodenum
questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter is a ring of muscle at the bottom of the esophagus. It guards the opening into the stomach, relaxing to let food pass and closing to keep stomach contents from flowing back up. It is also called the cardiac sphincter because it opens into the cardia, the region of the stomach around the esophageal opening.
notes: Correct. The lower esophageal sphincter guards the entrance to the stomach.
The opening from the pharynx into the esophagus is guarded by the upper esophageal sphincter. Pick this if the question asks about the sphincter at the top of the esophagus.
The ileocecal sphincter guards the junction where the ileum empties into the cecum of the large intestine. That is the answer for the valve between the small and large intestines.
The pyloric sphincter guards the opening from the stomach into the duodenum. It would be the answer for the sphincter at the far end of the stomach.
questions.answerText: The opening from the esophagus into the stomach

questions.q: A patient has burning pain behind the breastbone after meals as stomach contents rise into the esophagus. Which sphincter has most likely weakened?
options: Pyloric sphincter
Ileocecal sphincter
Lower esophageal sphincter
Upper esophageal sphincter
questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter normally closes the bottom of the esophagus so acidic stomach contents stay in the stomach. When it weakens, stomach contents flow back up and irritate the esophageal lining, which is felt as heartburn behind the sternum because the esophagus runs through the thorax there. Long-term reflux of this kind is called GERD.
notes: The pyloric sphincter controls the passage from the stomach into the duodenum, at the far end of the stomach. It is the answer if the question involves food leaving the stomach too slowly or too fast.
The ileocecal sphincter sits between the small and large intestines in the lower right abdomen, far from the chest. It would be the answer for backflow from the cecum into the ileum.
Correct. A weak lower esophageal sphincter lets stomach contents back up into the esophagus.

The upper esophageal sphincter sits at the top of the esophagus, where it joins the pharynx. It would matter for a problem where food or liquid comes up into the throat, not for acid entering the lower esophagus.

questions.q: Which description matches gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)?
options: An eroded sore forms in the wall of the stomach or duodenum
Stomach contents flow back through a weak lower esophageal sphincter
Small pouches bulge outward through weak spots in the colon wall
Part of the stomach pushes up through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm
questions.why: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, happens when the lower esophageal sphincter at the bottom of the esophagus is weak. Acidic stomach contents flow back up into the esophagus and irritate its lining, which is felt as heartburn behind the sternum. The name itself tells you the two organs involved, gastro for stomach and esophageal for esophagus.
notes: An eroded sore in the wall of the stomach or duodenum is a peptic ulcer. It is the answer for a sore that begins in the mucosa and can perforate the wall.
Correct. GERD is reflux of stomach contents through a weak lower esophageal sphincter.
Small pouches bulging through weak spots in the colon wall describe diverticulosis. Choose it for a question about the large intestine.
Part of the stomach pushing up through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm is a hiatal hernia. Pick it for a question about the stomach moving into the thorax.
questions.answerText: Stomach contents flow back through a weak lower esophageal sphincter

questions.q: Which structure forms the floor of the oral cavity?
options: Hard palate
Cheeks
Uvula
Mylohyoid muscle
questions.why: The oral cavity is bounded by the lips in front, the cheeks on the sides, the hard and soft palate above, and the mylohyoid muscle below. The tongue rests on this muscular floor and fills most of it, which is why students often name the tongue as the floor. The lingual frenulum anchors the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.
notes: The hard palate is the bony front part of the roof of the mouth. It sits above the tongue, so it is the answer for the roof, not the floor.
The cheeks form the lateral walls of the oral cavity, built around the buccinator muscle. Choose them for the sides of the mouth, not the floor.
The uvula hangs from the back edge of the soft palate, at the top of the mouth. It would be the answer for the projection that helps close off the nasopharynx during swallowing.
Correct. The mylohyoid muscle forms the floor of the oral cavity.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a wall of the oral cavity with the structure that forms it?
options: Lateral walls: the cheeks
Roof: the tongue
Anterior wall: the uvula of the soft palate
Floor: the hard palate
questions.why: The walls of the oral cavity are the lips in front, the cheeks on each side, the hard and soft palate above, and the mylohyoid muscle below, with the tongue resting on it. Only the pairing of the cheeks with the lateral walls matches this layout. The other choices put real mouth structures in the wrong position.
notes: Correct. The cheeks form the lateral walls of the mouth.
The tongue rests on the floor of the mouth, above the mylohyoid muscle, so it is not the roof. The roof is formed by the hard and soft palate.
The uvula hangs at the back of the soft palate, near the opening to the oropharynx. The anterior wall of the mouth is formed by the lips.
The hard palate is part of the roof of the mouth, above the tongue. Pick it for the bony front part of the roof.

questions.q: How many teeth are in a complete adult (permanent) set?
questions.why: The permanent set has 32 teeth, 16 in each jaw. In each half of each jaw there are two incisors, one canine, two premolars, and three molars, which adds up to eight per quarter and 32 in all. The count includes the third molars, or wisdom teeth.
notes: Twenty is the number of deciduous, or baby, teeth. Pick it for a child's first set.
Twenty-four has no basis in either set. It usually comes from mixing up the number of teeth per jaw or forgetting a whole tooth type.
Twenty-eight is the count students get if they leave out the four wisdom teeth. Many adults do have 28 teeth after wisdom teeth are removed, but the full set has 32.
Correct. A complete permanent set has 32 teeth.

questions.q: How many teeth are in the deciduous (baby) set?
questions.why: The deciduous teeth are the first set, which erupt in early childhood and are later shed. There are 20 of them, five in each half of each jaw: two incisors, one canine, and two molars. They are gradually replaced by the 32 permanent teeth.
notes: Sixteen is the number of permanent teeth in one jaw, half of the adult set. It is a common mix-up between one jaw and the whole mouth.
Correct. The deciduous set has 20 teeth.
Twenty-eight is the adult count without the four wisdom teeth. It does not apply to the baby set.
Thirty-two is the number of permanent teeth in a complete adult set. Pick it for the adult count.

questions.q: Which substance covers the crown of a tooth and is the hardest material in the body?
options: Cementum
Pulp
Dentin
Enamel
questions.why: Enamel is a heavily mineralized layer that covers the crown, the part of the tooth above the gum. It is the hardest substance in the body, which lets it withstand the forces of chewing. Enamel contains no living cells, so once it is lost it cannot grow back.
notes: Cementum is a calcified layer that covers the root, not the crown. Choose it for the covering of the part of the tooth inside the socket.
Pulp is the soft tissue in the center of the tooth, holding nerves and blood vessels. It is the softest part, not the hardest.
Dentin forms the bulk of the tooth beneath the enamel. It is hard and bone-like but softer than enamel. Pick it for the main body of the tooth.
Correct. Enamel covers the crown and is the hardest substance in the body.

questions.q: What does the pulp cavity of a tooth contain?
options: Bone marrow and fat cells
Enamel and dentin
Saliva and mucus
Blood vessels and nerves
questions.why: The pulp cavity is the hollow center of the tooth. It is filled with pulp, a soft connective tissue that carries blood vessels and nerves. The pulp extends down into each root as the root canal, where the vessels and nerves enter through a small opening at the tip of the root.
notes: Bone marrow and fat are found inside bones, not teeth. Teeth sit in bony sockets, but the tooth itself has pulp at its center.
Enamel and dentin are the hard outer layers of the tooth that surround the pulp cavity. They form its walls, not its contents.
Saliva and mucus are secretions of the salivary and lingual glands that bathe the outside of the teeth. They do not fill the inside of a tooth.
Correct. The pulp cavity holds the blood vessels and nerves of the tooth.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares dentin and enamel?
options: Dentin forms the bulk; enamel is harder and covers the crown
Enamel forms the bulk; dentin is harder and covers the crown
Both cover only the root and attach to the socket
Both are soft tissues that hold the nerves of the tooth
questions.why: Most of a tooth is made of dentin, a hard, bone-like tissue that surrounds the pulp cavity. Over the crown, the dentin is capped by enamel, the hardest substance in the body. Over the root, the dentin is covered by cementum instead.
notes: Correct. Dentin is the bulk of the tooth and enamel is the harder cap on the crown.
This reverses the two layers. Enamel is the thin, very hard covering of the crown, and dentin lies beneath it as the main body of the tooth.
The root is covered by cementum, which helps attach the tooth to its socket. Enamel stays on the crown, and dentin runs through both crown and root.
The soft tissue holding the nerves is the pulp, at the center of the tooth. Dentin and enamel are both hard mineralized tissues.
questions.answerText: Dentin forms the bulk; enamel is harder and covers the crown

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the crown and the root of a tooth?
options: Crown is above the gum; root sits in the bony socket
Root is above the gum; crown sits in the bony socket
Both lie in the socket and are covered by cementum
Both lie above the gum and are covered by enamel
questions.why: A tooth has two main regions. The crown is the visible part that projects above the gingiva, or gum, and is covered by enamel. The root is the part anchored in the bony socket of the maxilla or mandible and is covered by cementum. The narrow region where they meet, at the gum line, is the neck.
notes: Correct. The crown is above the gum and the root is in the socket.
This swaps the two regions. The part you can see when someone smiles is the crown.
Only the root lies in the socket and is covered by cementum. The crown is exposed and covered by enamel.
Only the crown lies above the gum and wears enamel. The root is hidden in the socket.
questions.answerText: Crown is above the gum; root sits in the bony socket

questions.q: What anchors the root of a tooth to the bone of its socket?
options: Pulp
Gingiva
Lingual frenulum
Periodontal ligament
questions.why: The periodontal ligament is a layer of dense fibrous connective tissue between the cementum of the root and the bony wall of the socket. Its fibers anchor the tooth firmly while allowing a tiny amount of give during chewing. This tooth-in-socket arrangement is a fibrous joint called a gomphosis.
notes: The pulp is the soft tissue inside the tooth with its nerves and blood vessels. It lies within the tooth rather than attaching it to the jaw.
The gingiva, or gum, is the mucous membrane covering the jaw bone and surrounding the neck of each tooth. It seals around the tooth but does not hold the root in the bone.
The lingual frenulum is a fold of mucous membrane that anchors the tongue to the floor of the mouth. Pick it for the tongue, not the teeth.
Correct. The periodontal ligament anchors the root to the socket.

questions.q: Which statement correctly matches a type of tooth with its main job?
options: Incisors: broad crowns that grind
Molars: broad crowns that grind
Premolars: chisel edges that cut
Canines: flat edges that grind
questions.why: Tooth shape follows function. Incisors at the front have chisel-shaped edges for cutting, canines are pointed for tearing, and premolars and molars have broad crowns with raised cusps for crushing and grinding. Molars, at the back of the jaw, have the broadest grinding surfaces.
notes: Incisors are the front teeth with thin, chisel-shaped edges used for cutting and biting off food. The broad grinding crown belongs to the back teeth.
Correct. Molars have broad, cusped crowns for grinding.
Premolars sit between the canines and molars and have cusps for crushing and grinding. The chisel edge for cutting belongs to the incisors.
Canines are the single pointed teeth beside the incisors, used for tearing and piercing. A flat grinding surface does not fit their shape.

questions.q: The teeth commonly called wisdom teeth are which teeth?
options: Third molars
Canines
Second premolars
First molars
questions.why: Each half of each jaw in the permanent set has three molars. The third molars are the last teeth at the back of the jaw and usually erupt last, in the late teens or early twenties, which is why they are called wisdom teeth. They are often removed when there is not enough room in the jaw.
notes: Correct. Wisdom teeth are the third molars.
The canines are the pointed teeth beside the incisors, near the front of the mouth. Pick them for the teeth used for tearing.
The second premolars sit just in front of the first molars. They are not the last teeth in the jaw.
The first molars are the most forward of the three molars and erupt in childhood. Choose them for the first permanent molars, not the last ones.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue?
options: Both arise outside the tongue and only move it forward
Intrinsic change its shape; extrinsic move its position
Extrinsic change its shape; intrinsic move its position
Both lie within the tongue and only change its shape
questions.why: Intrinsic means within. The intrinsic tongue muscles begin and end inside the tongue and alter its shape and size, which matters for speech and swallowing. The extrinsic muscles arise from structures outside the tongue and insert into it, so they move the whole tongue side to side and in and out.
notes: Only the extrinsic muscles arise outside the tongue, and they move it in several directions, not just forward. The intrinsic muscles lie within it.
Correct. Intrinsic muscles change shape and extrinsic muscles change position.
This swaps the two groups. Muscles that are entirely within the tongue can reshape it, while muscles anchored outside can pull it into new positions.
Only the intrinsic muscles lie entirely within the tongue. The extrinsic muscles reach it from outside and move it as a whole.
questions.answerText: Intrinsic change its shape; extrinsic move its position

questions.q: What are the small projections on the surface of the tongue that carry taste buds and help it grip food?
options: Villi
Rugae
Teniae coli
Papillae
questions.why: The upper surface of the tongue is covered with tiny projections called papillae. They give the tongue its rough texture, which helps it grip and move food during chewing, and many of them carry taste buds.
notes: Villi are finger-like projections of the small intestine lining that increase surface area for absorption. They are in the small intestine, not on the tongue.
Rugae are the folds of the inner lining of the stomach that flatten as the stomach fills. Pick them for the stomach, not the tongue.
The teniae coli are three bands of longitudinal muscle running along the colon. They would be the answer for the large intestine.
Correct. Papillae carry taste buds and help grip food.

questions.q: Which sequence lists the regions of the pharynx from superior to inferior?
options: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx
Nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, oropharynx
Laryngopharynx, oropharynx, nasopharynx
Oropharynx, nasopharynx, laryngopharynx
questions.why: The pharynx is a funnel-shaped tube behind the nasal cavity, mouth, and larynx. Its regions are named for what lies in front of them. The nasopharynx is highest, behind the nasal cavity; the oropharynx is in the middle, behind the mouth; and the laryngopharynx is lowest, behind the larynx, where it leads into the esophagus.
notes: Correct. From top to bottom the regions are the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, behind the larynx. It cannot lie between the nasopharynx and the oropharynx.
This is the correct order read from bottom to top. Pick it if the question asked for inferior to superior.
The oropharynx lies behind the mouth, below the nasopharynx. Putting it first places the mouth above the nasal cavity.

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx carries only air and not food?
options: Oropharynx
Nasopharynx
Esophagus
Laryngopharynx
questions.why: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate. During swallowing, the soft palate and uvula rise to seal it off, so food never passes through it. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx, by contrast, carry both air and swallowed food.
notes: The oropharynx lies behind the mouth and carries both air and food. Pick it for the region that food enters through the fauces.
Correct. The nasopharynx carries only air.
The esophagus is not a region of the pharynx. It carries only food, the opposite of the correct answer.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest region and also carries both air and food before they separate. Choose it for the region that leads into the esophagus.

questions.q: At its lower end, the laryngopharynx opens into which two tubes?
options: Esophagus and larynx
Oral cavity and esophagus
Larynx and nasal cavity
Trachea and nasopharynx
questions.why: The laryngopharynx is where the paths for food and air separate. Behind, it continues downward as the esophagus, which carries food to the stomach. In front, it opens into the larynx, which leads to the trachea and lungs. During swallowing the larynx is covered so food goes into the esophagus.
notes: Correct. The laryngopharynx leads into the esophagus and the larynx.
The oral cavity opens into the oropharynx through the fauces, higher up. Only the esophagus in this pair is correct.
The nasal cavity opens into the nasopharynx at the top of the pharynx. It does not connect to the laryngopharynx.
The trachea lies below the larynx, so the laryngopharynx reaches it only by way of the larynx. The nasopharynx lies above, not below.

questions.q: In the neck and thorax, where does the esophagus lie relative to the trachea?
options: Lateral to the trachea
Anterior to the trachea
Posterior to the trachea
Inside the trachea
questions.why: The esophagus runs down the neck and through the mediastinum directly behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column. The back wall of the trachea has no cartilage, which lets the esophagus bulge forward slightly as a swallowed bite passes. Lower down, the esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm to reach the stomach.
notes: Lateral to the trachea is where the common carotid arteries run on each side. The esophagus is in the midline behind the trachea.
Anterior to the trachea would place the esophagus just under the skin of the front of the neck, where the thyroid gland lies instead.
Correct. The esophagus lies behind the trachea.
The esophagus and trachea are separate tubes. Food and air share a path only in the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, above them.

questions.q: Most of the esophagus, in the neck and thorax, lacks a serosa. What forms its outermost layer instead?
options: Adventitia
Submucosa
Visceral peritoneum
Mucosa
questions.why: Most of the digestive tube is wrapped in a serosa, the visceral peritoneum, because those organs lie in the peritoneal cavity. The esophagus runs through the neck and thorax, outside that cavity, so its outer covering is instead an adventitia, a layer of fibrous connective tissue that blends with the surrounding tissues.
notes: Correct. The esophagus in the neck and thorax has an adventitia instead of a serosa.
The submucosa is the connective tissue layer just outside the mucosa, carrying vessels and the submucosal plexus. It lies deep in the wall, not on the outside.
The visceral peritoneum is the serosa that covers abdominal organs such as the stomach and intestines. Pick it for the outer layer of organs inside the peritoneal cavity.
The mucosa is the innermost layer, the lining in contact with food. It is the opposite end of the wall from the correct answer.

questions.q: Where is the upper esophageal sphincter?
options: Where the esophagus joins the cardia of the stomach
Where the laryngopharynx meets the esophagus
Where the mouth meets the oropharynx
Where the pylorus of the stomach meets the duodenum
questions.why: The esophagus is guarded by a ring of muscle at each end. The upper esophageal sphincter is at the top, where the laryngopharynx joins the esophagus, and it stays closed between swallows so air does not enter the esophagus. The lower esophageal sphincter is at the bottom, where the esophagus joins the stomach.
notes: The junction of the esophagus and stomach is guarded by the lower esophageal sphincter, also called the cardiac sphincter. Pick it for the bottom end of the esophagus.
Correct. The upper esophageal sphincter is where the laryngopharynx meets the esophagus.
The opening from the mouth into the oropharynx is the fauces. It is an opening, not a sphincter of the esophagus.
The junction of the stomach and duodenum is guarded by the pyloric sphincter. Choose it for the outlet of the stomach.
questions.answerText: Where the laryngopharynx meets the esophagus

questions.q: In the permanent set, moving back from the front of the jaw, which type of tooth comes directly after the canine?
options: Incisors
Premolars
Molars
Wisdom teeth
questions.why: In each half of each jaw, the permanent teeth run from front to back as two incisors, one canine, two premolars, and three molars. The premolars therefore sit right behind the canine. Their cusped crowns are the start of the crushing and grinding surface that continues back through the molars.
notes: The incisors are in front of the canine, at the very front of the jaw. Pick them for the chisel-shaped cutting teeth.
Correct. The premolars come directly after the canine.
The molars come after the premolars, at the back of the jaw. They are one step too far back.
The wisdom teeth are the third molars, the last teeth at the very back of the jaw. They are the farthest teeth from the canine, not the next ones.

questions.q: A cavity has worn through a patient's enamel and dentin, and the tooth now aches constantly. Which part of the tooth has the decay most likely reached?
options: Gingiva
Pulp
Enamel
Cementum
questions.why: A tooth has layers from the outside in: enamel over the crown, dentin beneath it, and the pulp cavity at the center. Enamel has no nerves, so decay there is often painless. Once decay passes through the dentin and reaches the pulp, it contacts the nerves and blood vessels there, which causes the constant ache.
notes: The gingiva is the gum tissue around the tooth, outside it entirely. Gum disease affects it, but tooth decay works inward through the hard layers.
Correct. Decay through enamel and dentin reaches the pulp and its nerves.
The enamel is the outermost layer and has already been worn through. It contains no nerves, so it is not the source of the ache.
Cementum covers the root, below the gum. Decay coming down through the crown passes enamel and dentin to the pulp rather than heading for the root surface.

questions.q: Below the gum line, a dentist begins cleaning the outer surface of a tooth's root. Which covering does the instrument touch first?
options: Pulp
Enamel
Dentin
Cementum
questions.why: The root of a tooth is the part held in the bony socket below the gum. Its outer surface is covered by cementum, a calcified, bone-like layer that also gives attachment to the periodontal ligament. Beneath the cementum lies dentin, and at the center is the pulp.
notes: The pulp lies at the center of the tooth, inside the dentin. It is the deepest part, not the outer surface.
Enamel covers the crown above the gum line, not the root. Pick it if the dentist were working on the visible chewing surface.
Dentin is the bulk of the tooth beneath the cementum. The instrument would reach it only after passing through the cementum.
Correct. Cementum covers the outer surface of the root.

questions.q: A newborn cannot push her tongue past her gums, and the fold of tissue tying the underside of her tongue to the floor of the mouth looks unusually short. Which structure is involved?
options: Uvula
Lingual frenulum
Palatine tonsil
Soft palate
questions.why: The lingual frenulum is a midline fold of mucous membrane that anchors the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth. When it is unusually short or attached too far forward, it restricts how far the tongue can move, a condition commonly called tongue-tie. This can interfere with feeding and, later, with speech.
notes: The uvula hangs from the back of the soft palate and helps seal off the nasopharynx during swallowing. It is not attached to the tongue.
Correct. A short lingual frenulum restricts the tongue and causes tongue-tie.
The palatine tonsil is lymphatic tissue on the side wall of the oropharynx, between the palatal arches. It does not tie down the tongue.
The soft palate is the muscular back part of the roof of the mouth. It forms the roof, not a fold beneath the tongue.

questions.q: Imaging shows that the top of a patient's stomach has slid upward through the opening in the diaphragm that normally passes the esophagus. Through which opening did it move?
options: Fauces
Vena caval foramen
Aortic hiatus
Esophageal hiatus
questions.why: The esophagus passes from the thorax into the abdomen through the esophageal hiatus, an opening in the diaphragm. In a hiatal hernia, part of the stomach pushes up through this same opening into the thorax. This can weaken the barrier at the lower esophageal sphincter and is linked with heartburn.
notes: The fauces is the opening from the mouth into the oropharynx, far above the diaphragm. It would be the answer for the back of the mouth.
The vena caval foramen passes the inferior vena cava through the diaphragm on its way to the right atrium. It carries a vein, not the digestive tube.
The aortic hiatus is the opening at the back of the diaphragm that passes the aorta. Pick it for the path of the aorta from the thorax into the abdomen.
Correct. A hiatal hernia occurs through the esophageal hiatus.

questions.q: A patient with a sore throat opens wide, and swollen, red masses of lymphatic tissue are visible on the side walls of the throat between the palatal arches. In which region of the pharynx are they located?
options: Nasopharynx
Oropharynx
Oral cavity proper
Laryngopharynx
questions.why: The palatine tonsils sit in the side walls of the throat between the two palatal arches, just behind the fauces. That places them in the oropharynx, the part of the pharynx directly behind the mouth. Because the oropharynx can be seen through an open mouth, swollen palatine tonsils are easy to spot in tonsillitis.
notes: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate, and holds the pharyngeal tonsil. It cannot be seen just by opening the mouth.
Correct. The palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx.
The oral cavity proper is the space inside the teeth. The tonsils lie behind it, past the fauces, in the throat rather than in the mouth itself.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, behind the larynx. It lies too deep to be seen through an open mouth.

questions.q: A dentist examines a 5-year-old and counts 20 teeth: incisors, canines, and molars, but no premolars. What does this tell the dentist?
options: A complete permanent set
A permanent set without wisdom teeth
A complete deciduous set
Missing premolars from injury
questions.why: The deciduous set has 20 teeth made up of incisors, canines, and molars only, with no premolars. The permanent premolars come in later, replacing the deciduous molars. A count of 20 with this mix of tooth types is exactly what a complete baby set looks like.
notes: A complete permanent set has 32 teeth and includes eight premolars. Twenty teeth with no premolars cannot be a permanent set.
A permanent set without wisdom teeth still has 28 teeth, including premolars. This choice confuses the two sets.
Correct. Twenty teeth with no premolars is a complete deciduous set.
Premolars are not missing here. They are simply not part of the deciduous set, so their absence is normal at this age.

questions.q: A swallowed bolus moves down the esophagus and passes through the esophageal hiatus. At about which vertebral level is this, and how does the outer layer of the esophagus change below it?
options: At the cricoid cartilage; the adventitia gives way to a serosa.
At about T10; the adventitia gives way to a serosa.
At the cricoid cartilage; the serosa gives way to an adventitia.
At about T10; the serosa gives way to an adventitia.
questions.why: The esophagus begins at the level of the cricoid cartilage and runs down through the mediastinum. It reaches the stomach by passing through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus, at about the level of T10. Above the diaphragm, in the neck and thorax, its outer layer is an adventitia. Below the diaphragm the short abdominal segment lies in the abdominal cavity, so it has a serosa.
notes: The cricoid cartilage marks where the esophagus begins, at the lower end of the laryngopharynx, not where it passes through the diaphragm.
Correct. The hiatus is at about T10, and the short segment below the diaphragm has a serosa instead of an adventitia.
The cricoid level is the top of the esophagus, and the outer layer there is already an adventitia. The hiatus is at about T10.
The level is right, but the change runs the other way. The esophagus has an adventitia above the diaphragm and a serosa below it.
questions.answerText: At about T10; the adventitia gives way to a serosa.

questions.q: A child is born with a gap in the bony front part of the roof of the mouth. Which structure is affected, and which space would the mouth then open into?
options: The uvula; the mouth would open into the nasopharynx.
The soft palate; the mouth would open into the nasal cavity.
The hard palate; the mouth would open into the nasal cavity.
The hard palate; the mouth would open into the oropharynx.
questions.why: The roof of the oral cavity is the palate. The hard palate is its bony front part, formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The soft palate behind it is skeletal muscle. Because the palate separates the nasal cavity from the mouth, a gap in the hard palate would leave the mouth open to the nasal cavity above.
notes: The uvula is the soft finger-shaped tab hanging from the back edge of the soft palate. It is not bone and is not part of the front of the roof.
The soft palate is the back of the roof and is skeletal muscle, not bone. The bony front part is the hard palate.
Correct. The hard palate is the bony front of the roof of the mouth, and it separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity above.
The structure is right, but the mouth already opens into the oropharynx through the fauces. The palate separates the mouth from the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: The hard palate; the mouth would open into the nasal cavity.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: The muscularis of the stomach has one more layer of smooth muscle than the rest of the canal. Which layer is the extra one?
options: The outer longitudinal layer
The middle circular layer
The muscularis mucosae
The inner oblique layer
questions.why: Most of the canal has a muscularis of two smooth muscle layers, an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer. The stomach adds a third, an inner oblique layer whose fibers run at an angle, so its muscularis runs oblique, circular, then longitudinal from the inside out. The extra layer lets the stomach churn and mix its contents, not just squeeze them forward.
notes: The outer longitudinal layer runs along the whole canal, so it is not unique to the stomach. It would be the answer if the question asked which muscularis layer of the stomach is outermost.
The stomach does have a circular layer, but so does every other region of the canal, so it is not the extra one. Pick it if the question asked which stomach muscle layer sits between the other two.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin sheet of smooth muscle inside the mucosa, not part of the muscularis, and every region of the canal has one. Choose it if the question asked which part of the mucosa is made of smooth muscle.
Correct. The inner oblique layer is found in the stomach and nowhere else in the canal.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which list names the four regions of the stomach?
options: Fundus, body, pyloric part, and duodenum
Cardia, body, lesser curvature, and pyloric part
Cardia, fundus, rugae, and pyloric part
Cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part
questions.why: The stomach is divided into four regions. The cardia surrounds the opening from the esophagus, the fundus bulges above and to the left of the cardia, the body is the large central portion, and the pyloric part connects the body to the duodenum. Named features such as the rugae and the curvatures are found on these regions but are not regions themselves.
notes: The duodenum is the first region of the small intestine, just past the pyloric sphincter, so it is not part of the stomach, and this list leaves out the cardia. It would fit a question about where food goes after leaving the stomach.

The lesser curvature is the short, concave medial border of the stomach, an edge rather than a region, and this list also leaves out the fundus. The lesser curvature would be the answer if the question asked where the lesser omentum attaches to the stomach.

Rugae are the folds of the inner stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills, a feature of the lining rather than a region. Pick rugae if the question asked what lets the stomach lining expand with a meal.
Correct. The cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part are the four regions of the stomach.
questions.answerText: Cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: The pyloric part of the stomach has three subdivisions. In what order does food meet them as it moves toward the duodenum?
options: Pyloric antrum, pyloric canal, pylorus
Pylorus, pyloric canal, pyloric antrum
Pyloric canal, pyloric antrum, pylorus
Pyloric antrum, pylorus, pyloric canal
questions.why: The pyloric part funnels food from the body of the stomach toward the small intestine. It begins with the wider pyloric antrum next to the body, narrows into the pyloric canal, and ends at the pylorus. The pylorus is guarded by the pyloric sphincter, which opens into the duodenum.
notes: Correct. Food passes the pyloric antrum, then the pyloric canal, then the pylorus at the junction with the duodenum.
This is the correct order run backward, from the duodenum toward the body of the stomach. It would be right only if the question asked for the order moving away from the duodenum.
This puts the narrow canal before the wide antrum. The antrum is the broad first part next to the body, and it narrows into the canal, not the other way around.
This places the pylorus in the middle, but the pylorus is the final part of the stomach, where the pyloric sphincter meets the duodenum. The canal must come before it.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which region of the small intestine begins at the pyloric sphincter and is mostly retroperitoneal?
options: The jejunum
The stomach
The duodenum
The ileum
questions.why: The small intestine runs duodenum, jejunum, then ileum. The duodenum is the first and shortest region, about 25 cm (10 inches), and it curves in a C shape from the pyloric sphincter around the head of the pancreas. It lies mostly behind the peritoneum, pressed against the posterior abdominal wall, which is what retroperitoneal means. The jejunum and ileum, by contrast, hang within the peritoneal cavity on the mesentery.
notes: The jejunum is the middle region, about 1 m (3 feet) long, and it hangs from the posterior wall on the mesentery inside the peritoneal cavity. Pick it if the question asked for the middle region of the small intestine.
The stomach sits just before the pyloric sphincter and lies within the peritoneal cavity, held by the omenta. Choose it if the question asked which organ the greater omentum hangs from.
Correct. The duodenum starts at the pyloric sphincter and lies mostly behind the peritoneum.

The ileum is the last and longest region, about 2 m (6 feet), and it ends at the ileocecal sphincter, not the pyloric sphincter. It would be the answer if the question asked which region joins the large intestine.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which three surface features are found on the large intestine and on no other part of the canal?
options: Teniae coli, rugae, and circular folds
Teniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices
Rugae, haustra, and teniae coli
Circular folds, villi, and microvilli
questions.why: Three features identify the large intestine. The teniae coli are three flat bands of longitudinal smooth muscle running along the colon. They are shorter than the wall, so the wall bunches up between them into pouches called haustra. Small fat-filled pouches of visceral peritoneum, the omental appendices, hang from the surface of the colon, mostly along the teniae coli.
notes: Only the teniae coli belong to the large intestine here. Rugae are stomach folds and circular folds are permanent ridges of the small intestine wall.
Correct. The teniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices are found only on the large intestine.
Haustra and teniae coli belong to the colon, but rugae are folds of the stomach lining that flatten as it fills. Pick rugae for a question about the stomach.

Circular folds, villi, and microvilli are the three nested surface features of the small intestine that increase its surface area for absorption. Choose this set if the question asked about the small intestine.
questions.answerText: Teniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What are gastric pits?
options: Folds of the stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills
Openings in the stomach lining that lead down to the gastric glands
Finger-like projections of the small intestine mucosa
Pouches of the colon wall formed by the teniae coli
questions.why: The stomach lining is dotted with tiny pits called gastric pits. Each pit leads down into gastric glands, which are the secreting glands of the stomach, so the secretions made in the glands empty into the bottom of the pits and rise to the surface. The pits are microscopic and are seen on slides, unlike the large rugae seen on a model.
notes: Folds of the stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills are the rugae. Pick rugae if the question asked how the stomach expands to hold a meal.
Correct. Gastric pits are openings in the stomach lining that lead to the gastric glands.
Finger-like projections of the small intestine mucosa are the villi. Choose villi for a question about absorptive surface area in the small intestine.
Pouches of the colon wall formed by the teniae coli are the haustra. They would be the answer for a question about the puckered look of the large intestine.
questions.answerText: Openings in the stomach lining that lead down to the gastric glands

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which region of the stomach surrounds the opening where the esophagus enters?
options: The cardia
The pyloric part
The fundus
The body
questions.why: The cardia is the small region of the stomach that surrounds the opening from the esophagus. Its name comes from its position near the heart, just below the diaphragm. The lower esophageal sphincter, also called the cardiac sphincter, guards this opening.
notes: Correct. The cardia surrounds the opening where the esophagus enters the stomach.
The pyloric part is the region that connects the body to the duodenum at the exit end of the stomach. Choose it if the question asked which region leads to the small intestine.
The fundus is the rounded portion that bulges above and to the left of the cardia. Pick it if the question asked for the dome-shaped top of the stomach.
The body is the large central portion of the stomach. It would be the answer if the question asked for the biggest region of the stomach.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What is the first and shortest region of the small intestine?
options: The duodenum
The jejunum
The cecum
The ileum
questions.why: The duodenum is the first and shortest region of the small intestine, about 25 cm (10 inches) long, and it curves from the pyloric sphincter of the stomach. Bile and pancreatic juice enter the small intestine here at the major duodenal papilla. After it come the jejunum, about 1 m (3 feet) long, and the ileum, the longest region at about 2 m (6 feet).
notes: Correct. The duodenum is the first and shortest region, about 25 cm (10 inches) long.
The jejunum is the middle region of the small intestine, about 1 m (3 feet) long. Pick it if the question asked for the region between the duodenum and the ileum.
The cecum is the pouch at the start of the large intestine, on the far side of the ileocecal valve. Choose it if the question asked where the large intestine begins.

The ileum is the last and longest region, about 2 m (6 feet), ending at the ileocecal sphincter. It would be the answer if the question asked for the longest region or the one that joins the large intestine.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What are the finger-like projections of the small intestine mucosa called?
options: Teniae coli
Villi
Rugae
Haustra
questions.why: Villi are finger-like projections of the mucosa that give the small intestine lining a velvety look. They greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients. Each villus holds a lacteal, a lymphatic capillary that absorbs dietary fats, and its surface cells carry even smaller microvilli.
notes: Teniae coli are three bands of longitudinal muscle running along the colon, part of the muscle layer rather than the mucosa. Choose them if the question asked what forms the haustra.
Correct. Villi are the finger-like projections of the small intestine mucosa.
Rugae are folds of the inner stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills. Pick rugae if the question asked about the stomach lining rather than the small intestine.
Haustra are the pouches that give the colon its puckered look. They would be the answer for a question about the wall of the large intestine.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What are the folds of the inner stomach lining that flatten out as the stomach fills?
options: Villi
Haustra
Plicae circulares
Rugae
questions.why: Rugae are folds of the inner stomach lining. When the stomach is empty they lie in ridges, and as a meal arrives they flatten out so the stomach can stretch and hold more. This fits the stomach's role as a holding reservoir and mixing chamber.
notes: Villi are finger-like projections of the small intestine mucosa that increase surface area for absorption. Pick villi for a question about the absorptive lining of the small intestine.
Haustra are the pouches of the colon formed by the teniae coli. Choose them for a question about the puckered look of the large intestine.

Plicae circulares, or circular folds, are permanent ridges of the mucosa and submucosa in the small intestine, and they do not flatten out. They would be the answer for the largest folds of the small intestine wall.
Correct. Rugae are the stomach folds that flatten as the stomach fills.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What is the ring of smooth muscle that controls the exit from the stomach into the duodenum?
options: The upper esophageal sphincter
The lower esophageal sphincter
The pyloric sphincter
The ileocecal sphincter
questions.why: The pyloric sphincter is the ring of smooth muscle between the pylorus and the duodenum. It controls the exit from the stomach, letting the liquefied stomach contents into the small intestine a little at a time. Each sphincter in the canal is named for where it sits, so the pyloric sphincter belongs at the pylorus.
notes: The upper esophageal sphincter guards the top of the esophagus, where it meets the laryngopharynx. Choose it if the question asked which sphincter a bolus passes first after the pharynx.
The lower esophageal sphincter guards the entrance to the stomach from the esophagus, not the exit. Pick it if the question asked which sphincter keeps stomach contents out of the esophagus.
Correct. The pyloric sphincter controls the passage from the stomach into the duodenum.
The ileocecal sphincter sits where the ileum meets the large intestine, far downstream. It would be the answer if the question asked where the small intestine ends.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What is the pouch where the large intestine begins, just below the ileocecal valve?
options: The ascending colon
The rectum
The cecum
The ileum
questions.why: The cecum is the blind pouch at the start of the large intestine, just below the ileocecal valve where the ileum enters. The vermiform appendix hangs from it. From the cecum, material moves up into the ascending colon.
notes: The ascending colon is the first part of the colon, which rises from the cecum up the right side of the abdomen. It would be the answer if the question asked where material goes right after the cecum.
The rectum is the straight segment near the end of the large intestine, anterior to the sacrum and coccyx. Choose it if the question asked where feces are stored before elimination.
Correct. The cecum is the pouch at the start of the large intestine.
The ileum is the last region of the small intestine, which empties into the large intestine at the ileocecal valve. Pick it if the question asked which region lies just before the valve.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What are the three bands of longitudinal muscle that run the length of the colon called?
options: Teniae coli
Rugae
Haustra
Omental appendices
questions.why: In the cecum and colon, the outer longitudinal layer of the muscularis is gathered into three flat bands called the teniae coli instead of forming a complete sheet. The bands are shorter than the wall, so the wall bunches up between them into pouches called haustra. The teniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices together mark the large intestine.
notes: Correct. The teniae coli are the three bands of longitudinal muscle along the colon.
Rugae are folds of the inner stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills. Choose rugae for a question about the stomach.
Haustra are the pouches of the colon wall, formed by the pull of the teniae coli. Pick haustra if the question asked about the puckered pouches rather than the muscle bands.

Omental appendices are small fat-filled pouches of peritoneum that hang from the surface of the colon, mostly along the teniae coli. They are fat, not muscle, so they would be the answer for the fatty tags on the colon surface.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: What are the microscopic projections of the absorptive cells that form the brush border called?
options: Rugae
Plicae circulares
Villi
Microvilli
questions.why: Microvilli are microscopic projections of the plasma membrane on each absorptive cell of the small intestine. Packed together, they look like the bristles of a brush under the microscope, which is why they are called the brush border. They are the smallest of the three surface features, after the circular folds and villi, that expand the absorptive surface.
notes: Rugae are folds of the stomach lining that flatten as the stomach fills. Choose rugae for a question about the stomach.

Plicae circulares are permanent circular ridges of the mucosa and submucosa, the largest of the small intestine's folds. They would be the answer if the question asked for the biggest surface feature of the small intestine wall.
Villi are finger-like projections of the whole mucosa, each made of many cells. Pick villi if the question asked about the projections that give the lining its velvety look.
Correct. Microvilli are the tiny projections on each absorptive cell that form the brush border.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Food leaving the stomach passes through the pyloric sphincter. Which region does it enter next?
options: The cecum
The jejunum
The duodenum
The esophagus
questions.why: The pyloric sphincter sits between the pylorus of the stomach and the duodenum. Food that passes it enters the duodenum, the first region of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice are added. From there it continues into the jejunum and then the ileum.
notes: The cecum is the pouch at the start of the large intestine, reached only after the whole small intestine. Choose it if the question asked where food goes after passing the ileocecal valve.
The jejunum is the middle region of the small intestine, reached only after the duodenum. Pick it if the question asked where food goes after the duodenum.
Correct. Food passing the pyloric sphincter enters the duodenum.
The esophagus comes before the stomach and delivers food to it through the lower esophageal sphincter. It would be the answer if the question asked which region food leaves to enter the stomach.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: The duodenum, jejunum, and ileum are the three regions of which organ?
options: The pharynx
The large intestine
The small intestine
The stomach
questions.why: The small intestine is the long, coiled region of the canal where most absorption happens, and it has three regions. The duodenum comes first, curving from the pyloric sphincter, the jejunum is the middle region, and the ileum is the last and longest, joining the large intestine at the ileocecal sphincter.
notes: The pharynx also has three regions, but they are the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx. Choose it if the question listed those throat regions.
The large intestine is made of the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal. Pick it if the question listed those regions instead.
Correct. The duodenum, jejunum, and ileum make up the small intestine.
The stomach is divided into the cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part. It would be the answer if the question listed those four regions.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: The ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid segments are the four parts of which structure?
options: The stomach
The colon
The rectum
The small intestine
questions.why: The colon is the long main portion of the large intestine, and it has four parts named for their direction or shape. The ascending colon rises on the right, the transverse colon crosses the abdomen, the descending colon drops on the left, and the S-shaped sigmoid colon leads into the rectum. The large intestine as a whole also includes the cecum, rectum, and anal canal, which are not parts of the colon.
notes: The stomach also has four regions, but they are the cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part. It would be the answer if the question listed those.
Correct. The ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid segments make up the colon.

The rectum is a single straight segment that follows the sigmoid colon, not one of the four parts of the colon. Choose it if the question asked for the straight portion anterior to the sacrum and coccyx.
The small intestine is divided into the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Pick it if the question listed those three regions.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: The ileum joins the large intestine at which structure?
options: The internal anal sphincter
The pyloric sphincter
The lower esophageal sphincter
The ileocecal valve
questions.why: The ileum is the last and longest region of the small intestine. It ends at the ileocecal sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle where it opens into the cecum of the large intestine. Together with folds of mucosa, this sphincter forms the ileocecal valve, which keeps the contents of the large intestine from moving back into the ileum.
notes: The internal anal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle around the anal canal, at the very end of the tract, far from the ileum. Choose it if the question asked which smooth muscle sphincter surrounds the anal canal.
The pyloric sphincter is at the exit of the stomach into the duodenum, at the start of the small intestine. Pick it if the question asked where the small intestine begins.
The lower esophageal sphincter guards the entrance of the stomach from the esophagus. It would be the answer if the question asked which sphincter weakens in GERD.
Correct. The ileum joins the cecum at the ileocecal valve.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which region of the stomach is the rounded portion that bulges above and to the left of the cardia?
options: The cardia
The body
The pyloric part
The fundus
questions.why: The fundus is the rounded, dome-shaped portion of the stomach that bulges above and to the left of the cardia, just under the diaphragm. Because it sits higher than the opening from the esophagus, it often holds swallowed air. The four regions in order are the cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part.
notes: The cardia is the region that surrounds the opening from the esophagus, just below and to the right of the fundus. Choose it if the question asked where food enters the stomach.
The body is the large central portion of the stomach, below the fundus. Pick it if the question asked for the biggest region of the stomach.
The pyloric part is the region that connects the body to the duodenum, at the opposite end from the fundus. It would be the answer if the question asked which region leads to the small intestine.
Correct. The fundus is the rounded portion above and to the left of the cardia.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: Which disorder of the canal is stomach contents flowing back up through a weak lower esophageal sphincter and irritating the esophagus?
options: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Hiatal hernia
Peptic ulcer
Diverticulosis
questions.why: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, happens when the lower esophageal sphincter is weak and lets acidic stomach contents flow back up into the esophagus. The esophagus has no protection against stomach acid, so it becomes irritated, and the person feels heartburn behind the breastbone. The name itself traces the path: gastro (stomach) to esophageal (esophagus), with reflux meaning backflow.
notes: Correct. GERD is backflow of stomach contents through a weak lower esophageal sphincter.

A hiatal hernia is part of the stomach pushing up through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm. It can occur alongside reflux, but it is a hernia, not the backflow itself. It would be the answer for a question about the stomach moving through the diaphragm.
A peptic ulcer is an eroded sore in the wall of the stomach or duodenum, not a backflow problem. Pick it if the question described a sore eating into the lining.
Diverticulosis is small pouches bulging outward through weak spots in the colon wall. Choose it for a question about the large intestine wall.

questions.topic: Stomach, small intestine and large intestine
questions.q: A patient has pain in the lower right abdomen from inflammation of the narrow, worm-like tube attached to the cecum. Which disorder is this?
options: Colorectal cancer
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Peptic ulcer
