If it is blocked, the gallbladder is cut off, but the main route from the hepatic ducts to the common hepatic duct, common bile duct, and duodenum stays open. Trapped bile in the gallbladder is what often leads to cholecystitis.
notes: The pancreatic duct does not pass through the cystic duct, so pancreatic juice still drains. This would be the answer if the stone were at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, where the two systems share a passage.

Bile leaves the liver through the hepatic ducts, which are above the blockage and still open. This would happen only if the stone blocked the common hepatic duct, the single duct that carries all bile out of the liver.
The cystic duct and the pancreatic duct do not connect, so bile has no path into the pancreatic duct from here. Students pick this when they picture all the ducts as one connected tube.
Correct. The gallbladder is cut off, but the main bile route stays open.
questions.answerText: Bile is cut off from the gallbladder but still reaches the duodenum

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: At which raised opening in the duodenal lining do bile and pancreatic juice enter the small intestine?
options: The pyloric sphincter
The ileocecal valve
The renal papilla
The major duodenal papilla
questions.why: A papilla is a small nipple-shaped bump. The major duodenal papilla is the raised opening on the inner wall of the duodenum where the hepatopancreatic ampulla empties bile and pancreatic juice, with the sphincter of Oddi controlling the flow. It is the last stop on the path of bile.
notes: The pyloric sphincter is the ring of smooth muscle between the stomach and the duodenum. Pick it for what controls stomach emptying.
The ileocecal valve is where the ileum empties into the cecum, at the end of the small intestine. It would be the answer for the junction of the small and large intestines.
A renal papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid in the kidney, where urine drips into a minor calyx. Pick it for a kidney question; it shares only the word papilla.
Correct. Bile and pancreatic juice enter at the major duodenal papilla.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the acini and the pancreatic islets?
options: Both send their products through the pancreatic duct to the duodenum
Acini send pancreatic juice through ducts to the duodenum, and islets release hormones into the blood
Acini release bile into the duodenum, and islets store it between meals
Islets send pancreatic juice through ducts to the duodenum, and acini release hormones into the blood
questions.why: The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. The acini are the exocrine part, sending pancreatic juice through ducts that empty into the duodenum. The islets are the endocrine part, with no ducts, so their hormones pass directly into the blood.
notes: Only the acini use the duct system. Endocrine tissue such as the islets has no ducts, which is the defining difference between endocrine and exocrine glands.
Correct. Acini are exocrine and islets are endocrine.
Neither part of the pancreas handles bile. Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, so pick those organs for bile production and storage.
This swaps the two jobs. Acini are the exocrine clusters that use ducts, and the islets are the endocrine clusters that release into the blood.
questions.answerText: Acini send pancreatic juice through ducts to the duodenum, and islets release hormones into the blood

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which region of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve of the duodenum?
options: The head
The fundus
The tail
The body
questions.why: The pancreas has a head, body, and tail. The head is the widest part, and it sits nestled in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum on the right. The body crosses behind the stomach, and the tail tapers toward the spleen on the left.
notes: Correct. The head of the pancreas sits in the curve of the duodenum.
The fundus is a region of the gallbladder and of the stomach, not the pancreas. Students pick it by mixing up the regions of the three organs that share the word body.
The tail is the tapered left end of the pancreas, reaching toward the spleen. It would be the answer for the region nearest the spleen.
The body is the central part of the pancreas, crossing behind the stomach. Pick it for the middle region between the head and tail.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which wide, leaky capillaries run between the plates of hepatocytes?
options: The pulmonary capillaries
The hepatic sinusoids
The bile canaliculi
The lacteals
questions.why: Sinusoids are a special type of capillary with wide, winding channels and large gaps in their walls. In the liver, the hepatic sinusoids run between the plates of hepatocytes and carry blood from the portal triads toward the central vein. Their leakiness lets hepatocytes exchange materials easily with the blood flowing past.
notes: Pulmonary capillaries wrap around the alveoli in the lungs for gas exchange. Pick them for the capillaries of the respiratory membrane.
Correct. The hepatic sinusoids run between the hepatocyte plates.
The bile canaliculi are tiny channels between hepatocytes that collect bile, not blood. Pick them for the first channels on the path of bile.
Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries inside the villi of the small intestine that absorb fats. They would be the answer for a question about fat absorption in the intestine.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: The ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver, is a remnant of which fetal vessel?
options: The umbilical vein
An umbilical artery
The ductus arteriosus
The ductus venosus
questions.why: Before birth, the umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus, running up to the liver. After birth it closes and becomes a fibrous cord, the ligamentum teres, which runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament. Each fetal shunt and vessel leaves a named remnant, so it helps to learn them as pairs.
notes: Correct. The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein.
The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. They would be the answer for those paired cords.
The ductus arteriosus connected the pulmonary trunk to the aorta and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Pick it for the remnant between the pulmonary trunk and aorta.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Students confuse it with the teres because both remnants are on the liver.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A gallstone lodges at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, and the patient develops pancreatitis as well as blocked bile. Why can one stone affect the pancreas?
options: The bile duct and main pancreatic duct share that passage, so pancreatic juice is trapped too
The pancreas and gallbladder are one organ joined by the cystic duct
The stone blocks the pyloric sphincter, so stomach contents back up into the pancreas
Gallstones form inside the pancreas and travel down to the ampulla
questions.why: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct meet at the hepatopancreatic ampulla before emptying into the duodenum. A stone stuck there blocks the shared passage, so pancreatic juice cannot drain and backs up in the pancreas, which can inflame it. This shared anatomy is one of the main ways gallstones trigger pancreatitis.
notes: Correct. The shared ampulla means one stone blocks both bile and pancreatic juice.
The pancreas and gallbladder are separate organs, and the cystic duct connects only the gallbladder. This mixes up the bile and pancreatic duct systems, which meet only at the ampulla.
The pyloric sphincter is between the stomach and duodenum, upstream of the ampulla, and the stomach does not drain into the pancreas. Pick the pyloric sphincter for a question about stomach emptying.

Gallstones form in the gallbladder, not the pancreas. Students pick this because the stone ends up near the pancreas, but it traveled there from the gallbladder through the cystic and common bile ducts.
questions.answerText: The bile duct and main pancreatic duct share that passage, so pancreatic juice is trapped too

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares hepatitis and cirrhosis?
options: Hepatitis affects the gallbladder, and cirrhosis affects the liver
Cirrhosis is inflammation of the liver, and hepatitis is replacement of liver tissue by scar tissue
Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, and cirrhosis is replacement of liver tissue by scar tissue
Both are names for yellowing of the skin from a buildup of bilirubin
questions.why: Both disorders affect the liver, but they describe different processes. Hepatitis (hepat for liver, itis for inflammation) is inflammation, commonly from a viral infection. Cirrhosis is what can follow long-term damage, when healthy liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue and liver function is lost.
notes: Both disorders affect the liver. Inflammation of the gallbladder is cholecystitis, so pick that name for an inflamed gallbladder.
This swaps the two definitions. The itis ending in hepatitis is the clue that it is the inflammation, while cirrhosis is the scarring.
Correct. Hepatitis is inflammation and cirrhosis is scarring.
Yellowing of the skin and eyes from bilirubin buildup is jaundice, a sign that liver disease can cause. Pick jaundice for the yellow color, not for either of these disorders.
questions.answerText: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, and cirrhosis is replacement of liver tissue by scar tissue

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Gallstones are hardened deposits that can block the bile ducts. In which organ do they usually form?
options: The pancreas
The gallbladder
The kidney
The urinary bladder
questions.why: Gallstones form in the gallbladder, where bile is stored and concentrated. As the gallbladder removes water from bile, some bile components can harden into stones. A stone that slips out can lodge in the cystic duct, the common bile duct, or the ampulla and block the flow of bile.
notes: The pancreas does not store bile and is not where gallstones form, though a gallstone at the ampulla can cause pancreatitis. Pick the pancreas for the organ inflamed in pancreatitis.
Correct. Gallstones form in the gallbladder.
The kidney is where kidney stones form, from substances in urine. Pick it for a stone that blocks a ureter, not a bile duct.
The urinary bladder stores urine, and stones there come from urine, not bile. Students pick it because of the shared word bladder.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A child with mumps has swelling of the glands the virus infects. Where would that swelling show?
options: In the right upper quadrant of the abdomen
At the back of the throat beside the uvula
Under the tongue in the floor of the mouth
In front of and below the ears
questions.why: Mumps is a viral infection that inflames and enlarges the parotid glands. The parotids sit anterior and inferior to each ear, over the masseter muscle and the angle of the jaw. When they swell, the face looks puffy in front of and below the ears, which is the classic look of mumps.
notes: The right upper quadrant holds the liver and gallbladder. Pick it for pain or swelling from hepatitis or cholecystitis.
The back of the throat near the uvula is where the palatine tonsils sit. Swelling there would suggest tonsillitis, not mumps.
Under the tongue is where the sublingual glands lie. Swelling there would point to the sublingual or submandibular glands, not the classic site of mumps.
Correct. The parotid glands are in front of and below the ears.
questions.answerText: In front of and below the ears

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder, is most often caused by what?
options: A gallstone blocking the cystic duct
Scarring of the liver tissue
A viral infection of the liver
A buildup of bilirubin in the skin
questions.why: The gallbladder drains only through the cystic duct. When a gallstone blocks that duct, bile is trapped inside the gallbladder, and the trapped bile irritates and inflames its wall. That is why cholecystitis and gallstones so often appear together, with pain in the right upper quadrant.
notes: Correct. A gallstone blocking the cystic duct is the usual cause.
Scarring of liver tissue is cirrhosis, the result of long-term liver damage. It would be the answer for a scarred liver with lost function.
A viral infection of the liver causes hepatitis. Pick it for the most common cause of liver inflammation.
A buildup of bilirubin causes jaundice, the yellowing of the skin and eyes. Jaundice can follow a blocked bile duct, but it is a sign, not the cause of gallbladder inflammation.
questions.answerText: A gallstone blocking the cystic duct

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A patient develops yellowing of the skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin. What is this condition called?
options: Mumps
Cirrhosis
Pancreatitis
Jaundice
questions.why: Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by a buildup of bilirubin, a yellow pigment that is normally cleared by the liver into bile. It often signals liver disease or a blocked bile duct, such as from a gallstone. It is a sign that points to a problem rather than a disease of one organ.
notes: Mumps is a viral infection that swells the parotid glands. It would be the answer for swelling in front of the ears.
Cirrhosis is scarring of the liver that can lead to jaundice, but it is the underlying damage, not the yellow color itself. Pick it for liver tissue replaced by scar tissue.
Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas. Pick it for an inflamed pancreas, for example after a gallstone blocks the ampulla.
Correct. Yellowing from bilirubin buildup is jaundice.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Fat arrives in the duodenum mainly with meals. Why is it useful that the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals?
options: Stored bile is released into the blood to reach the small intestine
The gallbladder adds fat-digesting enzymes to bile while it is stored
A concentrated supply of bile can be released when fatty food arrives
Storing bile lets the gallbladder make more bile between meals
questions.why: The liver makes bile all the time, but bile is needed mainly when a fatty meal reaches the duodenum. Storing bile in the gallbladder and concentrating it by removing water builds up a strong supply between meals. When fat arrives, the gallbladder contracts and sends that concentrated bile down the cystic and common bile ducts right when it is needed.
notes: Bile travels through ducts, not the blood, from the gallbladder to the duodenum. Students choose this when they confuse exocrine secretion through ducts with endocrine release into the blood.
Bile contains no digestive enzymes, and the gallbladder adds none. The fat-digesting enzymes come from the pancreas, so pick the pancreas for the source of enzymes.
Correct. Storage lets a concentrated supply be released with a fatty meal.
The gallbladder makes no bile; it only stores and concentrates what the liver produces. Pick the liver for the organ that makes bile.
questions.answerText: A concentrated supply of bile can be released when fatty food arrives

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: The main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct join at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. What does this mean for where their secretions arrive?
options: Bile and pancreatic juice enter the jejunum rather than the duodenum
Bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum together at the major duodenal papilla
Pancreatic juice flows up the cystic duct to be stored in the gallbladder
Bile enters the stomach while pancreatic juice enters the duodenum
questions.why: Because the two ducts merge at the ampulla, bile and pancreatic juice exit through the same opening, the major duodenal papilla on the wall of the duodenum. The sphincter of Oddi controls that shared exit. Both secretions are therefore delivered together to the first part of the small intestine, right where food leaves the stomach.
notes: The jejunum is the middle part of the small intestine, beyond the duodenum. Pick it for the segment between the duodenum and the ileum, not for where these ducts open.
Correct. Both secretions enter the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
The cystic duct carries only bile to and from the gallbladder, and pancreatic juice is never stored. Pick the cystic duct for bile storage.
No bile duct opens into the stomach; both secretions enter the duodenum. Students pick this when they assume bile must work in the stomach because the stomach comes first.
questions.answerText: Bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum together at the major duodenal papilla

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement describes what saliva does in the mouth?
options: It absorbs nutrients from food directly into the blood
It moistens and lubricates food and begins its breakdown
It neutralizes the stomach acid that enters the duodenum
It breaks fat into small droplets so enzymes can reach it
questions.why: Saliva is the watery secretion of the salivary glands. It keeps the mouth moist and clean, lubricates food so it can be chewed into a soft mass and swallowed, and begins chemical digestion with salivary amylase acting on starch. Dissolving food in saliva also lets the taste buds detect it.
notes: Absorbing nutrients into the blood happens mainly in the small intestine, through its villi. Pick the small intestine for absorption.
Correct. Saliva moistens, cleanses, and lubricates food and begins its breakdown.
Neutralizing stomach acid in the duodenum is the job of the bicarbonate in pancreatic juice. That would be the answer for the pancreas, not saliva.
Breaking fat into small droplets is the job of bile from the liver. Pick bile for emulsifying fat in the duodenum.
questions.answerText: It moistens and lubricates food and begins its breakdown

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which list names the three large pairs of salivary glands?
options: Buccal, submandibular, and sublingual
Lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual
Parotid, submandibular, and lingual
Parotid, submandibular, and sublingual
questions.why: Three large pairs of glands make most of the saliva. The parotid glands lie in front of and below the ears, the submandibular glands lie along the inner side of the mandible, and the sublingual glands lie beneath the tongue. Many small minor salivary glands scattered through the lining of the mouth add a little more.
notes: Buccal glands are minor salivary glands in the lining of the cheeks. They are real salivary glands but small ones, and they would fit a question asking for examples of minor salivary glands.
The lacrimal glands make tears and sit above the lateral corner of each eye, so they are not salivary glands. Students pick them because they are another paired gland of the head.
The lingual glands are small glands within the tongue that secrete mucus and watery fluid. They are minor glands, so they would be the answer only for a question about glands in the tongue itself.
Correct. The parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands are the three large pairs.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: The parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear. Where does its duct open into the mouth?
options: Beside the second upper molar
Near the lingual frenulum
On the inside of the lower lip
Onto the floor of the mouth
questions.why: The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland and sits between the skin and the masseter muscle, in front of and below the ear. Its duct crosses the cheek and pierces the buccinator to open into the mouth beside the second upper molar. You can feel the small bump of this opening with your tongue on the inside of your cheek.
notes: Correct. The parotid duct opens beside the second upper molar.
Ducts opening near the lingual frenulum belong to the submandibular glands. Pick this location for a question about where the submandibular ducts open.
The inside of the lip holds small labial glands, which are minor salivary glands with their own tiny openings. No large salivary gland drains there, so students pick this only by guessing.
Ducts opening onto the floor of the mouth belong to the sublingual glands, which lie beneath the tongue. That would be the answer for the sublingual glands.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which salivary gland lies along the inner side of the mandible, with ducts that open near the lingual frenulum?
options: Minor lingual glands
Sublingual gland
Parotid gland
Submandibular gland
questions.why: The submandibular glands lie in the floor of the mouth along the inner side of the body of the mandible, as their name (below the mandible) suggests. Their ducts run forward and open near the lingual frenulum, the fold under the tongue. They produce a large share of the saliva in the resting mouth.
notes: Lingual glands are small minor glands within the tongue that secrete mucus and watery fluid. They are the answer for glands inside the tongue itself, not a large gland beside the mandible.
The sublingual glands lie just beneath the tongue, above the submandibular glands, and their ducts open onto the floor of the mouth. Choose them for the smallest of the three large pairs.

The parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear, over the masseter muscle, and its duct opens beside the second upper molar. It is the answer for the largest salivary gland and the one swollen in mumps.
Correct. The submandibular glands lie along the inner mandible and open near the lingual frenulum.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement describes what saliva does?
options: Carries most of the digestive enzymes into the duodenum
Moistens the mouth and starts breaking down food
Breaks fat into tiny droplets so it can be digested
Absorbs water from waste and helps form the feces
questions.why: Saliva is the watery secretion of the salivary glands. It keeps the mouth moist and clean, lubricates food so it can be shaped into a ball and swallowed, and begins the chemical breakdown of food while it is still being chewed. The three large pairs of salivary glands make most of it.
notes: Pancreatic juice from the acini of the pancreas carries most of the digestive enzymes into the duodenum. That is the answer for a question about the exocrine pancreas.
Correct. Saliva moistens, cleanses and lubricates, and it starts the breakdown of food.
Breaking fat into tiny droplets is the job of bile, which the liver makes and the gallbladder stores. Pick it for a question about what bile does in the duodenum.
Absorbing water and forming feces is the job of the large intestine, not a secretion at all. Choose it for a question about the colon.
questions.answerText: Moistens the mouth and starts breaking down food

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A child with mumps has painful swelling in front of and just below the ear, over the angle of the jaw. Which salivary gland is inflamed?
options: Sublingual gland
Submandibular gland
Parotid gland
Palatine tonsil
questions.why: Mumps is a viral infection that inflames and enlarges the parotid glands. The parotid gland lies anterior and inferior to the ear, between the skin and the masseter muscle, so when it swells the cheek in front of the ear puffs out. The location of the swelling points straight to this gland.
notes: The sublingual gland lies under the tongue in the floor of the mouth. Swelling of this gland would show inside the mouth beneath the tongue, not on the side of the face.

The submandibular gland lies along the inner side of the mandible, under the jaw rather than in front of the ear. Swelling there would show beneath the jawline, which is where you would point for this gland.
Correct. The parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear and is the gland swollen in mumps.

The palatine tonsils are lymphatic tissue at the back of the mouth between the palatal arches, not salivary glands. They would be the answer for swelling seen at the back of the throat in tonsillitis.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: What does the liver produce, and where does it sit?
options: Bile; upper left abdomen, behind the stomach
Gastric juice; upper left abdomen, below the diaphragm
Bile; upper right abdomen, below the diaphragm
Pancreatic juice; upper right abdomen, under the ribs
questions.why: The liver is the largest gland in the body. It sits just below the diaphragm, mostly in the upper right abdomen under the lower ribs, with its left lobe reaching across the midline. Its digestive product is bile, which drains through the bile ducts to the duodenum.
notes: Bile is right, but the upper left abdomen behind the stomach is where the pancreas body and tail lie, not the liver. Students choose this when they place the liver on the wrong side.
Gastric juice comes from the gastric glands of the stomach, which sits in the upper left abdomen below the diaphragm. This pairing describes the stomach, not the liver.
Correct. The liver makes bile and lies mostly in the upper right abdomen below the diaphragm.
Pancreatic juice is made by the acini of the pancreas, which lies behind the stomach. Pick pancreatic juice for a question about the exocrine pancreas.
questions.answerText: Bile; upper right abdomen, below the diaphragm

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: On the anterior surface, which fold of peritoneum separates the right and left lobes of the liver?
options: Falciform ligament
Lesser omentum
Greater omentum
Transverse mesocolon
questions.why: The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that suspends the liver from the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. On the front of the liver it marks the boundary between the large right lobe and the smaller left lobe. A fibrous cord in its free edge, the ligamentum teres, is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.
notes: Correct. The falciform ligament divides the right and left lobes on the front of the liver.
The lesser omentum connects the stomach and duodenum to the underside of the liver and carries vessels to it. Pick it for a question about which fold joins the stomach to the liver.
The greater omentum hangs from the stomach like a fatty apron over the intestines. It is the answer for the largest peritoneal fold, not for a fold on the liver.
The mesocolon binds the transverse and sigmoid colon to the posterior abdominal wall. Choose it for a question about how the colon is anchored.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: What are hepatocytes?
options: Leaky capillaries running between liver cell plates
Pancreatic cell clusters that make digestive juice
The liver's working cells, arranged in plates
Tiny channels between liver cells that collect bile
questions.why: Hepatocytes are the functional cells of the liver, the cells that make bile and do the liver's processing work. They are arranged in plates, called hepatic laminae, that radiate through each lobule. Blood flows past them in sinusoids on one side, and the bile they make drains into canaliculi between neighboring cells.
notes: Wide, leaky capillaries running between the plates of liver cells are the hepatic sinusoids. Pick them for a question about the blood channels inside a liver lobule.
Clusters of pancreatic cells that make digestive juice are the acini of the pancreas. That is the answer for the exocrine part of the pancreas, not the liver.
Correct. Hepatocytes are the liver's functional cells, stacked in plates called hepatic laminae.
Tiny channels between hepatocytes that collect bile are bile canaliculi, the first step in the bile pathway. They are the answer for where bile goes right after the cells make it.
questions.answerText: The liver's working cells, arranged in plates

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which three structures make up a portal triad at the corner of a liver lobule?
options: Cystic duct, hepatic artery branch, hepatic portal vein branch
Bile duct, hepatic artery branch, hepatic portal vein branch
Bile duct, hepatic artery branch, hepatic vein branch
Bile duct, central vein, hepatic portal vein branch
questions.why: A portal triad sits at each corner of a liver lobule and carries traffic in both directions. A branch of the hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood in, a branch of the hepatic portal vein brings nutrient-rich blood from the gut in, and a bile duct carries bile out. The two incoming blood supplies mix in the sinusoids as they flow past the hepatocytes.
notes: The cystic duct carries bile to and from the gallbladder outside the liver, so it is not found in a lobule. Pick it for a question about the duct that connects the gallbladder to the bile pathway.
Correct. The triad is a bile duct, a hepatic artery branch, and a hepatic portal vein branch.
The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava and are not part of the triad. They would be the answer for the vessels carrying blood away from the liver.
The central vein runs through the middle of each lobule and collects blood after it passes the hepatocytes. It is the answer for the vessel at the center of the lobule, not at its corners.
questions.answerText: Bile duct, hepatic artery branch, hepatic portal vein branch

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: The liver receives blood from two sources. Which statement correctly describes what each one delivers?
options: Portal vein brings nutrient-rich gut blood; hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood
Both vessels bring oxygenated blood from the aorta, one to each liver lobe
Hepatic veins bring nutrient-rich gut blood; hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood
Portal vein brings oxygenated blood; hepatic artery brings nutrient-rich gut blood
questions.why: The liver's blood supply is unusual. The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood collected from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas, so the liver can process absorbed substances before they reach the rest of the body. The hepatic artery, which arises from the celiac trunk, brings oxygenated blood to keep the liver tissue alive.
notes: Correct. The portal vein brings gut blood rich in nutrients, and the hepatic artery brings oxygen.
Only the hepatic artery comes from the aorta. Students pick this when they forget that the liver has a portal vein, a vein that brings blood in rather than taking it out.
The hepatic veins carry blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava, so they do not deliver anything to it. They would be the answer for the vessels that drain the liver.

This reverses the two vessels. Arteries carry blood from the aorta, so the oxygenated supply comes through the hepatic artery, while the portal vein collects blood that has already passed through the gut.
questions.answerText: Portal vein brings nutrient-rich gut blood; hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: What does the gallbladder do?
options: Stores and concentrates bile until it is needed
Produces enzyme-rich juice for the duodenum
Produces bile from the blood that passes through it
Absorbs water from waste and helps form feces
questions.why: The gallbladder is a small pear-shaped sac on the underside of the liver. It does not make bile. Instead it receives bile from the liver through the cystic duct, stores it, and concentrates it by removing water, then releases it into the duodenum after a meal.
notes: Correct. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile.
Enzyme-rich juice for the duodenum comes from the acini of the pancreas. That is the answer for a question about pancreatic juice.
Bile is produced by the liver's hepatocytes, not the gallbladder. Pick this for a question about what the liver makes.
Absorbing water from waste and forming feces is the job of the large intestine. Students pick this because the gallbladder also removes water, but it removes it from bile, not from waste.
questions.answerText: Stores and concentrates bile until it is needed

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Without a detour into the gallbladder, which sequence traces bile from the liver cells to the duodenum?
options: Canaliculi, hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, common bile duct, ampulla
Hepatic ducts, canaliculi, common hepatic duct, common bile duct, ampulla
Canaliculi, common bile duct, hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, ampulla
Canaliculi, hepatic ducts, cystic duct, main pancreatic duct, ampulla
questions.why: Bile drains along a path of widening ducts. The tiny bile canaliculi between hepatocytes collect it, the right and left hepatic ducts gather it and merge into the common hepatic duct, and the common hepatic duct becomes the common bile duct once the cystic duct joins. The common bile duct meets the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens into the duodenum.
notes: Correct. Bile moves from canaliculi to hepatic ducts, then the common hepatic duct, the common bile duct, and the ampulla.
This puts the hepatic ducts ahead of the canaliculi, but the canaliculi are the smallest channels and collect bile right where the cells make it. The larger ducts come after.
This places the common bile duct second, but the common bile duct only forms after the common hepatic duct is joined by the cystic duct. It is the last duct before the ampulla, not an early one.

The cystic duct leads to and from the gallbladder, which the question excludes, and bile never travels up the main pancreatic duct. Choose the cystic duct only for a question about bile going into storage.
questions.answerText: Canaliculi, hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, common bile duct, ampulla

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: After a patient's gallbladder is removed, bile still reaches the intestine. Using the duct anatomy, how does it get there?
options: It drains through the accessory pancreatic duct and into the duodenum instead
It drains into the stomach along a channel in the lesser omentum
It enters the blood and is carried to the duodenum by the hepatic veins
It drains from the common hepatic duct straight into the common bile duct
questions.why: The gallbladder only stores and concentrates bile, and it sits on a side branch, the cystic duct. The liver keeps making bile, which flows from the hepatic ducts into the common hepatic duct and then straight into the common bile duct, the hepatopancreatic ampulla, and the duodenum. Without the gallbladder, bile simply trickles in steadily instead of being stored and released in larger amounts.
notes: The accessory pancreatic duct drains part of the pancreas separately into the duodenum and is not connected to the bile ducts. Pick it for a question about the smaller pancreatic duct.
The lesser omentum is a fold of peritoneum linking the stomach and duodenum to the liver, not a channel for bile. It is the answer for a question about which fold carries vessels to the liver.
The hepatic veins carry blood from the liver to the inferior vena cava and never carry bile. Students pick this when they confuse the liver's blood vessels with its bile ducts.
Correct. Bile takes the main path from the common hepatic duct into the common bile duct and on to the duodenum.
questions.answerText: It drains from the common hepatic duct straight into the common bile duct

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Where does the pancreas lie, and how is it positioned relative to the peritoneum?
options: Under the right lobe of the liver, intraperitoneal
Beside the stomach in the upper left, intraperitoneal
Posterior to the stomach, retroperitoneal
Anterior to the stomach, inside the greater omentum
questions.why: The pancreas lies posterior to the stomach, stretching from its head in the curve of the duodenum to its tail near the spleen. It is retroperitoneal, meaning it lies behind the peritoneum against the posterior abdominal wall instead of hanging in the peritoneal cavity. Its ducts empty into the duodenum.
notes: The underside of the right lobe of the liver is where the gallbladder sits. Pick this location for a question about the gallbladder.
An intraperitoneal organ beside the stomach in the upper left abdomen describes the spleen. That would be the answer for the spleen, which is covered by peritoneum.
Correct. The pancreas is behind the stomach and retroperitoneal.
The greater omentum hangs in front of the intestines from the stomach, and the pancreas is behind the stomach, not in front of it. This description fits the fatty apron of the greater omentum.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which list names the three regions of the pancreas?
options: Right, left, and caudate lobes
Cardia, body, and pylorus
Head, body, and tail
Fundus, body, and neck
questions.why: The pancreas is divided into a head, a body and a tail. The wide head sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum, the body runs behind the stomach, and the tapered tail reaches toward the spleen. The main pancreatic duct runs through all three regions toward the head.
notes: The right and left lobes, with the smaller caudate and quadrate lobes, are lobes of the liver. Choose them for a question about liver anatomy.
The cardia, body and pylorus are regions of the stomach. This set would fit a question about the parts of the stomach between the esophagus and the duodenum.
Correct. The pancreas has a head, body, and tail.
Fundus, body and neck are the three regions of the gallbladder, from its broad end to its tapered end. Pick this set for a question about the gallbladder.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: What are the acini of the pancreas?
options: Ducts that carry pancreatic juice into the duodenum
Plates of liver cells that make bile and process absorbed nutrients
Exocrine clusters that make pancreatic juice, about 99 percent
Endocrine clusters that make hormones, about 1 percent
questions.why: Most of the pancreas is made of acini, small grape-like clusters of exocrine cells (cells that release their product into ducts). They produce pancreatic juice, which drains through the pancreatic ducts into the duodenum. The acini make up about 99 percent of the gland, while the scattered pancreatic islets make up the remaining 1 percent.
notes: The ducts that carry juice into the duodenum are the main and accessory pancreatic ducts. The acini make the juice, and the ducts only carry it.
Plates of liver cells are hepatic laminae made of hepatocytes. They are the answer for the functional tissue of the liver, not the pancreas.
Correct. Acini are the exocrine clusters that make pancreatic juice and form most of the gland.
Endocrine clusters that make hormones, about 1 percent of the gland, are the pancreatic islets. Pick them for a question about the endocrine part of the pancreas.
questions.answerText: Exocrine clusters that make pancreatic juice, about 99 percent

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the exocrine and endocrine parts of the pancreas?
options: Acini and islets both send juice through ducts to the duodenum
Islets send juice through ducts to the duodenum; acini release hormones
Acini send juice through ducts to the duodenum; islets release hormones
Acini release hormones into ducts; islets make bile for the duodenum
questions.why: The pancreas is two glands in one. Its exocrine part, the acini, makes pancreatic juice and sends it through ducts into the duodenum. Its endocrine part, the pancreatic islets, makes hormones that pass into the blood rather than into a duct. The acini make up about 99 percent of the gland and the islets about 1 percent.
notes: Only the acini send their product through ducts. The islets are endocrine, so their hormones go into the blood, which is the whole difference between the two parts.
This reverses the two. Exocrine glands use ducts, and the acini are the clusters that empty through the pancreatic duct, so the islets cannot be the duct-using part.
Correct. Acini are the exocrine part and islets are the endocrine part.
Bile is made by the liver, not the pancreas, and hormones do not travel in ducts. Students pick this when they mix up the pancreas with the liver.
questions.answerText: Acini send juice through ducts to the duodenum; islets release hormones

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A gallstone lodges at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, and the patient develops pancreatitis. Why can a gallstone there inflame the pancreas?
options: Bile and pancreatic ducts share that passage, so pancreatic juice backs up
The gallbladder sits inside the pancreas, so its swelling presses on the gland
The pancreas makes the bile, so blocked bile damages the pancreas
The stone travels up the cystic duct and lodges inside the pancreas
questions.why: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct meet at the hepatopancreatic ampulla before they open into the duodenum. Because both secretions pass through that short shared channel, a stone lodged there blocks bile and pancreatic juice at once. The trapped pancreatic juice backs up into the pancreas, which can inflame it.
notes: Correct. The shared ampulla means one stone can block both the bile duct and the pancreatic duct.
The gallbladder sits on the underside of the liver, not inside the pancreas. This is a location mix-up, since the gallbladder and pancreas are linked only through the ducts.
The liver makes bile, and the pancreas makes pancreatic juice. Pick the liver for a question about where bile is produced.
The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the common bile duct and leads nowhere near the pancreas. Students pick this when they think of the cystic duct as a route into the pancreas.
questions.answerText: Bile and pancreatic ducts share that passage, so pancreatic juice backs up

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the alimentary canal from the accessory digestive organs?
options: The canal is the tube food passes through; accessory organs lie outside it
The canal makes every digestive secretion; accessory organs only absorb food
The canal includes the liver and pancreas; accessory organs are the intestines
Food passes through both; accessory organs are the widest parts of the tube
questions.why: The alimentary canal is one continuous muscular tube from the mouth to the anus, and food passes through every part of it. The accessory organs (the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas) are not part of that tube. The teeth and tongue work on food in the mouth, and the glandular organs add their secretions to the canal through ducts.
notes: Correct. Food passes through the canal, while the accessory organs help from outside the tube.
Much of the digestive secretion comes from accessory organs such as the salivary glands, liver, and pancreas, and absorption happens in the canal. This choice reverses the roles of the two groups.
The liver and pancreas are accessory organs, and the intestines are part of the canal. This choice reverses the two groups.
Food never passes through the accessory organs, so this cannot be right. Students pick it when they think of the gallbladder or pancreas as pouches of the tube rather than separate organs with ducts.
questions.answerText: The canal is the tube food passes through; accessory organs lie outside it

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: What are gallstones, and what can they block?
options: Hardened deposits from the kidney that can block the ureter
Scar tissue in the liver that replaces healthy liver tissue
Hardened deposits from the gallbladder that can block the bile ducts
Hardened deposits in a salivary gland that can block the gland's duct
questions.why: Gallstones are hardened deposits that form inside the gallbladder from substances in stored bile. A stone can leave the gallbladder and lodge in the cystic duct, the common bile duct, or the hepatopancreatic ampulla, blocking the flow of bile. A blocking stone can inflame the gallbladder (cholecystitis) or, at the ampulla, the pancreas.
notes: Hardened deposits that form in the kidney and block the ureter are kidney stones. Pick this for a question about the urinary tract.
Scar tissue replacing healthy liver tissue is cirrhosis. Choose it for a question about long-term liver damage and loss of liver function.
Correct. Gallstones form in the gallbladder and can block the bile ducts.
Stones can form in a salivary gland and block its duct, but they are salivary stones, not gallstones. This would be the answer for a swollen salivary gland during meals.
questions.answerText: Hardened deposits from the gallbladder that can block the bile ducts

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Which description matches jaundice?
options: Yellowing of skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin
Replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue
Inflammation of the gallbladder from a blocking stone
Inflammation of the liver, often from a viral infection
questions.why: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment made when old red blood cells are broken down. The liver normally clears it into bile. When the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, bilirubin builds up in the blood and tints the skin and the whites of the eyes yellow. Jaundice is therefore a sign of a problem rather than a disease of its own.
notes: Correct. Jaundice is yellowing of the skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin.
Replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue is cirrhosis. It can also lead to jaundice, but it is the answer for scarring of the liver.
Inflammation of the gallbladder, often from a blocking gallstone, is cholecystitis. Pick it for a question about an inflamed gallbladder.
Inflammation of the liver, commonly from a viral infection, is hepatitis. Hepatitis can cause jaundice, but the inflammation itself is the answer for a question about hepatitis.
questions.answerText: Yellowing of skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Where would a single gallstone have to lodge to block both bile and pancreatic juice at the same time?
options: Hepatopancreatic ampulla
Common hepatic duct
Accessory pancreatic duct
Cystic duct
questions.why: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct meet at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, a short widened channel just before the duodenum. This is the only place in the system where bile and pancreatic juice share one passage. A stone stuck there backs bile up toward the liver and pancreatic juice up into the pancreas at the same time, which can cause both jaundice and pancreatitis.
notes: Correct. The hepatopancreatic ampulla is the shared passage for bile and pancreatic juice.
The common hepatic duct carries bile from the liver before the cystic duct joins it, well above the pancreas. A stone there blocks bile from the liver but not pancreatic juice.
The accessory pancreatic duct empties separately into the duodenum and carries only pancreatic juice. Blocking it would not stop bile at all, so it fits a question about the duct of Santorini.

A stone in the cystic duct blocks the gallbladder's outlet and can cause cholecystitis, but bile from the liver and pancreatic juice can still reach the duodenum. Pick it for a stone that affects only the gallbladder.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A dentist sees saliva coming from a small opening inside the cheek, opposite the upper second molar. Which gland makes this saliva, and which muscle does its duct pierce to reach the mouth?
options: The parotid gland; the buccinator muscle.
The submandibular gland; the buccinator muscle.
The parotid gland; the mylohyoid muscle.
The sublingual gland; the masseter muscle.
questions.why: The parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear, over the masseter muscle. Its duct runs forward across the masseter, passes through the buccinator muscle of the cheek, and opens on the inside of the cheek opposite the upper second molar. An opening in the cheek at that spot always points to the parotid.
notes: Correct. The parotid duct runs across the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.
The submandibular duct runs under the lining of the floor of the mouth and opens beside the lingual frenulum, not in the cheek.
The gland is right, but the mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth. The parotid duct passes through the buccinator in the cheek.
The sublingual gland drains through many small ducts into the floor of the mouth. Its ducts do not reach the cheek.
questions.answerText: The parotid gland; the buccinator muscle.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A small stone blocks the single duct that opens on a bump beside the lingual frenulum. Which gland swells, and where would you feel it?
options: The sublingual gland, just under the lining below the tongue.
The submandibular gland, over the masseter muscle.
The parotid gland, in front of and below the ear.
The submandibular gland, along the inner surface of the mandible.
questions.why: Start with the opening: the single duct that ends on a small bump on each side of the lingual frenulum is the submandibular duct. Then trace it back. It runs under the lining of the floor of the mouth to the submandibular gland, which lies along the inner surface of the body of the mandible. A blocked duct would make that gland swell.
notes: The sublingual gland lies under the tongue, but it drains through many small ducts along the floor of the mouth, not one duct beside the frenulum.
The gland is right, but the gland over the masseter is the parotid. The submandibular gland lies along the inner surface of the mandible.
The parotid lies in front of and below the ear, but its duct opens inside the cheek opposite the upper second molar, not beside the frenulum.
Correct. The submandibular duct opens beside the lingual frenulum, and the gland lies along the inner surface of the body of the mandible.
questions.answerText: The submandibular gland, along the inner surface of the mandible.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A drawing of the floor of the mouth shows two salivary glands. One drains through a single duct beside the lingual frenulum. The other drains through many small ducts along the floor. Which one is which, and which one sits higher?
options: The single duct drains the submandibular; the many ducts drain the sublingual, which sits higher.
The single duct drains the parotid; the many ducts drain the submandibular, which sits higher.
The single duct drains the sublingual; the many ducts drain the submandibular, which sits higher.
The single duct drains the submandibular; the many ducts drain the sublingual, which sits lower.
questions.why: Both glands sit in the floor of the mouth, but they drain differently. The submandibular gland sends its saliva through one submandibular duct that opens beside the lingual frenulum. The sublingual gland, the smallest of the three, drains through many small ducts along the floor of the mouth. It lies just under the lining, above the submandibular gland.
notes: Correct. The sublingual gland drains through many small ducts and lies above the submandibular gland.
The parotid duct opens inside the cheek, not beside the frenulum. The two glands in the floor of the mouth are the submandibular and sublingual.
This swaps the two. The submandibular has one duct beside the frenulum, and the sublingual, with many small ducts, lies above it.
The ducts are matched correctly, but the sublingual gland lies just under the lining, above the submandibular gland, not below it.
questions.answerText: The single duct drains the submandibular; the many ducts drain the sublingual, which sits higher.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: On a liver slide, you find a corner of a lobule with a small vein, a small artery, and a duct. Blood from those two vessels flows through which channels, and into which vessel?
options: Through the bile canaliculi, into the bile duct of the triad.
Through the hepatic sinusoids, into the central vein.
Through the hepatic sinusoids, into the hepatic portal vein.
Through the bile canaliculi, into the central vein.
questions.why: A vein, an artery, and a duct together at a lobule corner make a portal triad: a branch of the hepatic portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery, and a bile duct. Blood from the two vessels mixes in the hepatic sinusoids, the leaky capillaries between the plates of hepatocytes, and flows toward the center. The central vein collects it there. Bile travels the other way, out through the canaliculi to the bile duct.
notes: This is the path of bile, not blood. Bile moves from the canaliculi out to the bile duct, the opposite direction from blood.
Correct. Blood from the portal triad flows through the sinusoids past the hepatocytes to the central vein in the middle of the lobule.
The channels are right, but the portal vein brings blood into the liver. The sinusoids drain into the central vein at the lobule's center.
The bile canaliculi carry bile between hepatocytes, outward toward the portal triad. They do not carry blood.
questions.answerText: Through the hepatic sinusoids, into the central vein.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: Looking at the inferior surface of the liver, you see a small square lobe between the gallbladder and a fibrous cord. Which lobe is it, and what is the cord a remnant of?
options: The quadrate lobe; the cord is the remnant of the fetal umbilical artery.
The caudate lobe; the cord is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.
The quadrate lobe; the cord is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.
The left lobe; the cord is the falciform ligament.
questions.why: The liver has four lobes. The right and left lobes are seen from the front, while the quadrate and caudate lobes are seen from below and behind. The quadrate lobe is the small square lobe on the inferior surface between the gallbladder and the ligamentum teres. The ligamentum teres (round ligament) is a fibrous cord from the umbilicus to the liver, and it is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.
notes: The lobe is right, but the ligamentum teres is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein. The remnant of the umbilical artery is the medial umbilical ligament, on the inside of the anterior abdominal wall.
The caudate lobe is on the posterior surface beside the inferior vena cava. The square lobe beside the gallbladder is the quadrate lobe.
Correct. The quadrate lobe sits between the gallbladder and the ligamentum teres, which is what remains of the fetal umbilical vein.
The left lobe is seen from the front, over the stomach. The falciform ligament is a peritoneal fold, and the cord in its free edge is the ligamentum teres.
questions.answerText: The quadrate lobe; the cord is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A gallstone lodges in the common bile duct where it runs through the head of the pancreas. Which ducts lie upstream of the stone and would fill with bile that cannot get past it?
options: Only the main pancreatic duct and the hepatopancreatic ampulla below the stone.
The common hepatic duct, the hepatic ducts, and the cystic duct with the gallbladder.
Only the right and left hepatic ducts; the gallbladder still empties freely.
Only the cystic duct and the gallbladder; the hepatic ducts still drain freely.
questions.why: Trace the biliary tree from the top. The right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct from the gallbladder joins it to form the common bile duct, which runs behind the first part of the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas. Every duct above that point drains into the common bile duct, so a stone there blocks the hepatic ducts, the common hepatic duct, and the cystic duct and gallbladder.
notes: The main pancreatic duct and the ampulla lie downstream, where the common bile duct ends. Bile from above never reaches them past the stone.
Correct. All of these drain into the common bile duct, so all of them lie upstream of a stone lodged in it.
The gallbladder empties through the cystic duct into the common bile duct, so it is blocked by the stone as well.
The hepatic ducts empty into the common hepatic duct, which joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct. A stone there blocks them too.
questions.answerText: The common hepatic duct, the hepatic ducts, and the cystic duct with the gallbladder.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A stone blocks the hepatopancreatic ampulla. Which pancreatic duct can still deliver pancreatic juice to the duodenum, and where does it open?
options: The main pancreatic duct, at the major duodenal papilla.
The main pancreatic duct, at the minor duodenal papilla.
The accessory pancreatic duct, at the minor duodenal papilla.
The accessory pancreatic duct, at the major duodenal papilla.
questions.why: The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) runs the length of the gland and joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. The smaller accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini) drains part of the head and opens on its own at the minor duodenal papilla, a little above the major papilla. A stone in the ampulla blocks the main duct but not the accessory duct.
notes: The main pancreatic duct joins the common bile duct at the ampulla, so a stone in the ampulla blocks it.
The main pancreatic duct opens through the ampulla at the major papilla. It is the accessory duct that uses the minor papilla.
Correct. The accessory pancreatic duct opens on its own at the minor duodenal papilla, so it bypasses the blocked ampulla.
The duct is right, but the major papilla is where the blocked ampulla opens. The accessory duct opens at the minor papilla.
questions.answerText: The accessory pancreatic duct, at the minor duodenal papilla.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A stained pancreas slide shows mostly dark clusters of gland cells around tiny ducts, with scattered pale, round patches. If a disease destroyed only the pale patches, which tissue would be lost?
options: The pancreatic islets, the endocrine tissue, about 1 percent of the gland.
The acini, the exocrine tissue, about 99 percent of the gland.
The pancreatic islets, the exocrine tissue, about 99 percent of the gland.
The acini, the endocrine tissue, about 1 percent of the gland.
questions.why: On a stained slide the pancreas shows two tissues. The acini are the darker clusters of gland cells around tiny ducts, the exocrine part that makes pancreatic juice and forms about 99 percent of the gland. Scattered among them are the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans), pale round patches that are the endocrine part and form about 1 percent of the gland. A disease of the pale patches destroys the islets.
notes: Correct. The pale patches are the islets, the endocrine part, which make up about 1 percent of the gland.
The acini are the darker clusters around tiny ducts that make up most of the gland. The pale patches scattered among them are the islets.
The islets are the pale patches, but they are the endocrine part and only about 1 percent of the gland. The acini are the exocrine part.
The acini are exocrine, sending pancreatic juice through ducts. The endocrine tissue is the islets, the pale patches.
questions.answerText: The pancreatic islets, the endocrine tissue, about 1 percent of the gland.

questions.topic: Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas
questions.q: A tumor grows in the part of the pancreas that sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum. Which region is this, and which duct that is not part of the pancreas runs through it?
options: The tail of the pancreas; the common bile duct.
The head of the pancreas; the common bile duct.
The head of the pancreas; the main pancreatic duct.
The body of the pancreas; the cystic duct.
questions.why: The head of the pancreas is its wide end, sitting in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum to the right of the midline. The common bile duct, which carries bile from the liver and gallbladder, runs down behind the first part of the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas. It then joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. A tumor in the head lies right beside that duct.
notes: The tail is the narrow left end near the spleen. The region in the curve of the duodenum is the head.
Correct. The head sits in the curve of the duodenum, and the common bile duct runs through the head on its way to the ampulla.
The region is right, but the main pancreatic duct is the pancreas's own duct. The question asks for the duct from outside the gland.
The body crosses the midline behind the stomach. The cystic duct runs from the neck of the gallbladder and ends where it joins the common hepatic duct, so it never reaches the pancreas.
questions.answerText: The head of the pancreas; the common bile duct.

questions.q: In digestive physiology, what does the term motility refer to?
options: Movement of material through the tract by smooth muscle contraction
Release of fluid, ions, and enzymes into the lumen from glands
Enzymatic breakdown of large molecules into their absorbable subunits
Transfer of nutrients across the epithelium into blood or lymph
questions.why: Motility is the muscular work of the tract: contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle that mixes and propels contents. Releasing fluid and enzymes is secretion, breaking molecules apart is digestion, and moving nutrients across the epithelium is absorption. All four happen at once in a fed gut, but only motility is muscle work.
questions.answerText: Movement of material through the tract by smooth muscle contraction

questions.q: Which digestive process describes glands releasing water, enzymes, and ions into the lumen of the tract?
options: Secretion
Motility
Digestion
Absorption
questions.why: Secretion is the movement of substances from cells and glands into the lumen, and it supplies the enzymes and fluid the rest of digestion depends on. Digestion is the chemical breakdown that those enzymes then carry out. Absorption runs the opposite direction, lumen to blood. Motility is the muscular mixing and propulsion that keeps secretions in contact with food.

questions.q: Chemical digestion is best defined as which of the following?
options: Grinding of food into smaller particles by the teeth and stomach
Enzymatic breaking of chemical bonds to yield absorbable subunits
Packaging of nutrients for transport in blood or lymph
Movement of ions and water into the lumen from glands
questions.why: Chemical digestion uses hydrolytic enzymes to cleave bonds, turning starch into monosaccharides and protein into amino acids. Grinding is mechanical digestion, which is a form of motility and changes particle size but not chemical structure. Packaging for transport happens inside the enterocyte after absorption. Moving ions and water into the lumen is secretion.
questions.answerText: Enzymatic breaking of chemical bonds to yield absorbable subunits

questions.q: Absorption in the digestive tract refers to movement in which direction?
options: From the cytoplasm of a gland cell into the duct it drains
From the blood and glands into the lumen of the tract
From the lumen across the epithelium into blood or lymph
From one segment of the tract into the next segment
questions.why: Absorption is the one-way trip that makes eating useful: nutrients cross the enterocyte and enter capillaries or lacteals. Movement from blood into the lumen is secretion, which supplies fluid and enzymes. Movement between segments is motility. Gland cell to duct is also secretion, described at the cellular level.
questions.answerText: From the lumen across the epithelium into blood or lymph

questions.q: Which region of the digestive tract is the principal site of nutrient absorption?
options: The small intestine
The large intestine
The esophagus
The stomach
questions.why: The small intestine combines an enormous surface area from folds, villi, and microvilli with the enzymes and transporters that finish digestion, so nearly all carbohydrate, protein, and fat absorption happens there. The stomach absorbs almost nothing of nutritional value, mostly alcohol and a few lipid soluble drugs. The large intestine absorbs water, electrolytes, and some vitamins made by bacteria, not the bulk of nutrients. The esophagus is a conduit only.

questions.q: Which region of the tract completes water and electrolyte absorption and compacts the residue into feces?
options: The stomach
The proximal duodenum
The mid jejunum
The large intestine
questions.why: The colon receives roughly 1.5 L of watery residue each day and returns most of that water and its salts to the body, leaving about 100 to 150 mL in stool. The duodenum and jejunum absorb far more water in absolute terms, but they hand off a still fluid chyme rather than forming feces. The stomach neither concentrates the residue nor absorbs meaningful water.

questions.q: About how much fluid enters the lumen of the digestive tract each day from ingestion plus secretion combined?
options: About 9 liters
About 25 liters
About 1 liter
About 3 liters
questions.why: Roughly 2 L is swallowed and about 7 L is secreted as saliva, gastric juice, pancreatic juice, bile, and intestinal fluid, for a total near 9 L. About 1 liter is what a person drinks in a modest day, and about 3 liters would cover ingestion plus saliva alone. About 25 liters overstates it badly; that figure is closer to daily glomerular filtration territory in the kidney, not the gut. Because almost all 9 L is reabsorbed, small failures of absorption produce large fluid losses.

questions.q: Chewing food into smaller pieces is classified as which of the four digestive processes?
options: Absorption, because surface area for uptake increases
Secretion, because saliva is released at the same time
Digestion, because chemical bonds in starch are broken
Motility, specifically mechanical digestion
questions.why: Chewing is skeletal muscle work that reduces particle size and increases surface area, so it is grouped with motility as mechanical digestion. Nothing chemical happens: no covalent bond in starch or protein is broken by the teeth. Secretion is the saliva released alongside chewing, and absorption does not occur in the mouth to any meaningful extent.

questions.q: A parietal cell in the stomach wall moves H+ into the gastric lumen. Which digestive process is this?
options: Absorption
Secretion
Digestion
Motility
questions.why: Anything a cell releases into the lumen is secretion, regardless of what it later does there. The acid then supports digestion by activating pepsinogen, but the release itself is the secretory step. Absorption would be H+ moving from lumen into blood, the opposite direction. Motility describes the churning that mixes the acid with food.

questions.q: Rings of contraction appear at intervals along the small intestine, relax, and reappear between the old sites, sloshing chyme back and forth with little forward movement. Which process is this?
options: Secretion
Motility
Absorption
Digestion
questions.why: This describes segmentation, a motility pattern whose job is mixing rather than propulsion. It supports digestion and absorption by keeping chyme in contact with enzymes and the brush border, but the contractions themselves are muscle work. Digestion is enzymatic bond breaking, and secretion is the release of the enzymes doing that work.

questions.q: Glucose crosses the apical membrane of an enterocyte on SGLT1 and leaves the cell into a capillary. Which process does this represent?
options: Secretion
Mechanical digestion
Chemical digestion
Absorption
questions.why: Nutrient moving from lumen through the epithelium into blood is the definition of absorption. Secretion would be glucose moving the other way. Chemical digestion is what produced the free glucose in the first place, when brush border maltase cleaved a disaccharide, but the transport step itself is absorption. No muscle is involved, so nothing here is mechanical digestion.

questions.q: Pepsin cleaves peptide bonds inside a protein chain in the stomach lumen. Which process is this?
options: Absorption
Mechanical digestion
Secretion
Chemical digestion
questions.why: Breaking a covalent bond with a hydrolytic enzyme is chemical digestion by definition. The release of pepsinogen from chief cells was secretion, an earlier and separate step. Absorption comes later, once peptides are reduced to amino acids and small peptides at the brush border. Mechanical digestion would be the churning that exposed more of the protein to the enzyme.

questions.q: A drug sharply increases the rate at which chyme is propelled through the small intestine. Which process is most directly compromised, and why?
options: Mechanical digestion, because there is less churning
Secretion, because glands cannot keep up with the flow
Absorption, because contact time with the mucosa falls
Motility, because the muscle fatigues at high rates
questions.why: Absorption depends on time spent against the brush border, so faster transit means nutrients and water leave before they can be taken up, which is why rapid transit causes diarrhea. Secretion is largely reflex driven and does not simply fail at high flow. Motility is the thing being increased, not impaired. Mechanical digestion continues; the problem is that the products are swept past the absorptive surface.
questions.answerText: Absorption, because contact time with the mucosa falls

questions.q: A patient loses the brush border enzyme lactase. Which digestive process fails first for lactose?
options: Absorption, because the brush border glucose transporter is missing
Secretion, because less intestinal fluid is released into the lumen
Motility, because segmentation slows and mixing is reduced
Digestion, because lactose is never cleaved to monosaccharides
questions.why: Lactase is the enzyme that performs the final digestive step, so without it lactose stays a disaccharide. Absorption then fails as a consequence, but the transporters themselves are intact and would carry glucose and galactose perfectly well if the sugar were cleaved, so the primary failure is digestive. Secretion and motility are not the primary lesion, though the unabsorbed sugar draws water in osmotically and speeds transit as a downstream effect.
questions.answerText: Digestion, because lactose is never cleaved to monosaccharides

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a region of the tract with the process that dominates there?
options: Colon and chemical digestion of dietary protein
Esophagus and secretion of digestive enzymes
Mouth and absorption of most dietary nutrients
Stomach and mechanical mixing with acid secretion
questions.why: The stomach churns food into chyme while parietal and chief cells secrete acid and pepsinogen, so motility and secretion dominate there. The mouth secretes and chews but absorbs essentially nothing. Protein digestion is complete before the colon, which handles water and electrolytes. The esophagus performs peristalsis and secretes only lubricating mucus, not enzymes.
questions.answerText: Stomach and mechanical mixing with acid secretion

questions.q: A person has surgery that speeds gastric emptying so that a meal reaches the jejunum in minutes instead of hours. Predict the effect on chemical digestion and then on absorption in the small intestine.
options: Digestion falls but absorption rises because the mucosa is exposed to a larger load
Digestion improves because the meal reaches the enzymes sooner, and absorption improves along with it
Digestion is unchanged and absorption improves because more chyme is delivered per minute
Both fall, because enzymes have less time to act and products have less contact time with the mucosa
questions.why: Digestion and absorption are both time dependent, so dumping a bolus into the intestine faster than the enzymes and transporters can process it leaves nutrients undigested and unabsorbed. Arriving sooner does not help when the limiting factor is duration of contact, not delay in delivery. A larger load per minute saturates transporters rather than driving more uptake, and the unabsorbed solute holds water in the lumen, which speeds transit further and makes the problem worse.
questions.answerText: Both fall, because enzymes have less time to act and products have less contact time with the mucosa

questions.q: Cholera toxin locks open the Cl- channel on the apical membrane of intestinal crypt cells, so Cl- and water pour into the lumen. Using the four processes, explain the resulting diarrhea.
options: Digestion is blocked, so osmotically active nutrients are left to hold water in the lumen
Motility stops, so secreted fluid pools in the small intestine and cannot move on
Secretion exceeds absorption, so net fluid movement into the lumen overwhelms the colon
Absorption of nutrients stops, so the mucosa can no longer recover water from residue
questions.why: Stool water is the balance of two processes, and cholera drives secretion far above the roughly 1.5 to 2 L per day the colon can absorb, so the excess appears as watery stool. Digestion and nutrient transport are undamaged, which is exactly why oral rehydration with glucose and salt still works: SGLT1 driven Na+ and water absorption is intact. Motility is not stopped, and pooled fluid without net secretion would not produce this volume.
questions.answerText: Secretion exceeds absorption, so net fluid movement into the lumen overwhelms the colon

questions.q: A patient has most of the ileum surgically removed. Trace the consequences through the four processes and identify the most specific loss.
options: Absorption fails for bile salts and vitamin B12, which are taken up only in the ileum
Motility of the entire tract stops, because the pacemaker for the gut lies in the ileum
Digestion of starch fails, because the ileum supplies most of the brush border amylase
Secretion of pancreatic enzymes fails, so digestion of all three macronutrients is lost
questions.why: The ileum is the only site with the Na+ coupled bile salt transporter and the intrinsic factor B12 receptor, so its loss produces bile salt wasting and B12 deficiency even when the rest of the tract works. Pancreatic secretion is unaffected because the pancreas and its duct are untouched. Pacemaker activity comes from interstitial cells of Cajal distributed along the whole tract, not from an ileal center. Starch is digested by brush border enzymes concentrated in the duodenum and jejunum, upstream of the resection.
questions.answerText: Absorption fails for bile salts and vitamin B12, which are taken up only in the ileum

questions.q: A drug blocks contraction of smooth muscle throughout the digestive tract while leaving glands and epithelium intact. Predict the sequence of consequences.
options: Absorption rises because contents remain in contact with the mucosa indefinitely
Nothing changes because digestion and absorption do not require muscle activity
Secretion stops first, and digestion and absorption fail because no enzymes are released
Mixing and propulsion stop, so enzymes contact food poorly and unabsorbed contents stagnate
questions.why: Motility is what brings substrate and enzyme together and what moves the products along to fresh absorptive surface, so blocking it degrades digestion and absorption indirectly even though neither process needs muscle itself. Secretion is glandular and reflex driven, so it continues. Indefinite contact does not raise total absorption because the layer against the mucosa is quickly stripped of nutrients and nothing renews it. The prediction that nothing changes ignores that stagnant contents also permit bacterial overgrowth.
questions.answerText: Mixing and propulsion stop, so enzymes contact food poorly and unabsorbed contents stagnate

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of peristalsis?
options: Clearing residue from the tract between meals
Propulsion of contents along the tract in one direction
Mixing of contents with little net movement
Grinding of solid particles against a closed sphincter
questions.why: Peristalsis is a progressive wave of contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, so material is squeezed forward. Mixing with little net movement is segmentation. Grinding against a closed pylorus is gastric retropulsion, a specialized stomach behavior. Clearing residue between meals is the job of the migrating motor complex.
questions.answerText: Propulsion of contents along the tract in one direction

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of segmentation in the small intestine?
options: Mixing chyme with digestive secretions and exposing it to the brush border
Sweeping bacteria and residual debris out of the small intestine during fasting
Generating the pressure that opens the lower esophageal sphincter
Rapidly propelling chyme toward the ileocecal valve
questions.why: Segmentation is alternating contraction of nonadjacent rings of circular muscle, which chops and sloshes chyme so enzymes reach it and fresh material contacts the absorptive surface. It moves contents only slowly forward, so rapid propulsion is not its role. Fasting cleanup belongs to the migrating motor complex, and sphincter opening is a separate reflex event.
questions.answerText: Mixing chyme with digestive secretions and exposing it to the brush border

questions.q: When does the migrating motor complex occur?
options: Continuously, whether fed or fasting
Immediately after a meal enters the stomach
During fasting, between meals
Only during sleep
questions.why: The migrating motor complex is the fasting pattern; feeding abolishes it and replaces it with the fed pattern of segmentation and short peristaltic waves. It is not restricted to sleep, though it is easier to record at night. It is not continuous, which is the point: it is a cycle that appears only when the tract is empty enough to need sweeping.

questions.q: About how often does a migrating motor complex cycle recur in the fasting state?
options: Every 3 to 5 minutes
