Every 20 to 30 minutes
Every 90 to 120 minutes
Every 8 to 10 hours
questions.why: The cycle repeats roughly every 90 to 120 minutes until the next meal interrupts it. Intervals of 3 to 5 minutes are closer to the frequency of gastric slow waves and peristaltic waves in a fed stomach. Twenty to thirty minutes is too frequent to allow the quiescent phase that begins each cycle, and 8 to 10 hours would leave residue sitting in the tract most of the night.

questions.q: Which motility pattern is described as the housekeeper of the small intestine?
options: Haustral churning
The migrating motor complex
Receptive relaxation
Segmentation
questions.why: The migrating motor complex sweeps undigested residue, sloughed cells, and bacteria from the stomach through the ileum, which is why losing it permits small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Segmentation mixes rather than sweeps. Haustral churning is a colonic pattern. Receptive relaxation is the vagally mediated relaxation of the stomach as food arrives, not a propulsive pattern at all.

questions.q: Which cells generate the slow waves that set the basic rhythm of gastrointestinal smooth muscle?
options: Enterochromaffin like cells
Interstitial cells of Cajal
Chief cells
Goblet cells
questions.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the tract, producing rhythmic depolarizations that spread through gap junctions to smooth muscle. Enterochromaffin like cells release histamine and drive acid secretion. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and goblet cells secrete mucus, neither of which has any pacemaker role.

questions.q: What is the approximate frequency of gastric slow waves?
options: About 12 per minute
About 30 per minute
About 60 per minute
About 3 per minute
questions.why: The stomach paces at roughly 3 slow waves per minute, and the duodenum runs faster at about 12 per minute, which helps drive contents distally down the frequency gradient. Thirty and sixty per minute are far above anything gastrointestinal smooth muscle produces and are closer to respiratory or cardiac rates. Slow waves set the maximum contraction rate; whether a wave produces a contraction depends on whether it reaches threshold.

questions.q: During a peristaltic wave, what happens to the circular muscle immediately behind the bolus?
options: It contracts and relaxes rhythmically without net change
It is unaffected, since only longitudinal muscle acts
It relaxes, widening the lumen behind the bolus
It contracts, narrowing the lumen behind the bolus
questions.why: Contraction of circular muscle behind the bolus squeezes it forward while the segment ahead relaxes and the longitudinal muscle there shortens to widen the receiving segment. Relaxation behind the bolus would let it slide backward. Both muscle layers participate, which is why the wave has both a pushing and a receiving component.
questions.answerText: It contracts, narrowing the lumen behind the bolus

questions.q: A recording from the jejunum shows rings of contraction that appear, relax, and reappear between the previous sites, with contents moving only a few centimeters over several minutes. Which pattern is this?
options: Segmentation
Phase III of the migrating motor complex
Mass movement
Peristalsis
questions.why: Alternating, nonprogressive rings with almost no net transit is the signature of segmentation, the dominant fed pattern in the small intestine. Peristalsis would show a wave traveling steadily in one direction. Phase III of the migrating motor complex is a strong sweeping series that moves contents rapidly and appears only in fasting. Mass movement is a colonic event that pushes a large volume over a long distance at once.

questions.q: A fasting volunteer shows a burst of strong contractions that begins in the stomach and travels to the terminal ileum, then falls quiet for about 90 minutes before repeating. What is being recorded?
options: Receptive relaxation
Segmentation
The gastrocolic reflex
The migrating motor complex
questions.why: A propagating burst that starts proximally, sweeps to the ileum, and cycles every 90 minutes in a fasting subject is the migrating motor complex. Segmentation is nonpropagating and belongs to the fed state. The gastrocolic reflex is triggered by a meal and acts on the colon. Receptive relaxation is a brief gastric event as food arrives and produces no traveling contraction.

questions.q: A volunteer eats a meal partway through a fasting motility recording. What happens to the migrating motor complex?
options: Its cycle length lengthens to about four hours but it continues
It is unchanged, since it is driven by an intrinsic clock
It is abolished and replaced by the fed pattern of segmentation
It becomes stronger and faster to move the meal along
questions.why: Feeding switches the tract from the fasting sweeping pattern to the fed mixing pattern, and the migrating motor complex does not resume until the meal has been cleared. Strengthening it would defeat the purpose of holding a meal in place long enough to digest and absorb it. The cycle does not simply slow, and it is not immune to feeding, since it is under hormonal and neural control including motilin.
questions.answerText: It is abolished and replaced by the fed pattern of segmentation

questions.q: Plasma motilin rises during a fast. What does this predict?
options: Contraction of the gallbladder and release of pancreatic enzymes
Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
Onset of a migrating motor complex
A burst of segmentation in the jejunum
questions.why: Motilin peaks cyclically during fasting and initiates phase III of the migrating motor complex, which is why motilin receptor agonists speed gastric emptying. Segmentation is the fed pattern and is not motilin driven. Gallbladder contraction and enzyme release are cholecystokinin effects triggered by fat and protein in the duodenum. Lower esophageal sphincter relaxation is a swallow triggered vagal event.
questions.answerText: Onset of a migrating motor complex

questions.q: If interstitial cells of Cajal were selectively destroyed in a segment of small intestine, what would you predict?
options: Normal motility, since smooth muscle sets its own rhythm from the myenteric plexus
Faster transit because the pacemaker no longer restrains contraction
Sustained maximal contraction of that segment
Loss of the rhythmic slow wave and uncoordinated, ineffective contractions
questions.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal set the underlying electrical rhythm, so without them the smooth muscle loses its coordinated timing and contractions become weak and disorganized rather than propulsive. Sustained contraction would require continuous excitation, which is the opposite of losing the pacemaker. The myenteric plexus modulates the rhythm but does not generate it. Removing a pacemaker slows and disorders motility rather than speeding it.
questions.answerText: Loss of the rhythmic slow wave and uncoordinated, ineffective contractions

questions.q: Why does segmentation improve absorption even though it moves contents forward very slowly?
options: It increases the surface area of the mucosa by stretching the villi out flat
It repeatedly brings fresh chyme against the brush border and mixes it with enzymes
It raises luminal pressure so that nutrients are forced through the epithelium directly
It speeds transit so that more chyme passes the absorptive surface each minute
questions.why: Absorption is limited by contact between nutrients and the transporters on the microvilli, and segmentation keeps replacing the depleted layer next to the mucosa with fresh chyme. Villi are not flattened by segmentation, and flattening would reduce surface area rather than increase it. Luminal pressure does not force nutrients across the membrane; transporters do. Speeding transit is what segmentation specifically does not do.
questions.answerText: It repeatedly brings fresh chyme against the brush border and mixes it with enzymes

questions.q: A drug increases the frequency of segmentation contractions in the small intestine without affecting peristalsis. Predict the effect on intestinal transit time.
options: Transit speeds up, because more contractions mean more propulsion
Transit is unchanged, because segmentation does not affect movement at all
Transit reverses, because segmentation pushes contents proximally
Transit slows, because segmentation resists net forward movement
questions.why: Segmentation is effectively a series of temporary dams, so more of it holds chyme in place longer and lengthens transit time, which is why antidiarrheal strategies aim to increase segmenting activity. More contractions do not mean more propulsion when the contractions are nonprogressive. Segmentation does affect net movement, just in the retarding direction, and it does not drive contents backward.
questions.answerText: Transit slows, because segmentation resists net forward movement

questions.q: A patient loses the migrating motor complex after nerve damage. Predict the sequence that leads to symptoms of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
options: Gastric acid secretion falls, so swallowed bacteria survive and colonize the stomach and duodenum
Peristalsis reverses, so colonic bacteria are pumped backward through the ileocecal valve
Segmentation stops, so chyme is never mixed with enzymes and passes on undigested
Residue and bacteria are not swept distally, so counts rise and bacteria ferment nutrients first
questions.why: The migrating motor complex is the mechanical defense that keeps bacterial counts low in the small intestine, so losing it allows colonization, and those bacteria consume nutrients and deconjugate bile salts before the host can absorb them. Segmentation is a separate fed pattern and continues normally. Acid secretion is a chemical defense that is unaffected by loss of a motility pattern. Peristalsis does not reverse, and the ileocecal valve resists retrograde flow.
questions.answerText: Residue and bacteria are not swept distally, so counts rise and bacteria ferment nutrients first

questions.q: In achalasia the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax during swallowing and esophageal peristalsis is absent. Predict what happens to a swallowed bolus and why.
options: It is ground into smaller particles by sustained esophageal contraction and then absorbed
It passes normally, because gravity alone is sufficient to move it in an upright person
It accumulates in the esophagus, because neither the wave nor the sphincter opens
It is propelled into the stomach but then refluxes back, because the sphincter stays open
questions.why: Swallowing normally combines a propagated peristaltic wave with receptive relaxation of the sphincter ahead of it, and achalasia removes both, so the bolus is stuck above a closed sphincter. Gravity moves liquids somewhat but cannot substitute for peristalsis with solids or when the sphincter will not open. Reflux requires a sphincter that opens too easily, which is the opposite problem. The esophagus does not digest or absorb food.
questions.answerText: It accumulates in the esophagus, because neither the wave nor the sphincter opens

questions.q: An opioid drug reduces propulsive motility in the colon. Trace the two steps that lead to hard, dry stool.
options: Water absorption in the colon is directly blocked, so stool loses its water to evaporation
Colonic secretion increases, so more electrolytes are lost and stool becomes hard
Transit slows, so residue spends longer in the colon, and more water is absorbed from it
Segmentation stops, so chyme is never mixed and arrives at the rectum undigested
questions.why: Colonic water absorption is time dependent, so any slowing of transit means the residue is exposed to the absorptive epithelium longer and leaves with less water. Increased secretion would soften stool, not harden it. Digestion is complete before the colon, so mixing failure there is not the mechanism. Nothing evaporates from a sealed lumen; the water is absorbed into blood.
questions.answerText: Transit slows, so residue spends longer in the colon, and more water is absorbed from it

questions.q: Two manometry tracings are described. Tracing A shows a pressure peak that appears at successive sensors down the intestine at a steady speed. Tracing B shows peaks at alternating sensors that come and go without traveling. Classify each and predict which produces faster transit.
options: A is peristalsis and B is segmentation, and A produces faster transit
Both are peristalsis, and B produces faster transit because more sensors fire
A is segmentation and B is peristalsis, and A produces faster transit
A is peristalsis and B is segmentation, and B produces faster transit
questions.why: A traveling pressure wave that reaches sensors in sequence is peristalsis and moves contents along, while nonprogressive alternating peaks are segmentation, which mixes and retards transit. Reversing the labels misses that the defining feature of peristalsis is propagation in space and time. More sensors firing does not mean faster movement when the activity does not propagate; that is precisely why segmentation slows things down.
questions.answerText: A is peristalsis and B is segmentation, and A produces faster transit

questions.q: Which cells of the gastric mucosa secrete gastrin?
options: Parietal cells
G cells
I cells
S cells
questions.why: G cells in the gastric antrum release gastrin into the blood in response to peptides and distension. Parietal cells are the target of gastrin, not its source, and they secrete acid and intrinsic factor. I cells and S cells sit in the duodenal mucosa and release cholecystokinin and secretin respectively.

questions.q: What is the principal action of gastrin?
options: It stimulates insulin release before glucose is absorbed
It increases pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
It increases gastric acid secretion
It causes the gallbladder to contract
questions.why: Gastrin drives the parietal cell to secrete HCl, both directly and by stimulating histamine release from enterochromaffin like cells, and it also promotes gastric motility and mucosal growth. Pancreatic bicarbonate is the secretin response. Gallbladder contraction is a cholecystokinin effect. Anticipatory insulin release is the job of glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide.

questions.q: Which cells release secretin, and what stimulus triggers it?
options: K cells of the duodenum, in response to glucose arriving in chyme
G cells of the antrum, in response to peptides in the gastric lumen
I cells of the duodenum, in response to fatty acids and amino acids
S cells of the duodenum, in response to acid arriving from the stomach
questions.why: S cells sense the drop in duodenal pH as acidic chyme arrives and release secretin, which is why secretin is often called the acid hormone. G cells respond to peptides and release gastrin. I cells respond to fat and protein and release cholecystokinin. K cells respond to glucose and release glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide.
questions.answerText: S cells of the duodenum, in response to acid arriving from the stomach

questions.q: What is the principal action of secretin?
options: It stimulates the stomach to empty faster
It stimulates the pancreatic acinar cells to secrete their digestive enzymes
It stimulates the pancreatic duct cells to secrete a bicarbonate rich fluid
It stimulates the parietal cells to secrete more acid
questions.why: Secretin targets duct cells, which pour out bicarbonate that neutralizes acidic chyme and brings duodenal pH into the range pancreatic enzymes need. Enzyme secretion from acinar cells is the cholecystokinin response. Secretin actually inhibits acid secretion and slows gastric emptying, which makes sense as negative feedback on the very stimulus that released it.
questions.answerText: It stimulates the pancreatic duct cells to secrete a bicarbonate rich fluid

questions.q: Which cells release cholecystokinin, and what stimulus triggers it?
options: S cells of the duodenum, in response to a fall in luminal pH
G cells of the antrum, in response to distension of the stomach wall
D cells of the antrum, in response to acid in the gastric lumen
I cells of the duodenum, in response to fatty acids and amino acids
questions.why: I cells detect the products of fat and protein digestion in the duodenal lumen and release cholecystokinin, which then arranges for more of the enzymes and bile those nutrients require. S cells respond to acid with secretin. G cells respond to distension and peptides with gastrin. D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits rather than stimulates.
questions.answerText: I cells of the duodenum, in response to fatty acids and amino acids

questions.q: Which pair of effects belongs to cholecystokinin?
options: Insulin release and inhibition of glucagon
Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and gastric acid secretion
Pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction
Gastric acid secretion and gastric mucosal growth
questions.why: Cholecystokinin acts on pancreatic acinar cells to release enzymes and on the gallbladder smooth muscle to contract while the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, delivering both enzymes and bile to a fatty meal. Bicarbonate secretion is secretin's job. Acid secretion and mucosal growth belong to gastrin. Insulin release with anticipation of a meal belongs to glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide.
questions.answerText: Pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction

questions.q: What is the main metabolic action of glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide?
options: It stimulates bile salt synthesis in the liver
It stimulates insulin release from the pancreatic beta cells
It stimulates glucagon release from the pancreatic alpha cells
It stimulates bicarbonate release from pancreatic duct cells
questions.why: Glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide is an incretin: released by K cells when glucose is in the duodenum, it primes the beta cell so insulin rises before blood glucose does. It does not act on alpha cells to raise glucagon, which would oppose its purpose. Duct cell bicarbonate is secretin's action, and bile salt synthesis in the liver is not under gut hormone control in this way.
questions.answerText: It stimulates insulin release from the pancreatic beta cells

questions.q: What defines a short reflex in the digestive tract?
options: The reflex uses a circulating hormone rather than a nerve to reach its target
The reflex has a short latency but still passes through the vagus nerve to the brainstem
The entire reflex arc, from receptor to effector, lies within the enteric nervous system
The reflex travels through the spinal cord but does not reach the brainstem
questions.why: A short reflex is handled entirely by the gut's own neurons, which is why an isolated segment of intestine still shows coordinated peristalsis. A long reflex is the one that leaves the gut for the central nervous system and returns, whether by spinal cord or brainstem. Hormonal signaling is a separate mechanism, not a reflex arc. Anything that passes through the vagus is by definition long.
questions.answerText: The entire reflex arc, from receptor to effector, lies within the enteric nervous system

questions.q: Acidic chyme with a pH of 2 enters the duodenum. Which hormone rises, and what does it accomplish?
options: Gastrin rises and drives more acid secretion to finish protein digestion
Secretin rises and drives bicarbonate secretion that raises duodenal pH
Cholecystokinin rises and drives bicarbonate secretion from acinar cells
Glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide rises and slows acid delivery
questions.why: Low duodenal pH is the specific stimulus for S cells, and the bicarbonate that secretin calls up neutralizes the acid, closing a negative feedback loop. More acid would worsen the problem, so a gastrin response here makes no physiological sense. Cholecystokinin responds to fat and protein and acts on acinar cells for enzymes, not duct cells for bicarbonate. Glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide responds to glucose and acts on the beta cell.
questions.answerText: Secretin rises and drives bicarbonate secretion that raises duodenal pH

questions.q: After a meal high in cream and meat, the gallbladder contracts and the pancreas releases lipase and trypsinogen. Which hormone is responsible?
options: Cholecystokinin
Motilin
Secretin
Gastrin
questions.why: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin, which contracts the gallbladder and stimulates acinar enzyme secretion, exactly the two things a fatty, proteinaceous meal needs. Secretin would supply bicarbonate instead. Gastrin acts back in the stomach on acid. Motilin drives the fasting migrating motor complex, not a fed response.

questions.q: A protein rich meal distends the stomach and raises luminal peptide concentration. Predict the immediate hormonal consequence and its effect.
options: Secretin release rises, so gastric emptying slows
Gastrin release rises, so acid secretion increases
Cholecystokinin release rises, so the gallbladder contracts
Somatostatin release rises, so acid secretion increases
questions.why: Peptides and distension in the stomach are the classic G cell stimuli, and the gastrin released raises acid output, which activates more pepsinogen and continues protein digestion. Secretin comes later, once acid reaches the duodenum. Cholecystokinin also comes later, once digestion products reach the duodenum. Somatostatin does inhibit acid, so the somatostatin choice pairs the right hormone with the wrong direction.
questions.answerText: Gastrin release rises, so acid secretion increases

questions.q: An oral glucose load produces a larger insulin response than an intravenous infusion that raises blood glucose by the same amount. What explains the difference?
options: Oral glucose is absorbed faster than an intravenous infusion reaches the beta cell
Gut hormones such as glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide amplify insulin release
Gastrin released by the meal acts directly on the beta cell to release insulin
Intravenous glucose is partly removed by the liver before it can reach the pancreas
questions.why: This is the incretin effect: K cells sense luminal glucose and release glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide, which potentiates the beta cell response so insulin rises more for the same blood glucose. Oral glucose is not faster than an intravenous infusion, which is delivered straight into the blood. Gastrin acts on the stomach, not the beta cell. Intravenous glucose enters the systemic circulation and is not subject to a first pass through the liver.
questions.answerText: Gut hormones such as glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide amplify insulin release

questions.q: Smelling and thinking about food causes vagal fibers to stimulate gastric secretion before any food is swallowed. Is this a short or a long reflex, and why?
options: A short reflex, because it acts entirely on the stomach and nowhere else
A long reflex, because the arc passes through the central nervous system
A short reflex, because no circulating hormone is involved in the response
A long reflex, because it takes longer than a minute to produce an effect
questions.why: The defining feature of a long reflex is that the signal leaves the gut for the brain or cord and returns by autonomic fibers, and a smell cannot be detected by the enteric nervous system at all. Where the reflex ends is irrelevant to the classification; what matters is where the integration happens. Absence of a hormone does not make a reflex short, and the naming has nothing to do with latency.
questions.answerText: A long reflex, because the arc passes through the central nervous system

questions.q: A drug blocks the gastrin receptor on the parietal cell. Predict the effect on gastric pH and on circulating gastrin.
options: Gastric pH rises and circulating gastrin rises
Gastric pH rises and circulating gastrin falls
Gastric pH falls and circulating gastrin rises
Gastric pH falls and circulating gastrin falls
questions.why: Blocking the receptor removes a major drive on acid secretion, so less HCl is made and luminal pH climbs. Antral G cells are inhibited by low pH, so when acid falls that brake is released and gastrin secretion actually rises, a pattern seen with any effective acid suppressing drug. The two options predicting falling pH have the direct effect backward, and the option predicting falling gastrin misses the loss of negative feedback.
questions.answerText: Gastric pH rises and circulating gastrin rises

questions.q: Besides stimulating bicarbonate secretion, secretin slows gastric emptying. How does this fit the logic of the response?
options: Slowing delivery of acid gives the duodenum time to neutralize what has already arrived
It prevents nutrients from reaching the duodenum before the enzymes are secreted there
It raises the pressure inside the stomach so that mixing becomes more effective
It allows more time for the stomach to finish digesting protein completely
questions.why: Secretin is released by acid, and both of its main effects, adding bicarbonate and reducing the acid load arriving, push duodenal pH back up. That double action is a good example of a hormone attacking a disturbance from two sides. Gastric protein digestion is not the variable being regulated here. Enzyme timing is cholecystokinin's concern, and raising gastric pressure is not a secretin effect at all.
questions.answerText: Slowing delivery of acid gives the duodenum time to neutralize what has already arrived

questions.q: A tumor secretes gastrin continuously and independently of pH. Predict the sequence of consequences in the duodenum, ending with an effect on fat digestion.
options: Acid output falls because the gastrin receptor desensitizes over time, and bile salts precipitate
Acid output rises, secretin falls because the feedback loop is bypassed, and enzyme secretion stops
Acid output rises, but the duodenum neutralizes the extra load easily, so fat digestion is normal
Acid output rises, duodenal pH stays low, and lipase is inactivated so fat is poorly digested
questions.why: Unregulated gastrin drives acid output far above the bicarbonate capacity of the pancreas and duodenum, so duodenal pH stays acidic and lipase, which needs a near neutral pH, is denatured, producing fat in the stool. The duodenum cannot easily neutralize an output several times normal. Receptor desensitization does not rescue this. Secretin actually rises rather than falls, because the acid stimulus is present continuously.
questions.answerText: Acid output rises, duodenal pH stays low, and lipase is inactivated so fat is poorly digested

questions.q: A patient has the vagal branches to the stomach cut. Predict the effect on the cephalic phase of acid secretion and on gastrin release during a meal.
options: Cephalic acid secretion is largely lost and meal stimulated gastrin release is reduced
Cephalic acid secretion is unchanged because it is driven by gastrin, and gastrin rises
Cephalic acid secretion is lost but gastrin rises sharply because acid falls
Both cephalic secretion and gastrin release are unchanged because local reflexes take over
questions.why: The vagus is the entire efferent limb of the cephalic phase, and it also releases gastrin releasing peptide onto G cells, so cutting it removes both direct parietal cell stimulation and much of the neural drive to gastrin. Gastrin is not the cephalic phase mediator, so the claim that gastrin drives the cephalic phase reverses cause and effect. Falling acid does disinhibit G cells, but with the vagal drive gone the net gastrin response to a meal is still blunted. Local reflexes maintain some gastric phase activity but cannot substitute for a signal that originates in the brain.
questions.answerText: Cephalic acid secretion is largely lost and meal stimulated gastrin release is reduced

questions.q: Antral D cells release somatostatin when luminal pH falls below about 3, and somatostatin inhibits G cells. A drug blocks somatostatin receptors on G cells. Predict what happens to gastrin and to gastric pH.
options: Gastrin rises because the brake is removed, and gastric pH falls
Gastrin rises and gastric pH also rises, because gastrin inhibits parietal cells at high concentration
Gastrin is unchanged because acid inhibits G cells directly rather than through somatostatin
Gastrin falls because D cells compensate by releasing more, and gastric pH rises
questions.why: Somatostatin is the negative feedback that shuts gastrin off once the stomach is acidic, so blocking its receptor leaves G cells firing and acid output climbs, dropping pH. More somatostatin cannot help when its receptor is blocked. Gastrin does not become inhibitory at high concentration; it is a straightforward stimulator. The main pathway by which acid restrains gastrin is exactly this D cell loop, so blocking it is not silent.
questions.answerText: Gastrin rises because the brake is removed, and gastric pH falls

questions.q: A meal of 40 percent fat empties from the stomach much more slowly than an isocaloric low fat meal. Trace the hormonal mechanism and state why the delay is useful.
options: Fat in the duodenum releases motilin, which halts the migrating motor complex and stops emptying
Fat in the stomach releases gastrin, which contracts the pylorus and holds the meal back longer
Fat in the duodenum releases secretin, which slows emptying so that acid can be neutralized first
Fat in the duodenum releases cholecystokinin, which slows emptying so the duodenum is not overloaded
questions.why: Fatty acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells, and cholecystokinin both calls up bile and enzymes and applies a brake on gastric emptying, matching the delivery rate to the slowest step in digestion. Gastrin responds to peptides and distension, not fat, and it promotes emptying rather than blocking it. Secretin does slow emptying, but its stimulus is acid, not fat. Motilin belongs to the fasting state and is suppressed by a meal.
questions.answerText: Fat in the duodenum releases cholecystokinin, which slows emptying so the duodenum is not overloaded

questions.q: What triggers the cephalic phase of digestive control?
options: Distension of the stomach wall as the swallowed meal arrives in it
The sight, smell, taste, or thought of food before it is swallowed
Arrival of acidic and fatty chyme in the duodenum
A rise in blood glucose after nutrients are absorbed
questions.why: The cephalic phase is anticipatory: signals from the head prepare the stomach before food arrives. Gastric distension starts the gastric phase. Acidic chyme in the duodenum starts the intestinal phase. A rise in blood glucose is a metabolic consequence of absorption, well after all three phases are underway.
questions.answerText: The sight, smell, taste, or thought of food before it is swallowed

questions.q: Which nerve carries the efferent signal of the cephalic phase to the stomach?
options: The greater splanchnic nerve
The vagus nerve
The phrenic nerve
The pelvic nerve
questions.why: The vagus is the parasympathetic outflow to the foregut and midgut and is the entire efferent limb of the cephalic phase, which is why cutting it abolishes anticipatory acid secretion. The greater splanchnic nerve is sympathetic and generally inhibits digestion. The phrenic nerve serves the diaphragm. The pelvic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers to the distal colon and rectum, not the stomach.

questions.q: What initiates the gastric phase of digestive control?
options: A fall in duodenal pH as acid crosses the pylorus
Fatty acids and amino acids arriving in the duodenal lumen
Distension of the stomach and peptides in the gastric lumen
The taste and smell of food while it is chewed
questions.why: Stretch receptors and chemoreceptors in the stomach wall respond to the arrival of the meal itself, launching local reflexes and gastrin release. Fatty acids in the duodenum and a fall in duodenal pH are intestinal phase stimuli. Taste belongs to the cephalic phase, which has already peaked by the time the meal is in the stomach.
questions.answerText: Distension of the stomach and peptides in the gastric lumen

questions.q: Which control mechanisms dominate the gastric phase?
options: Local short reflexes in the enteric nervous system plus gastrin
Secretin and cholecystokinin acting back on the stomach itself
Sympathetic inhibition of the myenteric nerve plexus
Long vagal reflexes originating in the brainstem alone
questions.why: Once food is in the stomach, stretch and chemical stimuli are handled largely by the gut's own circuits and by gastrin released into the blood, though vagovagal reflexes contribute as well. The cephalic phase is the one that runs purely on long vagal reflexes. Secretin and cholecystokinin are intestinal phase hormones. Sympathetic activity opposes digestion rather than driving a phase of it.
questions.answerText: Local short reflexes in the enteric nervous system plus gastrin

questions.q: What event begins the intestinal phase of digestive control?
options: Emptying of the gallbladder
The first mass movement in the colon
Chewing and swallowing the first bite
Chyme entering the duodenum
questions.why: The intestinal phase begins when partly digested chyme crosses the pylorus and its acid, fat, and hypertonicity are sensed by the duodenal mucosa. Chewing belongs to the cephalic phase. Gallbladder emptying is a consequence of the intestinal phase, not its trigger. Colonic mass movements are a separate reflex and occur far downstream.

questions.q: Overall, what is the dominant effect of the intestinal phase on the stomach?
options: Inhibition of gastric secretion and emptying
No net effect, since the phases act only on the intestine
Stimulation of gastric motility but inhibition of secretion
Strong stimulation of gastric acid secretion
questions.why: Once chyme is in the duodenum the priority shifts to protecting the small intestine from being overloaded, so the enterogastric reflex plus secretin and cholecystokinin slow gastric emptying and reduce acid output. There is a brief early stimulatory component, but the sustained effect is inhibitory. The phase very much acts on the stomach, which is what makes it a feedback loop rather than a local event.
questions.answerText: Inhibition of gastric secretion and emptying

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of the acid secreted in response to a meal comes from the gastric phase?
options: Nearly all of it
About five percent
About twenty percent
About half to sixty percent
questions.why: The gastric phase supplies the largest share, roughly 50 to 60 percent, with the cephalic phase contributing about 30 percent and the intestinal phase only a small stimulatory fraction near 5 to 10 percent. Five percent is the intestinal phase share, and twenty percent understates the gastric contribution. Saying nearly all of it would leave no room for the substantial anticipatory response that survives even sham feeding.

questions.q: What is the enterogastric reflex?
options: A reflex in which gastric distension increases colonic motility
A reflex in which acid in the stomach stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate
A reflex in which chewing triggers salivary and gastric secretion
A reflex in which duodenal stimuli inhibit gastric secretion and motility
questions.why: The name reads in the direction of the signal: from the intestine back to the stomach, applying a brake when the duodenum is full, acidic, fatty, or hypertonic. Gastric distension increasing colonic motility is the gastrocolic reflex. Acid stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate is a hormonal response through secretin, not a named reflex. Chewing triggering secretion is the cephalic phase.
questions.answerText: A reflex in which duodenal stimuli inhibit gastric secretion and motility

questions.q: A volunteer chews and spits out food without swallowing any of it, and gastric acid secretion still rises measurably. Which phase is this, and what mediates it?
options: The gastric phase, mediated by gastrin
The cephalic phase, mediated by vagal efferents
The intestinal phase, mediated by cholecystokinin
The gastric phase, mediated by local stretch reflexes
questions.why: Sham feeding isolates the cephalic phase, since nothing reaches the stomach to distend it or supply peptides, and the response depends entirely on vagal outflow. Gastrin release does contribute, but only because the vagus stimulates G cells, so the initiating mediator is neural. Cholecystokinin requires nutrients in the duodenum, which never happens here. Stretch reflexes require a meal in the stomach.
questions.answerText: The cephalic phase, mediated by vagal efferents

questions.q: A meal of steak sits in the stomach, distending the wall and releasing peptides. Which phase is active, and what is the main consequence?
options: The cephalic phase, and salivation increases
The gastric phase, and acid and pepsinogen secretion rise
The intestinal phase, and gastric emptying slows
The gastric phase, and pancreatic bicarbonate secretion rises
questions.why: Distension and peptides are the defining gastric phase stimuli, and the response is more acid from parietal cells and more pepsinogen from chief cells, which continues protein digestion. Salivation belongs to the cephalic phase. Slowed emptying is the intestinal phase brake, which will follow once chyme crosses the pylorus. Pancreatic bicarbonate is a secretin response to acid already in the duodenum.
questions.answerText: The gastric phase, and acid and pepsinogen secretion rise

questions.q: Chyme with a pH of 2 and a high fat content arrives in the duodenum. Predict the effect on the rate of gastric emptying and name the phase.
options: Emptying slows, in the cephalic phase
Emptying speeds up, in the gastric phase
Emptying slows, in the intestinal phase
Emptying speeds up, in the intestinal phase
questions.why: Acid and fat in the duodenum are the two strongest signals for the enterogastric reflex and for secretin and cholecystokinin, all of which restrain the pylorus so the duodenum is not overwhelmed. Speeding emptying under those conditions would deliver more acid and fat than the duodenum could neutralize or emulsify. The cephalic phase has ended by this point, and the gastric phase concerns stimuli inside the stomach.
questions.answerText: Emptying slows, in the intestinal phase

questions.q: Why does the intestinal phase inhibit gastric emptying rather than simply increasing intestinal secretion?
options: Because the stomach cannot secrete acid and empty its contents at the same time in one phase
Because the duodenum can only process chyme at a limited rate, so intake must match that rate
Because inhibiting emptying is the only available way to raise duodenal pH
Because pancreatic enzymes are destroyed if chyme is delivered to them too slowly
questions.why: The intestinal phase is fundamentally a rate matching problem: bicarbonate, enzymes, and bile arrive at a finite rate, so the meal has to be metered out to stay within that capacity. The stomach can and does secrete while emptying. Raising duodenal pH also happens through bicarbonate secretion, so slowing delivery is not the only route. Slow delivery does not destroy enzymes; rapid delivery of acid is what inactivates them.
questions.answerText: Because the duodenum can only process chyme at a limited rate, so intake must match that rate

questions.q: Receptive relaxation allows the stomach to accept a large meal with little rise in pressure. Which phase and mechanism does it belong to?
options: The gastric phase, through a local myenteric reflex
The cephalic phase, through a vagovagal reflex
The intestinal phase, through cholecystokinin
The gastric phase, through gastrin
questions.why: Swallowing triggers a vagovagal reflex that relaxes the gastric fundus before food arrives, which is why volume can rise sharply without much pressure change. A local myenteric reflex cannot anticipate food that has not arrived. Cholecystokinin acts later and mainly on the pancreas and gallbladder. Gastrin increases secretion and motility rather than producing relaxation.
questions.answerText: The cephalic phase, through a vagovagal reflex

questions.q: A drug abolishes all vagal activity to the gut. Which phase is most reduced, and which is least affected?
options: The cephalic phase is most reduced and the intestinal phase is least affected
The intestinal phase is most reduced and the gastric phase is least affected
All three are reduced equally, since the vagus mediates all of them
The gastric phase is most reduced and the cephalic phase is least affected
questions.why: The cephalic phase has no mechanism other than vagal outflow, so it is essentially eliminated, while the intestinal phase relies heavily on hormones in the blood and on local reflexes that survive vagal loss. The gastric phase falls somewhere between, since it uses both local reflexes and gastrin. The phases are not equally vagal, which is exactly what makes this a useful distinction.
questions.answerText: The cephalic phase is most reduced and the intestinal phase is least affected

questions.q: A patient has a surgical vagotomy. Predict what happens to the cephalic phase, then to total meal stimulated acid output, and explain why the gastric phase is not abolished.
options: All three phases are lost, because the vagus is what initiates each one of them in sequence
The cephalic phase is lost and acid output falls, but the gastric phase persists on local reflexes and gastrin
The cephalic phase is lost but total acid output is unchanged, because the gastric phase compensates for it fully
The cephalic phase is unchanged because it is hormonally driven, and only the gastric phase is lost
questions.why: Removing the vagus takes out the entire anticipatory limb, so roughly a third of the acid response disappears, but distension and peptides still drive enteric reflexes and G cells, so the stomach still responds to a meal. Full compensation would make vagotomy useless as an acid reducing operation, which historically it was not. The cephalic phase is neural, not hormonal, which is why it is the phase most vulnerable to this lesion.
questions.answerText: The cephalic phase is lost and acid output falls, but the gastric phase persists on local reflexes and gastrin

questions.q: After surgery that removes the pylorus, a meal empties into the jejunum almost immediately. Explain, using the phases, why the patient feels lightheaded and has cramping shortly after eating.
options: The cephalic phase is exaggerated, so excess acid reaches the jejunum and irritates the mucosa
The gastric phase is prolonged, so the meal is overdigested before it ever leaves the stomach
The intestinal phase brake is bypassed, so a hypertonic load enters at once and draws in fluid
The intestinal phase is exaggerated, so too much bicarbonate is secreted and the blood becomes alkaline
questions.why: The intestinal phase normally meters delivery to match the duodenum's capacity, and losing the pylorus removes that regulation, so a concentrated meal pulls plasma water into the gut, causing distension, cramps, and a fall in circulating volume. The cephalic phase is unchanged by the surgery. The gastric phase is shortened, not prolonged, because the meal leaves at once. Bicarbonate secretion does not run away in this setting and would not produce cramping.
questions.answerText: The intestinal phase brake is bypassed, so a hypertonic load enters at once and draws in fluid

questions.q: During a meal, gastrin rises early and then falls even though food is still in the stomach. Explain the two mechanisms behind the fall.
options: The vagus fatigues, so the cephalic drive to the G cells fails after about ten minutes
The G cells are depleted of stored gastrin and cannot secrete more until they resynthesize it
Accumulating acid triggers D cell somatostatin, and duodenal chyme triggers the intestinal brake
Rising blood glucose after absorption directly inhibits the G cells of the antrum
questions.why: Two negative feedback loops close during a meal: the falling luminal pH turns on antral D cells whose somatostatin silences G cells, and duodenal signals inhibit gastric activity as a whole. Depletion is not the limiting factor; secretion is regulated, not exhausted. Blood glucose has no direct action on G cells. Vagal fibers do not fatigue on that timescale, and the cephalic phase ends because the stimulus ends, not because the nerve fails.
questions.answerText: Accumulating acid triggers D cell somatostatin, and duodenal chyme triggers the intestinal brake

questions.q: Two people eat the same meal. One is given a drug that blocks duodenal fat receptors. Predict the difference in gastric emptying rate and in duodenal pH at 30 minutes.
options: The treated person empties faster and has a lower duodenal pH
The treated person empties more slowly and has a higher duodenal pH
The treated person empties faster and has a higher duodenal pH
There is no difference, since acid rather than fat controls emptying
questions.why: Blocking the fat signal removes a major part of the intestinal phase brake, so the stomach empties faster and delivers acid to the duodenum more quickly than bicarbonate secretion can neutralize it, driving pH down. Slower emptying would require adding a brake rather than removing one. Faster delivery of acid cannot raise duodenal pH. Acid is one control signal, but fat is at least as powerful, so blocking it is not silent.
questions.answerText: The treated person empties faster and has a lower duodenal pH

questions.q: Which gastric cell secretes hydrochloric acid?
options: The parietal cell
The mucous neck cell
The enterochromaffin like cell
The chief cell
questions.why: Parietal cells, also called oxyntic cells, contain the H+/K+ ATPase that pumps protons into the lumen, and they also make intrinsic factor. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen. Mucous neck cells secrete the mucus and bicarbonate of the protective barrier. Enterochromaffin like cells release histamine, which stimulates the parietal cell but does not itself secrete acid.

questions.q: Which pump moves H+ across the apical membrane of the parietal cell into the gastric lumen?
options: The Na+/H+ exchanger
The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger
The Na+/K+ ATPase
The H+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: The H+/K+ ATPase, the proton pump, exchanges luminal K+ for cytoplasmic H+ using ATP directly, and it is the final common step that drugs called proton pump inhibitors block. The Na+/K+ ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane and maintains the Na+ gradient for other transport. The Na+/H+ exchanger handles pH regulation in many cells but is not the acid secreting pump here. The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger is basolateral and produces the alkaline tide.

questions.q: Which enzyme inside the parietal cell generates the H+ used for acid secretion?
options: Pepsinogen
Carbonic anhydrase
Enteropeptidase
Alcohol dehydrogenase
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 and water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ for secretion and HCO3- that leaves across the basolateral membrane. Pepsinogen is the inactive protein digesting enzyme secreted by chief cells. Enteropeptidase is a duodenal brush border enzyme that activates trypsinogen. Alcohol dehydrogenase in gastric mucosa metabolizes ethanol and has nothing to do with acid production.

questions.q: What is the alkaline tide?
options: The rise in gastric luminal pH during the interval between meals
The rise in venous blood pH as parietal cells export HCO3- during secretion
The rise in duodenal pH once pancreatic bicarbonate arrives from the duct
The layer of alkaline mucus that covers the gastric epithelium
questions.why: For every H+ pumped into the lumen, one HCO3- leaves the parietal cell into the blood on a Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, so blood draining the stomach becomes transiently alkaline after a meal. Luminal pH between meals is a different variable entirely. Duodenal neutralization is real but comes from the pancreas, not from parietal cell bicarbonate. The alkaline mucus layer is part of the barrier, not the tide.
questions.answerText: The rise in venous blood pH as parietal cells export HCO3- during secretion

questions.q: Which cells secrete pepsinogen?
options: D cells
G cells
Parietal cells
Chief cells
questions.why: Chief cells, in the base of the gastric glands, release pepsinogen, which is converted to active pepsin by acid. G cells secrete the hormone gastrin into blood. Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor. D cells release somatostatin, the local inhibitor of acid secretion.

questions.q: Which gastric secretion is required for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the ileum?
options: Gastric lipase
Mucus
Pepsinogen
Intrinsic factor
questions.why: Intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds B12 and is recognized by a receptor in the terminal ileum, and it is the only gastric product whose loss cannot be compensated for elsewhere. Pepsinogen contributes to protein digestion. Gastric lipase makes a modest contribution to fat digestion. Mucus protects the epithelium but has no role in B12 uptake.

questions.q: Which two substances make up the physical and chemical layers of the gastric mucosal barrier?
options: Mucus and bicarbonate
Pepsin and intrinsic factor
Histamine and gastrin
Bile salts and phospholipid
questions.why: Surface and mucous neck cells secrete a viscous mucus gel that traps a bicarbonate rich fluid, so the pH at the epithelial surface stays near neutral while the lumen sits near pH 2. Pepsin actively attacks the epithelium if the barrier fails, so it is a threat, not a defense. Histamine and gastrin stimulate acid secretion. Bile salts and phospholipid belong to bile and are among the substances that can damage the gastric barrier.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of gastric juice at peak secretion?
options: About 8
About 1.5 to 2
About 4 to 5
About 6.8
questions.why: Peak parietal cell output brings luminal pH down to roughly 1.5 to 2, which denatures proteins and activates pepsinogen. A pH of 4 to 5 is closer to what a partially buffered stomach shows during a large meal. About 6.8 is roughly the pH of saliva and of resting duodenal contents. About 8 is the pH of pancreatic juice, which is what neutralizes this acid downstream.

questions.q: A drug irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase. Predict the effect on gastric pH and on pepsin activity.
options: Gastric pH is unchanged because histamine bypasses the pump
Gastric pH rises and pepsin activity falls
Gastric pH rises and pepsin activity rises
Gastric pH falls and pepsin activity falls
questions.why: The proton pump is the final common step for all three stimulatory pathways, so blocking it raises luminal pH regardless of how the cell is stimulated. Pepsinogen requires an acid environment both to be converted to pepsin and for pepsin to work, so activity falls with the acid. Histamine acts upstream on the parietal cell receptor and cannot bypass a blocked pump.
questions.answerText: Gastric pH rises and pepsin activity falls

questions.q: A drug blocks the H2 histamine receptor on the parietal cell. Why does this reduce acid secretion even though gastrin and acetylcholine receptors are untouched?
options: Blocking the H2 receptor also destroys the H+/K+ ATPase in the membrane
Histamine normally inhibits acid secretion, so blocking it should raise acid instead
Histamine is the only stimulus that the parietal cell can respond to at all
Histamine from enterochromaffin like cells amplifies gastrin and acetylcholine signals
questions.why: Much of gastrin's effect is indirect, working through histamine release from enterochromaffin like cells, so removing the histamine arm blunts the whole system rather than just one third of it. Histamine is not the only stimulus, since acetylcholine and gastrin act directly as well. H2 blockade does not damage the pump; it reduces the signal that activates it. Histamine is stimulatory, not inhibitory, at the parietal cell.
questions.answerText: Histamine from enterochromaffin like cells amplifies gastrin and acetylcholine signals

questions.q: Long term use of a nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drug inhibits prostaglandin synthesis in the gastric mucosa. Predict the effect on the mucosal barrier.
options: Intrinsic factor secretion falls, so the epithelium loses its own protective coating
Acid secretion rises sharply while the mucosal barrier itself is unchanged
Mucus and bicarbonate secretion fall and mucosal blood flow falls, weakening defense
Pepsinogen secretion rises, so the epithelium is digested from the inside out
questions.why: Prostaglandins are the main local promoters of mucus and bicarbonate secretion and of the mucosal blood flow that carries away back diffusing acid, so blocking them leaves the epithelium exposed. The primary lesion is defensive failure rather than acid excess, though the acid present then does the damage. Pepsinogen output is not driven up by these drugs. Intrinsic factor has no barrier function.
questions.answerText: Mucus and bicarbonate secretion fall and mucosal blood flow falls, weakening defense

questions.q: Helicobacter pylori produces urease, which converts urea to ammonia. How does this help the bacterium survive and harm the stomach?
options: Ammonia binds intrinsic factor and prevents any vitamin B12 from being absorbed
Ammonia buffers acid around the organism and is toxic to the surface epithelium
Ammonia is an enzyme that digests the mucus layer of the barrier directly
Ammonia raises luminal pH enough to activate pepsin fully in the lumen
questions.why: The alkaline cloud of ammonia lets the organism live in a niche that would otherwise kill it, while the same ammonia and the associated inflammation damage surface cells and undermine the mucus and bicarbonate barrier. Ammonia is a small molecule, not an enzyme. Pepsin is activated by acid, not by alkalinization, so raising pH would reduce pepsin activity. Intrinsic factor is not the target here.
questions.answerText: Ammonia buffers acid around the organism and is toxic to the surface epithelium

questions.q: Pepsinogen is secreted in an inactive form. What converts it to active pepsin, and why does this matter for a patient on a proton pump inhibitor?
options: Enteropeptidase converts it, so suppression of acid has no effect on it
Acid converts it, so protein digestion in the stomach falls when acid is suppressed
Trypsin converts it, so it depends on pancreatic function rather than gastric pH
Bile salts convert it, so it depends on gallbladder emptying
questions.why: Low pH cleaves pepsinogen to pepsin and is also required for pepsin to be catalytically active, so raising gastric pH removes both steps. Enteropeptidase acts on trypsinogen in the duodenum, a different zymogen entirely. Trypsin activates other pancreatic zymogens, not pepsinogen. Bile salts emulsify fat and have no activating role for gastric enzymes. In practice, pancreatic proteases compensate well, so protein malnutrition is not a usual consequence.
questions.answerText: Acid converts it, so protein digestion in the stomach falls when acid is suppressed

questions.q: Strong alcohol strips the adherent mucus gel from a patch of gastric epithelium. Predict what happens to the pH at the epithelial surface and why that matters.
options: Surface pH falls, but this is harmless because gastric cells are acid resistant by themselves
Surface pH falls toward the luminal value of about 2, so acid and pepsin reach the cells directly
Surface pH rises toward 7, because bicarbonate is no longer trapped and diffuses freely inward
Surface pH is unchanged, because the tight junctions set the pH at the cell surface
questions.why: The mucus gel works by trapping bicarbonate against the epithelium, holding surface pH near 7 while the lumen sits near 2, so removing the gel collapses that gradient. Bicarbonate that is no longer trapped is simply washed into the lumen and neutralized, so surface pH cannot rise. Tight junctions limit paracellular leak but do not create a pH gradient. Gastric epithelial cells are not intrinsically acid proof; the barrier is what protects them, which is why barrier failure produces ulcers.
questions.answerText: Surface pH falls toward the luminal value of about 2, so acid and pepsin reach the cells directly

questions.q: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is given. Predict the effect on parietal cell acid output and explain the mechanism.
options: Acid output rises, because HCO3- can no longer leave the cell at all
Acid output falls, because the cell cannot generate H+ from CO2 and water
Acid output is unchanged, because the H+ comes from acid in the diet
Acid output falls, because the H+/K+ ATPase itself is destroyed by the drug
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase is the source of the H+ that the pump exports, so slowing it starves the pump of substrate. Bicarbonate exit is coupled to the same reaction, so it falls too rather than accumulating and driving secretion. The H+ is generated inside the cell from CO2 and water, not absorbed from the diet. The pump protein itself is intact; it simply has less H+ available.
questions.answerText: Acid output falls, because the cell cannot generate H+ from CO2 and water

questions.q: A patient takes a proton pump inhibitor for a year. Predict what happens to serum gastrin and explain the loop, then state what would happen to acid output if the drug were stopped abruptly.
options: Gastrin rises because low acid removes somatostatin inhibition, and stopping causes rebound acid
Gastrin rises because the drug stimulates G cells directly, and stopping the drug lowers acid below normal
Gastrin is unchanged, because G cells respond only to peptides and not to luminal pH
Gastrin falls because the parietal cell no longer signals the G cell, and stopping the drug changes nothing
questions.why: Antral D cells release somatostatin when luminal pH is low, so suppressing acid lifts that brake and gastrin climbs, which over months also increases parietal cell mass. When the drug is withdrawn, a high gastrin level acting on an expanded parietal cell population produces more acid than before, the rebound effect. G cells are sensitive to luminal pH, which is exactly what makes this loop work, and the drug acts on the parietal cell pump, not on G cells.
questions.answerText: Gastrin rises because low acid removes somatostatin inhibition, and stopping causes rebound acid

questions.q: A person takes daily aspirin and is also colonized with Helicobacter pylori. Explain why the combination is more likely to produce an ulcer than either factor alone.
options: Aspirin removes prostaglandin driven defense while the organism injures the epithelium
Both increase mucus production, which traps the bacteria against the epithelium
Aspirin activates pepsinogen directly and the organism secretes a pepsin of its own
Both raise acid secretion, so the total acid load on the mucosa roughly doubles
questions.why: An ulcer forms when aggressive factors exceed defensive ones, and this pair attacks from both sides: the drug disables mucus, bicarbonate, and mucosal blood flow while the infection inflames the epithelium and, in antral disease, drives gastrin and acid up. Aspirin does not raise acid secretion, so the doubling explanation is wrong. Mucus production falls rather than rises. Neither factor secretes or activates pepsin directly.
questions.answerText: Aspirin removes prostaglandin driven defense while the organism injures the epithelium

questions.q: An immune attack destroys parietal cells over several years. Predict the changes in gastric pH, serum gastrin, and red blood cell size, and explain the link.
options: Gastric pH rises, gastrin rises because acid no longer inhibits G cells, and red cells enlarge
Gastric pH falls, gastrin rises, and red cells become larger because of iron deficiency
Gastric pH rises, gastrin is unchanged, and red cell size is entirely unchanged
Gastric pH rises, gastrin falls because there are fewer target cells, and red cells become smaller
questions.why: Loss of parietal cells removes both acid and intrinsic factor, so pH climbs, G cells escape the somatostatin brake and secrete more gastrin, and B12 uptake in the ileum fails, producing large immature red cells. Gastrin is regulated by luminal pH rather than by the number of target cells, so it rises rather than falls. Losing acid secreting cells cannot lower pH, and iron deficiency produces small red cells, not large ones.
questions.answerText: Gastric pH rises, gastrin rises because acid no longer inhibits G cells, and red cells enlarge

questions.q: A patient secretes acid at three times the normal maximal rate. Trace why an ulcer forms in the duodenum rather than in the stomach.
options: The stomach is protected because acid cannot damage the very cells that produce it
The acid load exceeds bicarbonate capacity, and the duodenum lacks the gastric mucus barrier
Duodenal cells secrete their own pepsin, which digests the mucosa when acid is high
Acid is concentrated by water absorption as it passes the pylorus, so it is stronger in the duodenum
questions.why: The stomach is built to sit in acid, with a mucus and bicarbonate barrier and rapid cell turnover, while the duodenum relies on incoming pancreatic bicarbonate for protection, so overwhelming that supply exposes an unprepared epithelium. Producing acid does not by itself confer immunity; the barrier does, and it can still fail. The duodenum does not secrete pepsin. No water is absorbed at the pylorus, and acid is diluted rather than concentrated as it enters the duodenum.
questions.answerText: The acid load exceeds bicarbonate capacity, and the duodenum lacks the gastric mucus barrier

questions.q: Which cells of the pancreas secrete the bicarbonate rich component of pancreatic juice?
options: Alpha cells of the islets
Acinar cells
Duct cells
Beta cells of the islets
questions.why: Duct cells respond to secretin by secreting a watery, bicarbonate rich fluid that carries the enzymes and neutralizes chyme. Acinar cells make the enzymes themselves under cholecystokinin control. Islet beta and alpha cells secrete insulin and glucagon into blood and have no exocrine duct at all.

questions.q: Which of the following is a pancreatic enzyme secreted as an inactive zymogen?
options: Trypsinogen
Pancreatic lipase
Ribonuclease
Pancreatic amylase
questions.why: The proteases are secreted as zymogens, trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase, so that they cannot digest the pancreas itself. Amylase, lipase, and the nucleases are secreted in active form because starch, fat, and nucleic acids are not structural components of the pancreatic cell in a way that would be attacked. Activation of trypsinogen in the duodenum is the switch that turns the whole proteolytic system on.

questions.q: Which enzyme activates trypsinogen, and where is it located?
options: Enteropeptidase, on the duodenal brush border
Carbonic anhydrase, inside the acinar cell
Amylase, in pancreatic juice
Pepsin, in the stomach lumen
questions.why: Enteropeptidase, also called enterokinase, is anchored to the duodenal brush border and cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the remaining zymogens including more trypsinogen. Putting the activator outside the pancreas is the safety feature. Pepsin works in the stomach on dietary protein. Carbonic anhydrase supplies bicarbonate in duct cells, and amylase digests starch.
questions.answerText: Enteropeptidase, on the duodenal brush border

questions.q: Which statement about the composition of bile is correct?
options: Bile is composed mainly of bicarbonate, amylase, and water from the duct cells
Bile contains bile salts and lipase, which together digest fat in the duodenum
Bile contains bile salts, phospholipid, cholesterol, and bilirubin, but no enzymes
Bile contains bile salts and trypsin, which together digest protein in the duodenum
questions.why: Bile is a secretion of amphipathic molecules and waste products, and its digestive contribution is physical rather than enzymatic. Every option that puts an enzyme in bile makes the same mistake: lipase and trypsin are pancreatic products. Bile does contain a bicarbonate rich fluid added by the bile ducts, but amylase is not part of it.
questions.answerText: Bile contains bile salts, phospholipid, cholesterol, and bilirubin, but no enzymes

questions.q: From what molecule does the liver synthesize bile salts?
options: Phospholipid
Bilirubin
Cholesterol
Triglyceride
questions.why: Hepatocytes convert cholesterol to bile acids, which are then conjugated with glycine or taurine to form bile salts, and this is one of the body's few routes for disposing of cholesterol. Bilirubin is a separate waste product from heme, excreted in bile but not a precursor of bile salts. Triglyceride and phospholipid are lipids in their own right, not bile salt precursors, though lecithin is secreted alongside bile salts.

questions.q: Bilirubin in bile is derived from the breakdown of which molecule?
options: Dietary protein absorbed in the jejunum
Cholesterol from hepatocytes
Heme from aged red blood cells
Bile salts recycled from the ileum
questions.why: Macrophages break heme down to bilirubin, which travels to the liver, is conjugated with glucuronic acid, and is excreted in bile, giving stool its color. Cholesterol is the precursor of bile salts, a different bile component. Recycled bile salts return to be resecreted unchanged, not converted to bilirubin. Dietary protein is not a source of bile pigment.
questions.answerText: Heme from aged red blood cells

questions.q: What does the gallbladder do to bile between meals?
options: It stores bile and concentrates it by absorbing water and ions
It synthesizes new bile salts from cholesterol
It adds pancreatic enzymes to bile before release
It dilutes bile so that it does not damage the duodenal mucosa
questions.why: Between meals the sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile backs up into the gallbladder, where the epithelium removes water and salts so the stored bile becomes several fold more concentrated. Synthesis of bile salts is a hepatocyte function. Pancreatic enzymes join bile only where the ducts merge near the duodenum. Bile is concentrated rather than diluted, and it does not need dilution to be safe.
questions.answerText: It stores bile and concentrates it by absorbing water and ions

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of pancreatic juice, and what does that pH accomplish?
options: About 8, which neutralizes acidic chyme and creates the range pancreatic enzymes need
About 8, which keeps the duodenum acidic enough for pepsin to keep on working there
About 2, which continues the acid digestion begun in the stomach
About 5, which mildly buffers chyme without changing enzyme activity
questions.why: Pancreatic juice is alkaline at roughly pH 8 because of its bicarbonate, and raising duodenal pH toward neutral both protects the mucosa and puts lipase and the proteases in their working range. A pH of 2 would be gastric juice, not pancreatic. A pH of 5 would neither protect the mucosa nor activate the enzymes properly. Pepsin is inactivated rather than helped by the rise in pH, which is the intended outcome.
questions.answerText: About 8, which neutralizes acidic chyme and creates the range pancreatic enzymes need

questions.q: Bile salts are described as emulsifiers rather than digestive enzymes. What is the difference in what they do to a triglyceride?
options: They break large fat droplets into many small ones without breaking a covalent bond
They convert triglyceride into phospholipid so that it can cross the membrane
They carry intact triglyceride across the enterocyte membrane into the cell
They cleave the ester bonds that hold the three fatty acids to the glycerol backbone
questions.why: Emulsification is a physical change: the amphipathic bile salt coats droplet surfaces and keeps them from coalescing, so lipase has far more surface to work on. Cleaving ester bonds is what lipase does, and confusing the two is the most common error on this topic. Bile salts do not convert one lipid class to another. Intact triglyceride is not absorbed; its digestion products are.
questions.answerText: They break large fat droplets into many small ones without breaking a covalent bond

questions.q: A patient secretes normal pancreatic enzymes but almost no bicarbonate. Predict the effect on fat digestion and explain why.
options: Protein digestion falls but fat digestion is preserved, because lipase is acid stable
Fat digestion is normal, because lipase does not depend on pH
Fat digestion falls, because low duodenal pH inactivates pancreatic lipase
Fat digestion rises, because acid emulsifies fat more effectively
questions.why: Pancreatic lipase is the most pH sensitive of the digestive enzymes and is irreversibly denatured below about pH 4, so bicarbonate failure produces fat malabsorption even when enzyme output is normal. Lipase is very much pH dependent, which is precisely why bicarbonate matters. Acid does not emulsify fat; bile salts do. Proteases are more acid tolerant than lipase, so fat is the first casualty, not the last.
questions.answerText: Fat digestion falls, because low duodenal pH inactivates pancreatic lipase

questions.q: A stone completely blocks the common bile duct. Predict the effect on fat in the stool and on stool color.
options: Fat in the stool decreases and the stool becomes pale
Fat in the stool increases and the stool becomes pale
Fat in the stool increases and the stool becomes dark
Fat in the stool is unchanged and the stool becomes pale
questions.why: Without bile salts the fat is poorly emulsified and poorly carried to the brush border in micelles, so it passes into the stool, and without bilirubin reaching the intestine the pigment that normally colors stool is missing. Darkening would require more pigment, not less. Fat absorption cannot be unchanged when the emulsifier and micelle carrier are both absent, and it certainly does not improve.
questions.answerText: Fat in the stool increases and the stool becomes pale

questions.q: Once a small amount of trypsin forms in the duodenum, protease activity rises rapidly. What explains the acceleration?
options: Trypsin stimulates the acinar cells to release a further burst of enzyme
Trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, and more trypsinogen
Enteropeptidase is released into the lumen and multiplies as it circulates
Acid from the stomach progressively activates the remaining zymogens there
questions.why: Trypsin is the master activator, converting the other zymogens and its own precursor, so a small trigger produces a large and rapid response. It does not feed back on acinar secretion to produce this effect. Enteropeptidase stays anchored to the brush border and does not multiply. Acid is neutralized in the duodenum and is not what activates pancreatic zymogens.
questions.answerText: Trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, and more trypsinogen

questions.q: Why are pancreatic proteases secreted as inactive precursors while amylase is secreted in active form?
options: Zymogens are more stable at the acidic pH found inside the pancreatic duct
Active proteases would digest the pancreas itself, while starch is not part of it
Amylase requires acid activation, which happens only in the gastric lumen
Proteases must first be concentrated in the gallbladder before they are able to act
questions.why: The pancreas is largely protein, so a protease released in active form would attack the gland, whereas amylase can only find substrate in the diet. Pancreatic duct fluid is alkaline, not acidic, so pH stability is not the reason. Amylase needs no activation step at all. Proteases never enter the gallbladder, which handles bile only.
questions.answerText: Active proteases would digest the pancreas itself, while starch is not part of it

questions.q: Secretin and cholecystokinin arrive at the pancreas together after a mixed meal. Which cell does each act on, and what is the combined result?
options: Secretin acts on duct cells and cholecystokinin on acinar cells, giving enzymes in alkali
Secretin acts on acinar cells and cholecystokinin on duct cells, producing acidic juice
Both act on the duct cells, so a large volume of enzyme free fluid is produced
Both act on the acinar cells, so total enzyme output roughly doubles
questions.why: The division of labor matters: secretin supplies the alkaline vehicle and cholecystokinin supplies the enzymes, and only together do they deliver active enzymes into a pH where those enzymes work. If both acted on acinar cells there would be enzymes with no way to reach a workable pH. Reversing the targets would produce the wrong secretion from each cell type, and two duct signals would give volume without catalytic activity.
questions.answerText: Secretin acts on duct cells and cholecystokinin on acinar cells, giving enzymes in alkali

questions.q: After the gallbladder is removed, bile flows continuously from the liver into the duodenum. Predict the effect on digestion of a very large fatty meal.
options: Fat digestion is somewhat impaired, because no concentrated bolus can be delivered
Fat digestion improves, because bile is now always present in the duodenum
Fat digestion is unaffected, because bile salts are not needed for very large meals
Fat digestion becomes impossible, because bile is made only in the gallbladder
questions.why: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile so a large amount can be delivered exactly when a fatty meal arrives, and without it the steady trickle is adequate for ordinary meals but may fall short for a large fat load. Bile is made by hepatocytes, not by the gallbladder, so digestion is not impossible. Continuous presence is not an advantage when the need is episodic and large. Bile salts are needed most, not least, for large fatty meals.
questions.answerText: Fat digestion is somewhat impaired, because no concentrated bolus can be delivered

questions.q: Chronic pancreatitis destroys most acinar and duct tissue. Trace the consequences for fat digestion and predict which vitamins become deficient.
options: Lipase and bicarbonate both fall, so fat is malabsorbed and vitamins A, D, E, and K are lost
Bile salt synthesis fails, so fat is emulsified but not absorbed and vitamin B12 becomes deficient
Fat digestion is preserved by gastric lipase alone, so only the water soluble vitamins are lost
Only protein digestion fails, since pancreatic amylase is replaced by salivary amylase and bile digests fat
questions.why: Losing the pancreas removes both the enzyme that cleaves triglyceride and the bicarbonate that protects it, so undigested fat carries the fat soluble vitamins into the stool. Bile does not digest fat, it emulsifies, so it cannot cover for lipase. Bile salt synthesis is a liver function and is unaffected here, and B12 depends on intrinsic factor and the ileum. Gastric lipase contributes only a small fraction and cannot maintain normal fat digestion.
questions.answerText: Lipase and bicarbonate both fall, so fat is malabsorbed and vitamins A, D, E, and K are lost

questions.q: A rare deficiency of enteropeptidase is found in an infant with normal pancreatic secretion. Predict which macronutrient is malabsorbed and explain the two step reason.
options: Protein, because trypsinogen is never activated and the other proteases follow it
Carbohydrate, because the brush border enzymes require enteropeptidase for anchoring
All three equally, because enteropeptidase activates every pancreatic zymogen directly
Fat, because lipase must be cleaved from colipase by trypsin before it works
questions.why: Enteropeptidase performs only one job, cleaving trypsinogen, but trypsin is the activator of the whole proteolytic cascade, so the single missing step disables protein digestion downstream. Procolipase is activated by trypsin, so fat digestion is mildly affected, but lipase itself is secreted active and fat malabsorption is not the dominant problem. Carbohydrate digestion uses brush border enzymes that are secreted active and need no activation. Enteropeptidase acts on trypsinogen alone, not on each zymogen.
questions.answerText: Protein, because trypsinogen is never activated and the other proteases follow it

questions.q: A drug blocks the cholecystokinin receptor throughout the digestive tract. Predict the effect on pancreatic enzyme output, on gallbladder emptying, and on duodenal pH after a fatty meal.
options: Enzyme output falls but the gallbladder empties normally, since gallbladder contraction is purely a vagal reflex
Enzyme output falls and the gallbladder does not empty, while duodenal pH is largely preserved because secretin is unaffected
Enzyme output falls, the gallbladder does not empty, and duodenal pH falls sharply because bicarbonate secretion stops as well
Enzyme output is preserved but the gallbladder does not empty, so only fat digestion is affected
questions.why: Cholecystokinin has two main targets, acinar cells and gallbladder smooth muscle, so blocking its receptor removes both enzymes and bile while leaving the secretin driven duct cell bicarbonate response intact. Bicarbonate secretion is a secretin effect, so duodenal pH is not the variable that collapses here. Acinar enzyme release depends heavily on cholecystokinin and does not stay normal. Vagal input contributes to gallbladder contraction but the dominant fed signal is cholecystokinin.
questions.answerText: Enzyme output falls and the gallbladder does not empty, while duodenal pH is largely preserved because secretin is unaffected

questions.q: Bile flow is obstructed for several weeks. Predict the effect on emulsification, on micelle formation, and on the ability of blood to clot, and link the three.
options: Emulsification is normal because lipase can act on large droplets, and clotting is unaffected
Micelle formation fails but emulsification is preserved by phospholipid, so clotting improves
Emulsification fails but micelles still form normally, so only vitamin B12 absorption is lost
Emulsification and micelle formation both fail, so vitamin K is lost and clotting is impaired
questions.why: Bile salts perform both jobs, breaking fat into fine droplets and then ferrying the digestion products and fat soluble vitamins through the unstirred layer to the brush border, so obstruction removes both steps. Vitamin K is needed for the liver to make several clotting factors, so its loss lengthens clotting time. B12 depends on intrinsic factor and the ileum, not on bile. Lipase acting on large droplets is far too slow to maintain normal fat digestion, and nothing here would improve clotting.
questions.answerText: Emulsification and micelle formation both fail, so vitamin K is lost and clotting is impaired

questions.q: Which enzyme begins starch digestion, and where does it act?
options: Salivary amylase, in the mouth
Maltase, on the brush border
Pepsin, in the stomach
Pancreatic amylase, in the duodenum
questions.why: Salivary amylase starts cleaving the internal bonds of starch while food is still being chewed, though it accounts for only a modest share of total starch digestion. Pancreatic amylase continues the job in the duodenum. Maltase is a brush border enzyme that works on the products of amylase, not on intact starch. Pepsin digests protein and has no action on carbohydrate.

questions.q: What happens to salivary amylase when a bolus reaches the stomach?
options: It is converted to pancreatic amylase
It is activated by gastric acid and works faster
It is inactivated by gastric acid
