It is absorbed intact across the gastric mucosa
questions.why: Salivary amylase works best near neutral pH and is denatured as the bolus mixes with acid, which is why starch digestion pauses in the stomach and resumes in the duodenum. Acid activates pepsinogen, not amylase, and the two enzymes have opposite pH preferences. Enzymes are proteins and are digested rather than absorbed intact. Pancreatic amylase is a separate gene product made by the pancreas.
questions.answerText: It is inactivated by gastric acid

questions.q: What are the main products of pancreatic amylase acting on starch?
options: Branched glycogen and cellulose fibers
Free glucose and free galactose molecules only
Maltose, maltotriose, and alpha limit dextrins
The disaccharides sucrose and lactose
questions.why: Amylase is an endoenzyme that cuts internal alpha 1,4 bonds but cannot cut the alpha 1,6 branch points, so it leaves short oligosaccharides that brush border enzymes finish. Free monosaccharides are the product of the brush border step, not of amylase. Sucrose and lactose are dietary disaccharides, not products of starch digestion. Glycogen is a storage polysaccharide and cellulose is indigestible fiber.
questions.answerText: Maltose, maltotriose, and alpha limit dextrins

questions.q: Which enzyme is located on the brush border rather than being secreted into the lumen?
options: Lactase
Pepsin
Pancreatic amylase
Trypsin
questions.why: Lactase, along with sucrase, maltase, and alpha dextrinase, is anchored in the apical membrane of the enterocyte so the monosaccharides it releases appear right at the transporter that takes them up. Pancreatic amylase and trypsin are secreted into the lumen from the pancreas. Pepsin works in the gastric lumen. This membrane bound arrangement is why brush border damage causes carbohydrate malabsorption.

questions.q: By which transporter do glucose and galactose cross the apical membrane of the enterocyte?
options: A primary active ATPase specific for hexose sugars
GLUT5, by facilitated diffusion down a gradient
SGLT1, a Na+ dependent secondary active cotransporter
GLUT2, by facilitated diffusion down a gradient
questions.why: SGLT1 uses the inward Na+ gradient to drag glucose or galactose into the cell against its own concentration gradient, which is why these sugars can be absorbed almost completely. GLUT5 is the fructose carrier on the same membrane. GLUT2 is the basolateral exit route. There is no ATPase that pumps hexoses directly; the energy is spent by the Na+/K+ ATPase and used indirectly.
questions.answerText: SGLT1, a Na+ dependent secondary active cotransporter

questions.q: How does fructose cross the apical membrane of the enterocyte?
options: By Na+ dependent cotransport on SGLT1
By simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
By endocytosis in the form of vesicles
By facilitated diffusion on GLUT5
questions.why: Fructose moves down its concentration gradient on GLUT5 with no energy input, which is why fructose absorption saturates and why a large fructose load can be incompletely absorbed. SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose, not fructose. Fructose is a polar sugar and cannot cross the bilayer directly. Endocytosis is used for a few large molecules in the newborn gut, not for monosaccharides.

questions.q: By which transporter do monosaccharides leave the enterocyte across the basolateral membrane into the interstitial fluid?
options: GLUT5
GLUT2
The Na+/K+ ATPase
SGLT1
questions.why: GLUT2 in the basolateral membrane carries glucose, galactose, and fructose down their gradients out of the cell and into capillary blood. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are apical entry carriers. The Na+/K+ ATPase is also basolateral but moves Na+ and K+, indirectly powering SGLT1 by keeping intracellular Na+ low.

questions.q: Absorbed monosaccharides and amino acids leave the intestine in which vessel?
options: The lacteal of the villus
The thoracic duct
The hepatic portal vein
The hepatic artery
questions.why: Water soluble nutrients enter the capillaries of the villus and drain into the hepatic portal vein, so the liver processes them before they reach the rest of the body. The thoracic duct and the lacteal carry lymph and are the route for chylomicrons, not for sugars and amino acids. The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood to the liver rather than carrying nutrients away from the gut.

questions.q: A person lacks brush border lactase. Predict what happens to lactose after a glass of milk and why symptoms follow.
options: Lactose is converted to glucose in the stomach by simple acid hydrolysis
Lactose is absorbed intact and then excreted in the urine, causing dehydration
Lactose stays in the lumen, holds water, and is fermented by colonic bacteria
Lactose is digested by pancreatic amylase instead, so no symptoms follow at all
questions.why: Only monosaccharides can be absorbed, so an uncleaved disaccharide is an osmotically active solute that pulls water into the lumen and then feeds colonic bacteria, producing bloating, gas, and loose stool. Disaccharides are not absorbed intact by the small intestine. Pancreatic amylase cuts alpha 1,4 bonds in starch and cannot cleave the beta bond in lactose. Gastric acid is far too weak a hydrolytic agent to substitute for an enzyme.
questions.answerText: Lactose stays in the lumen, holds water, and is fermented by colonic bacteria

questions.q: A toxin blocks the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase in enterocytes. Predict the effect on glucose absorption and explain the link.
options: Glucose absorption rises, because more Na+ is available inside the cell for cotransport
Glucose absorption is unchanged, because SGLT1 hydrolyzes ATP on its own
Glucose absorption falls, because GLUT2 requires ATP to move glucose out
Glucose absorption falls, because intracellular Na+ rises and the SGLT1 gradient collapses
questions.why: SGLT1 is secondary active transport: it spends the Na+ gradient rather than ATP, and that gradient exists only because the pump keeps intracellular Na+ low. High intracellular Na+ removes the driving force, so glucose can no longer be taken up against its gradient. SGLT1 has no ATPase activity of its own, and GLUT2 is a facilitated carrier that needs no ATP.
questions.answerText: Glucose absorption falls, because intracellular Na+ rises and the SGLT1 gradient collapses

questions.q: In the same experiment where the Na+/K+ ATPase is blocked, what happens to fructose absorption?
options: It rises sharply, because SGLT1 no longer competes for the same site
It stops, because fructose is converted to glucose before absorption
It stops, because all sugar absorption requires the pump
It continues, because GLUT5 does not depend on the Na+ gradient
questions.why: Facilitated diffusion needs only a favorable concentration gradient, so fructose uptake persists while glucose uptake fails, and this dissociation is the cleanest way to show that the two sugars use different mechanisms. Not all sugar absorption is pump dependent, which is the point of the contrast. GLUT5 and SGLT1 are separate proteins and do not compete for a shared site. Fructose is absorbed as fructose and converted only later, in the liver.
questions.answerText: It continues, because GLUT5 does not depend on the Na+ gradient

questions.q: Pepsin works well in the stomach but has almost no activity once chyme reaches the duodenum. What explains the change?
options: Trypsin binds pepsin and carries it back to the stomach
Pepsin is absorbed across the duodenal wall as soon as it arrives
Bile salts emulsify pepsin, which prevents it from reaching protein
Bicarbonate raises the pH out of the acidic range pepsin requires
questions.why: Pepsin is an acid protease with an optimum near pH 2 and is essentially inert above pH 5, so pancreatic bicarbonate ends its activity as it hands off to the pancreatic proteases. Nothing transports enzymes backward up the tract. Enzymes are digested rather than absorbed intact. Bile salts act on lipid droplets, not on soluble proteins.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate raises the pH out of the acidic range pepsin requires

questions.q: Trypsin and carboxypeptidase both digest protein but are classified differently. What distinguishes them?
options: Trypsin is secreted in active form while carboxypeptidase is secreted as a zymogen
Trypsin works on the brush border while carboxypeptidase works out in the lumen
Trypsin acts at an acidic pH while carboxypeptidase acts at an alkaline pH
Trypsin is an endopeptidase cutting internal bonds, carboxypeptidase an exopeptidase
questions.why: Endopeptidases cut in the middle of a chain, producing many shorter fragments and many new ends, and exopeptidases then chew those ends down to free amino acids, so the two classes work in sequence. Both prefer the alkaline pH of the duodenum. Both are secreted as zymogens, trypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase. Both act in the lumen; peptidases on the brush border are a separate group.
questions.answerText: Trypsin is an endopeptidase cutting internal bonds, carboxypeptidase an exopeptidase

questions.q: Small peptides are absorbed faster than an equivalent mixture of free amino acids. What explains this?
options: Peptides are smaller than single amino acids and fit through the tight junctions
Peptides diffuse through the lipid bilayer more easily than amino acids do
Di and tripeptides enter on PepT1, an H+ coupled carrier that adds extra capacity
Peptides are absorbed by endocytosis, which has no capacity limit at all
questions.why: PepT1 uses an H+ gradient rather than the Na+ gradient and runs in parallel with several amino acid transporters, so the total uptake capacity for a peptide mixture exceeds that for free amino acids competing for the same carriers. Peptides are polar and do not cross the bilayer freely. Endocytosis is not the route in the mature gut. A dipeptide is by definition larger than one amino acid, and tight junctions do not pass nutrients.
questions.answerText: Di and tripeptides enter on PepT1, an H+ coupled carrier that adds extra capacity

questions.q: Where do absorbed amino acids go first after leaving the enterocyte, and why does that matter?
options: To skeletal muscle first, because muscle has the highest demand for them
To the systemic circulation by the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver entirely
To the liver by the hepatic portal vein, so the liver regulates what passes on
To the lymphatic system, so that they arrive slowly and steadily over hours
questions.why: Portal drainage gives the liver first access, allowing it to deaminate excess amino acids, build plasma proteins, and buffer the swing in nutrient concentration after a meal. The thoracic duct and lymphatic route belong to chylomicrons. Muscle receives amino acids only after they have passed the liver and entered the systemic circulation.
questions.answerText: To the liver by the hepatic portal vein, so the liver regulates what passes on

questions.q: Trace a molecule of starch from the mouth to the portal blood, naming the enzyme at each step and the apical transporter at the end.
options: Salivary amylase, then pepsin, then pancreatic amylase, then glucose taken up on GLUT5
Salivary amylase, pancreatic amylase, brush border maltase, then glucose on SGLT1
Pancreatic amylase alone, then brush border lactase, then glucose taken up on GLUT2
Salivary amylase, then pancreatic lipase, then brush border sucrase, then glucose on SGLT1
questions.why: Starch is attacked twice by amylase, in the mouth and again in the duodenum, then finished by membrane bound enzymes that release free glucose right at the SGLT1 carrier. Pepsin is a protease and plays no part. Lactase acts on lactose and GLUT2 is the basolateral exit, not the apical entry. Lipase and sucrase have the wrong substrates for this pathway.
questions.answerText: Salivary amylase, pancreatic amylase, brush border maltase, then glucose on SGLT1

questions.q: A child has a mutation that eliminates functional SGLT1. Predict the fate of dietary glucose and of dietary fructose, and explain the difference.
options: Both continue normally, because paracellular absorption compensates completely
Both fail, because all monosaccharides use SGLT1 to enter the enterocyte cell
Glucose absorption fails and causes osmotic diarrhea, while fructose continues
Glucose absorption continues on GLUT2 at the apical membrane, and fructose fails
questions.why: SGLT1 is the only meaningful apical route for glucose and galactose, so its loss leaves those sugars in the lumen where they draw water and cause severe diarrhea, while fructose has an independent carrier and is unaffected. Not all monosaccharides share SGLT1, which is exactly why the presentation is selective. GLUT2 is basolateral and cannot substitute for apical entry. Paracellular movement is far too small to replace a saturable active transporter.
questions.answerText: Glucose absorption fails and causes osmotic diarrhea, while fructose continues

questions.q: In celiac disease the immune response flattens the villi and shortens the microvilli. Predict which step of carbohydrate digestion fails first, and why protein digestion is less severely affected.
options: Salivary amylase fails first, so dietary starch is never cleaved at all
Gastric acid secretion fails first, so neither carbohydrate nor protein digestion begins
Pancreatic amylase secretion fails first, and proteases fail equally because they come from the same gland
Brush border disaccharide digestion fails first, while luminal pancreatic proteases work
questions.why: The lesion is in the epithelium, so the enzymes anchored there, lactase most conspicuously, disappear along with the transporters, while enzymes secreted from the pancreas into the lumen are untouched. Amino acid absorption still suffers because the transporters are on that same damaged membrane, but the digestive step itself survives. The pancreas and the salivary glands are not the site of injury, and gastric acid secretion is unrelated to a small intestinal mucosal lesion.
questions.answerText: Brush border disaccharide digestion fails first, while luminal pancreatic proteases work

questions.q: Ouabain is applied only to the basolateral surface of an intestinal epithelium mounted in a chamber. Predict the effect on glucose transport from the apical solution to the basolateral solution, and give the two steps.
options: Transport is unchanged, because ouabain must be applied apically to reach SGLT1
Transport falls, because ouabain blocks GLUT2 directly and glucose cannot leave the cell
Transport falls, because the Na+ gradient collapses first and SGLT1 then loses its driving force
Transport rises, because blocking the pump raises intracellular Na+ and pulls more glucose in
questions.why: Ouabain inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, and the effect on glucose is entirely indirect: intracellular Na+ climbs, the inward Na+ electrochemical gradient shrinks, and SGLT1 can no longer move glucose uphill. Ouabain has no action on GLUT2. Higher intracellular Na+ opposes cotransport rather than driving it, since the carrier needs Na+ to move inward. The pump is basolateral, so basolateral application is the correct way to reach it.
questions.answerText: Transport falls, because the Na+ gradient collapses first and SGLT1 then loses its driving force

questions.q: What do bile salts do to dietary fat in the duodenum?
options: They convert fatty acids directly into chylomicrons
They transport intact triglyceride into the enterocyte
They hydrolyze the ester bonds of the triglyceride
They emulsify it, breaking large droplets into small ones
questions.why: Bile salts are amphipathic, so they coat droplet surfaces and prevent the small droplets from merging back together, multiplying the surface available to lipase. Hydrolysis of ester bonds is what lipase does, and bile salts have no catalytic activity at all. Chylomicron assembly happens inside the enterocyte. Triglyceride is digested before absorption, not carried in intact.
questions.answerText: They emulsify it, breaking large droplets into small ones

questions.q: Which protein must bind to pancreatic lipase so that it can work at the surface of a bile salt coated fat droplet?
options: Colipase
Apoprotein B 48
Intrinsic factor
Enteropeptidase
questions.why: Bile salts on the droplet surface would otherwise displace lipase, and colipase anchors the enzyme to the lipid interface so hydrolysis can proceed. Apoprotein B 48 is a structural protein of the chylomicron, added later inside the cell. Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12. Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen and has no lipid role.

questions.q: What are the products of pancreatic lipase acting on a triglyceride?
options: One fatty acid and one diglyceride
Glycerol and cholesterol
Three free fatty acids and free glycerol
Two free fatty acids and one monoglyceride
questions.why: Pancreatic lipase removes the fatty acids at positions 1 and 3 and leaves the one at position 2 attached, so the products are two fatty acids and a 2 monoglyceride. Complete hydrolysis to glycerol is not what this enzyme does. A diglyceride is an intermediate rather than the end product. Cholesterol is a separate dietary lipid, not a product of triglyceride digestion.
questions.answerText: Two free fatty acids and one monoglyceride

questions.q: What is the function of a micelle in fat absorption?
options: It digests triglyceride into fatty acids and a monoglyceride
It carries digestion products through the watery layer to the brush border
It transports absorbed lipid through the lymph to the bloodstream
It stores excess fatty acids inside the enterocyte until they are needed again
questions.why: Fatty acids and monoglycerides are poorly soluble in water, and the micelle, built from bile salts with a hydrophobic interior, ferries them across the unstirred water layer to the membrane where they are released and diffuse in. Digestion is lipase's job. Transport in lymph is the chylomicron's job. Nothing is stored in the enterocyte in the normal course of a meal.
questions.answerText: It carries digestion products through the watery layer to the brush border

questions.q: Where inside the enterocyte are absorbed fatty acids and monoglycerides reassembled into triglyceride?
options: The mitochondrion, where fatty acids are oxidized
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum
The lysosome, where material is degraded
The nucleus, which directs the assembly
questions.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is the site of lipid synthesis, and resynthesizing triglyceride there keeps the intracellular free fatty acid concentration low, which maintains the inward gradient for further absorption. Mitochondria oxidize fatty acids rather than assembling them into triglyceride. Lysosomes degrade material, and the nucleus has no role in lipid assembly.

questions.q: What is a chylomicron?
options: A lipoprotein particle with a triglyceride core and a phospholipid and protein shell
A vesicle of ingested fat taken up whole by endocytosis at the apical surface of the cell
A complex of free fatty acids bound to albumin circulating in the blood
A bile salt aggregate that carries digested fat through the lumen
questions.why: The chylomicron is built inside the enterocyte to make a large amount of water insoluble lipid transportable in an aqueous medium, with apoprotein B 48 as its identifying protein. A bile salt aggregate is a micelle, which works in the lumen rather than in the blood. Fat is not taken up whole by endocytosis in the adult gut. Free fatty acids bound to albumin are how the blood carries fatty acids released from adipose tissue, a different transport form.
questions.answerText: A lipoprotein particle with a triglyceride core and a phospholipid and protein shell

questions.q: By what route do chylomicrons leave the intestinal villus?
options: Into the lacteal, then through lymph and the thoracic duct to the veins
Into the hepatic artery, then directly to the liver for processing
Into the lymph, then directly into the aorta and the systemic arteries
Into the capillary, then through the hepatic portal vein to reach the liver
questions.why: Chylomicrons are too large to cross the continuous basement membrane of the villus capillary, but lacteals have wide gaps between endothelial cells, so the lymphatic route is the only one available. Lymph then travels up the thoracic duct and empties into the venous system near the left subclavian vein. The portal vein carries sugars and amino acids. The hepatic artery brings blood to the liver, and lymph never drains into an artery.
questions.answerText: Into the lacteal, then through lymph and the thoracic duct to the veins

questions.q: Short and medium chain fatty acids differ from long chain fatty acids in their absorption route. Which route do they take?
options: They require micelles even more than the long chain fatty acids do
They are absorbed only in the colon after bacterial modification there
They are packaged into chylomicrons just as long chain fatty acids are
They pass directly into capillary blood and travel in the portal vein
questions.why: Shorter chains are water soluble enough to diffuse into the capillary without micelles or chylomicron packaging, so they reach the liver directly by the portal route. That is why medium chain triglyceride is useful when bile salts or lymphatic drainage are unavailable. They need micelles less, not more. Colonic bacteria do produce short chain fatty acids from fiber, but dietary short chain fats are absorbed in the small intestine.
questions.answerText: They pass directly into capillary blood and travel in the portal vein

questions.q: Why are chylomicrons taken up by lacteals rather than by the blood capillaries next to them?
options: Blood pressure in the capillary pushes chylomicrons back out into the interstitium
Chylomicrons carry a negative charge that repels them from capillary endothelium
Lacteals have wide gaps between endothelial cells, while capillaries do not
Lacteals actively pump chylomicrons inward using ATP from the endothelial cell
questions.why: Size and barrier structure decide the route: a chylomicron of about 100 nanometers or more cannot cross a continuous capillary basement membrane but passes easily between the loosely joined cells of a lacteal. Charge is not the determining factor. Lymphatic entry is passive and driven by interstitial pressure, not by an ATP powered pump. Capillary pressure is not what excludes them; the physical barrier is.
questions.answerText: Lacteals have wide gaps between endothelial cells, while capillaries do not

questions.q: A drug inhibits pancreatic lipase. Predict what appears in the stool and why.
options: Undigested triglyceride appears, because it cannot be reduced to absorbable units
Bile salts appear, because they are no longer recycled without lipase present
Chylomicrons appear, because they are unable to enter the lacteals of the villus
Free fatty acids appear, because they cannot be reassembled into triglyceride
questions.why: Absorption requires the digestion products, not the intact molecule, so blocking lipase leaves triglyceride in the lumen to be passed in the stool. Free fatty acids would imply digestion succeeded, which is the step being blocked. Bile salt recycling occurs in the ileum and does not depend on lipase. Chylomicrons are assembled inside the cell and never appear in the lumen.
questions.answerText: Undigested triglyceride appears, because it cannot be reduced to absorbable units

questions.q: A patient absorbs fat poorly because bile salt concentration in the duodenum is too low to form micelles. Which additional deficiency should you expect?
options: Deficiency of vitamin C and the B vitamins
Deficiency of iron and calcium only
Deficiency of vitamin B12 alone
Deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K
questions.why: The fat soluble vitamins dissolve in the lipid phase and depend on micelles to reach the brush border, so they are lost whenever micelle formation fails. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are water soluble and are absorbed by their own transporters independent of bile. Iron and calcium have dedicated transport systems and are not micelle dependent. Vitamin B12 requires intrinsic factor and the ileal receptor, a separate pathway.
questions.answerText: Deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K

questions.q: Why does plasma appear milky a few hours after a very fatty meal?
options: Undigested triglyceride is absorbed directly into the portal blood
Free fatty acids bound to albumin scatter light
Chylomicrons entering the blood from the thoracic duct scatter light
Bile salts absorbed from the ileum accumulate in plasma
questions.why: Chylomicrons are large enough to scatter visible light, and they enter the venous blood at the end of the lymphatic route a few hours after a fatty meal, before lipoprotein lipase clears them. Albumin bound fatty acids are molecularly dispersed and do not cloud plasma. Bile salts recirculate at low plasma concentration and are not turbid. Intact triglyceride is not absorbed into portal blood.
questions.answerText: Chylomicrons entering the blood from the thoracic duct scatter light

questions.q: A patient is fed medium chain triglyceride instead of long chain fat. Which two steps of the normal pathway are bypassed?
options: Resynthesis in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and entry into the portal vein
Gastric lipase action and pancreatic lipase action
Emulsification by bile salts and hydrolysis by lipase
Micelle dependent uptake and chylomicron packaging with lymphatic transport
questions.why: Medium chain fatty acids are soluble enough to reach and cross the membrane without micelles, and once inside they are not resynthesized into triglyceride or packaged, so they leave directly in portal blood. Emulsification and hydrolysis still occur to some extent, though far less is required. Entry into the portal vein is what these fats use, not what they bypass. Both lipases can still act on them.
questions.answerText: Micelle dependent uptake and chylomicron packaging with lymphatic transport

questions.q: A meal contains both butter and bread. Which nutrient appears first in the hepatic portal vein and which appears first in lymph, and what determines the split?
options: Both appear in the portal vein, because every vessel in the villus drains to the liver
Both appear in lymph, because the lacteal is the only vessel inside a villus at all
Long chain fat appears in the portal vein and glucose in lymph, because fat is denser
Glucose appears in the portal vein and long chain fat in lymph, set by particle size
questions.why: Small water soluble molecules such as glucose cross the capillary endothelium easily and drain to the liver, while chylomicrons are far too large for the capillary basement membrane and can only enter the leaky lacteal. Density is not the determining property. The villus contains both a capillary network and a lacteal, so neither route is the only one, and they do not both drain to the liver.
questions.answerText: Glucose appears in the portal vein and long chain fat in lymph, set by particle size

questions.q: Why does a fatty meal not simply diffuse into enterocytes as intact triglyceride, given that the membrane is made of lipid?
options: Triglyceride is destroyed by gastric acid long before it reaches the intestine
Triglyceride is far too polar a molecule to enter a lipid bilayer
Triglyceride cannot cross the aqueous layer and must be hydrolyzed and carried
Triglyceride is actively pumped back out of the enterocyte as fast as it enters
questions.why: The limiting barrier is water, not lipid: a droplet of triglyceride cannot approach the membrane through the unstirred aqueous layer, so digestion and micellar transport are what make the last few micrometers possible. Triglyceride is nonpolar, so the polarity explanation is backward. There is no pump exporting triglyceride from enterocytes into the lumen. Acid does not destroy triglyceride.
questions.answerText: Triglyceride cannot cross the aqueous layer and must be hydrolyzed and carried

questions.q: Trace a dietary triglyceride from the duodenal lumen to the systemic circulation in order.
options: Emulsification by bile salts, hydrolysis by lipase, micellar delivery, then chylomicron to the lacteal
Emulsification by bile salts, uptake of the intact droplet by endocytosis, then lacteal to thoracic duct to vein
Hydrolysis by gastric lipase, micelle formation in the stomach, then absorption in the duodenum into the portal vein
Hydrolysis by lipase, emulsification by bile salts, packaging into a micelle, then portal vein to liver
questions.why: The order matters because each step creates the conditions for the next: emulsification gives lipase surface area, hydrolysis gives micelles their cargo, micelles deliver that cargo to the membrane, and only then can the cell rebuild and export the lipid. Reversing emulsification and hydrolysis ignores that lipase works at an interface it needs bile salts to create. Intact droplets are not endocytosed. Gastric lipase contributes a little, but micelles cannot form in acid and absorption of long chain fat is not by the portal route.
questions.answerText: Emulsification by bile salts, hydrolysis by lipase, micellar delivery, then chylomicron to the lacteal

questions.q: A person cannot synthesize apoprotein B 48. Predict where dietary fat accumulates and what appears in the blood after a fatty meal.
options: Fat accumulates inside the enterocyte and plasma chylomicrons fail to appear
Fat is absorbed normally but is carried entirely in the portal vein
Fat accumulates in the lacteals and lymph becomes clear rather than milky
Fat remains undigested in the lumen and plasma chylomicrons are normal
questions.why: Digestion, micelle formation, and uptake all proceed normally, but without the structural apoprotein the enterocyte cannot assemble or export a chylomicron, so the resynthesized triglyceride is trapped in the cell and the postprandial rise in plasma chylomicrons never happens. The lumen contains digested fat, so it is not the site of accumulation. Long chain fat cannot switch to the portal route. Nothing reaches the lacteals to accumulate there.
questions.answerText: Fat accumulates inside the enterocyte and plasma chylomicrons fail to appear

questions.q: Bile flow into the duodenum is completely obstructed while pancreatic function is normal. Predict what happens to lipase action and to absorption, and explain why the two are affected differently.
options: Lipase acts normally but absorption fails because no chylomicrons can be assembled at all
Lipase cannot act at all, so no hydrolysis occurs anywhere and absorption fails completely
Lipase hydrolyzes some fat but slowly, and absorption fails because micelles cannot form
Lipase acts normally and absorption is normal, since bile salts only add color to the stool
questions.why: Bile salts serve two distinct roles, and losing them hurts both but not equally: hydrolysis is slowed because the droplets stay large, while transport across the unstirred layer is essentially abolished because there is nothing to solubilize the products. Lipase does not require bile salts absolutely, only to work efficiently. Bile salts do far more than color the stool. Chylomicron assembly is an intracellular process that does not need luminal bile.
questions.answerText: Lipase hydrolyzes some fat but slowly, and absorption fails because micelles cannot form

questions.q: An injury drains the thoracic duct externally so its lymph never reaches the blood. Predict the effect on absorption of long chain fat and of glucose, and explain the difference.
options: Long chain fat is absorbed but lost with the lymph, while glucose uses the portal vein
Long chain fat is never absorbed, because chylomicrons cannot leave the enterocyte at all
Glucose is lost and fat is unaffected, because glucose is carried in chylomicrons
Both are lost, because all absorbed nutrients travel in the lymph to the blood
questions.why: The two nutrient classes take different exits from the villus, so an interruption of lymphatic return removes fat and fat soluble vitamins from the body while leaving carbohydrate and amino acid absorption intact. Not all nutrients travel in lymph, and that separation is the whole point of the two routes. Absorption into the enterocyte and into the lacteal still occurs; the loss happens downstream. Glucose is never packaged into chylomicrons.
questions.answerText: Long chain fat is absorbed but lost with the lymph, while glucose uses the portal vein

questions.q: Which molecule does the liver store and release to keep blood glucose stable between meals?
options: Bilirubin
Triglyceride
Glycogen
Albumin
questions.why: The liver stores glucose as glycogen after a meal and breaks it back down during fasting, which is the main short term buffer for blood glucose. Triglyceride is stored mainly in adipose tissue, and liver triglyceride accumulation is a pathological finding rather than a glucose reserve. Albumin is a protein the liver exports, not a glucose store. Bilirubin is a waste product excreted in bile.

questions.q: Which plasma protein made by the liver is the main determinant of plasma colloid osmotic pressure?
options: Hemoglobin
Albumin
Fibrin
Intrinsic factor
questions.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and, because it stays in the capillary, it generates most of the osmotic force that pulls fluid back from the interstitium. Hemoglobin is inside red cells and made in bone marrow. Fibrin is the insoluble clot protein formed from fibrinogen, which is a liver product but a small fraction of plasma protein. Intrinsic factor comes from gastric parietal cells.

questions.q: The liver converts ammonia from amino acid breakdown into which molecule for excretion?
options: Urea
Creatinine
Bilirubin
Uric acid
questions.why: The urea cycle in hepatocytes converts toxic ammonia into urea, which the kidneys then excrete, and this is the body's main route for disposing of amino acid nitrogen. Uric acid comes from purine breakdown. Creatinine comes from muscle creatine phosphate. Bilirubin comes from heme and has nothing to do with nitrogen from amino acids.

questions.q: Where are bile salts reabsorbed during enterohepatic circulation?
options: In the stomach, along with acid and water
In the duodenum, by simple diffusion across the wall
In the terminal ileum, by Na+ coupled transport
In the colon, by facilitated diffusion into blood
questions.why: A specific Na+ dependent bile acid transporter in the terminal ileum recovers about 95 percent of secreted bile salts, which is why the ileum is the segment whose loss produces bile salt wasting. Reabsorbing them in the duodenum would defeat their purpose, since they are needed throughout the length of fat absorption. Only a small fraction is passively absorbed elsewhere. The stomach absorbs essentially nothing.
questions.answerText: In the terminal ileum, by Na+ coupled transport

questions.q: By which vessel do reabsorbed bile salts return to the liver?
options: The hepatic portal vein
The hepatic artery
The inferior vena cava directly
The thoracic duct
questions.why: Bile salts absorbed in the ileum enter the portal blood and are taken up by hepatocytes on their first pass, so very little reaches the systemic circulation. The thoracic duct carries chylomicrons. The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood in but is not the nutrient route from the gut. Blood entering the inferior vena cava has already passed through the liver.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of secreted bile salts is recycled rather than lost in the stool?
options: About 50 percent
About 95 percent
Essentially none, since bile salts are digested
About 20 percent
questions.why: Roughly 95 percent of the bile salt pool is recovered each cycle, so the liver needs to synthesize only the small amount lost in stool, and the pool can be recycled several times during a single meal. Recovering only 20 or 50 percent would require synthesis rates the liver cannot sustain. Bile salts are not digested; they are recovered intact by a specific transporter.

questions.q: Which liver cells phagocytose bacteria and debris arriving in portal blood from the intestine?
options: Kupffer cells
Stellate cells
Duct cells
Hepatocytes
questions.why: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids, positioned exactly where portal blood loaded with gut derived bacteria first arrives. Hepatocytes perform the metabolic and detoxification work but are not phagocytes. Stellate cells store vitamin A and produce collagen in injury. Duct cells line the bile ducts and add bicarbonate to bile.

questions.q: Which enzyme family in hepatocytes performs the first phase of drug and toxin metabolism?
options: The pancreatic zymogens
The brush border disaccharidases
The cytochrome P450 enzymes
The carbonic anhydrases
questions.why: Cytochrome P450 enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes oxidize drugs and toxins in phase I, adding or exposing a reactive group that phase II conjugation then attaches to glucuronate or sulfate. Carbonic anhydrase handles CO2 and bicarbonate chemistry. Pancreatic zymogens digest food in the intestinal lumen. Brush border disaccharidases finish carbohydrate digestion in the intestine.

questions.q: A person stops eating any source of vitamin A, yet takes many months to show signs of deficiency. Which liver function explains the delay?
options: Excretion, since the liver stops excreting vitamin A into bile
Storage, since the liver holds a large reserve of vitamin A
Detoxification, since the liver stops metabolizing vitamin A when intake falls
Synthesis, since the liver can manufacture vitamin A from cholesterol
questions.why: The liver is the body's main depot for vitamins A, D, and B12 as well as iron, and those reserves buffer months of inadequate intake, which is why deficiency of a stored nutrient appears slowly. Reduced metabolism of a vitamin is not what maintains plasma levels over months. Vitamin A is an essential nutrient, meaning the body cannot synthesize it. Reduced biliary excretion is a minor effect compared with mobilizing a large store.
questions.answerText: Storage, since the liver holds a large reserve of vitamin A

questions.q: A patient with advanced liver disease has a serum albumin far below normal. Predict the effect on fluid distribution and explain the mechanism.
options: Fluid moves into the interstitium, because plasma colloid osmotic pressure falls
Fluid moves into the plasma, because interstitial osmotic pressure falls
Fluid distribution is unchanged, because albumin crosses the capillary wall freely
Fluid moves into cells, because plasma becomes hypotonic to the cytoplasm
questions.why: Albumin normally holds fluid in the capillary by generating colloid osmotic pressure, so losing it tips the Starling balance toward filtration and produces edema and ascites. The direction is out of the plasma, not into it. Albumin is largely retained by the capillary wall, which is why it can generate an osmotic force at all. Plasma tonicity, which depends on small solutes like Na+, is not meaningfully changed by albumin.
questions.answerText: Fluid moves into the interstitium, because plasma colloid osmotic pressure falls

questions.q: A patient with severe liver failure bruises easily and bleeds after minor cuts. Which liver function has failed?
options: Phagocytosis by Kupffer cells
Storage of vitamin B12
Synthesis of clotting factors
Conjugation of bilirubin
questions.why: The liver makes fibrinogen, prothrombin, and most of the other clotting factors, so hepatocyte failure lengthens clotting time within days because several of these proteins have short half lives. B12 storage failure would take years to appear and would cause anemia, not bleeding. Failed bilirubin conjugation causes jaundice. Loss of Kupffer cell function raises infection risk rather than bleeding risk.

questions.q: A drug binds bile salts in the intestinal lumen so they cannot be reabsorbed. Predict the effect on hepatic cholesterol use and on blood LDL.
options: The liver stops making bile salts, and blood LDL rises
The liver uses more cholesterol to make replacement bile salts, and blood LDL falls
The liver converts bile salts back to cholesterol, and blood LDL rises
Bile salt synthesis is unchanged, and blood LDL falls because the drug is absorbed
questions.why: Interrupting the enterohepatic circulation removes the returning bile salts that normally inhibit synthesis, so the hepatocyte increases bile acid production, pulls cholesterol out of the blood by upregulating LDL receptors, and plasma LDL drops. Synthesis increases rather than stopping. Bile salts are not converted back to cholesterol. The drug works precisely because it is not absorbed.
questions.answerText: The liver uses more cholesterol to make replacement bile salts, and blood LDL falls

questions.q: An oral drug is largely inactivated before it ever reaches the systemic circulation, while the same drug given by injection is fully active. What accounts for the difference?
options: The drug is absorbed into lymph and heavily diluted before it reaches the blood
The kidney filters the oral form far more rapidly than the injected form
First pass metabolism, because absorbed drug crosses the liver in portal blood
Gastric acid destroys most of the drug before it can even be absorbed
questions.why: Everything absorbed by the portal route passes through the hepatocytes before entering the general circulation, so a drug that is a good substrate for cytochrome P450 can be largely metabolized on that first pass. Acid destruction is a different mechanism and would happen in the stomach rather than the liver. The lymphatic route is used by long chain fat, and it actually avoids the liver. The kidney cannot distinguish a molecule by its route of entry.
questions.answerText: First pass metabolism, because absorbed drug crosses the liver in portal blood

questions.q: Which liver function is being used when a person who has not eaten for 24 hours maintains a normal blood glucose?
options: Bile salt synthesis and secretion
Kupffer cell phagocytosis
Bilirubin conjugation and excretion
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
questions.why: After a day without food the liver first breaks down its glycogen and then makes new glucose from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids, keeping plasma glucose in range for the brain. Bilirubin handling is a waste disposal function. Bile salt synthesis serves fat digestion and continues, but it does not defend blood glucose. Kupffer cells are immune cells.

questions.q: Trace one bile salt molecule through a complete enterohepatic circuit, naming the site of each step.
options: Synthesized in the pancreas, secreted with the pancreatic juice, reabsorbed in the colon, and returned to the liver in the hepatic artery
Synthesized in the gallbladder, secreted directly into the duodenum, reabsorbed in the jejunum, and returned to the liver for reuse in the thoracic duct
Made in the hepatocyte, secreted in bile, stored in the gallbladder, released into the duodenum, reabsorbed in the ileum, returned in the portal vein
Synthesized in the hepatocyte, secreted into the portal vein, absorbed by the ileum from the blood, and then excreted unchanged in the stool
questions.why: The circuit runs liver to bile duct to gallbladder to duodenum to ileum to portal vein and back to the liver, and each site does a distinct job in it. The gallbladder stores and concentrates but does not synthesize. Bile salts are secreted into bile canaliculi, not into blood, and they are recovered from the lumen rather than from plasma. The pancreas makes enzymes and bicarbonate, not bile salts.
questions.answerText: Made in the hepatocyte, secreted in bile, stored in the gallbladder, released into the duodenum, reabsorbed in the ileum, returned in the portal vein

questions.q: In cirrhosis, hepatocyte function is lost progressively. Predict the direction of change in blood ammonia, serum albumin, and clotting time, and explain each.
options: Ammonia falls, albumin falls, and clotting time shortens, because all hepatic output declines together
Ammonia rises because the urea cycle fails, while albumin and clotting factors are not made
Ammonia rises, albumin rises because it is not being consumed, and clotting time shortens
Ammonia is unchanged because the kidney compensates, albumin falls, and clotting time is unchanged
questions.why: The key is to sort each variable by whether the liver makes it or disposes of it: substances the liver clears accumulate, and substances the liver synthesizes fall. Ammonia is cleared, so it rises, while albumin and clotting factors are made, so they fall and clotting slows. Ammonia cannot fall when its only disposal route is failing. Albumin is not conserved by lack of use, and the kidney cannot substitute for the urea cycle.
questions.answerText: Ammonia rises because the urea cycle fails, while albumin and clotting factors are not made

questions.q: After ileal resection a patient has both fatty stools and watery diarrhea. Explain the two separate mechanisms behind these findings.
options: Pancreatic enzyme output falls, causing fatty stools, and the colon is inflamed, causing diarrhea
Fat reaching the colon is fermented to gas, and the gas draws water in osmotically
Vitamin B12 deficiency damages the colonic epithelium, which causes both of the findings
Bile salt loss shrinks the pool so fat is malabsorbed, and colonic bile salts drive secretion
questions.why: Two consequences follow from the same lost transporter: too few bile salts remain for micelle formation, and the ones that escape into the colon act as secretagogues on colonic epithelium. Pancreatic output is unaffected by an ileal resection. Gas itself is not osmotically active in the way solutes are. B12 deficiency does occur here but affects blood and nerves, not colonic secretion.
questions.answerText: Bile salt loss shrinks the pool so fat is malabsorbed, and colonic bile salts drive secretion

questions.q: A patient with a portal systemic shunt has blood bypassing the liver from the intestine to the vena cava. Predict the effect on blood ammonia after a high protein meal and on the potency of an oral drug with heavy first pass metabolism.
options: Ammonia falls and the oral drug becomes less potent
Ammonia rises sharply and the oral drug becomes much more potent
Ammonia rises and the oral drug becomes less potent
Both are unchanged, since the shunt affects only blood pressure
questions.why: A shunt removes the liver's first crack at whatever the intestine absorbs, so ammonia from protein digestion enters the systemic circulation without being converted to urea, and a drug that would normally be largely metabolized on first pass arrives intact at much higher concentration. Ammonia cannot fall when its clearance step is bypassed, and a bypassed first pass makes the drug stronger rather than weaker. The shunt changes far more than pressure; it changes what the blood carries.
questions.answerText: Ammonia rises sharply and the oral drug becomes much more potent

questions.q: About how much fluid enters the colon each day, and about how much leaves in the stool?
options: About 1.5 liters enters and about 100 to 150 mL leaves
About 500 mL enters and about 400 mL leaves
About 3 liters enters and about 1.5 liters of it leaves
About 9 liters enters and about 1 liter leaves
questions.why: The small intestine has already recovered most of the roughly 9 liters that pass through the tract, so the colon receives about 1.5 liters and returns almost all of it, leaving stool about three quarters water by weight but only 100 to 150 mL in volume. Nine liters entering the colon would describe the total load on the whole tract. The other figures either understate the colon's daily load or overstate normal stool water.
questions.answerText: About 1.5 liters enters and about 100 to 150 mL leaves

questions.q: By which channel does Na+ enter the colonic epithelial cell from the lumen?
options: The Na+/H+ exchanger driven by luminal acid
SGLT1, cotransported with glucose
The epithelial Na+ channel, ENaC
The Na+/K+ ATPase on the apical membrane
questions.why: Colonic Na+ absorption is largely through ENaC in the apical membrane, driven by the low intracellular Na+ that the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase maintains, and it is the step that aldosterone upregulates. SGLT1 is a small intestinal carrier and there is little glucose left in the colon anyway. The Na+/K+ ATPase is basolateral, never apical. The Na+/H+ exchanger contributes in the small intestine but is not the main colonic route.

questions.q: Which hormone increases Na+ and water absorption in the colon?
options: Cholecystokinin
Gastrin
Secretin
Aldosterone
questions.why: Aldosterone acts on colonic epithelium much as it does on the distal nephron, increasing the number of ENaC channels and Na+/K+ ATPase units so more Na+, and therefore more water, is recovered. Secretin and cholecystokinin are duodenal hormones acting on the pancreas, gallbladder, and stomach. Gastrin acts on the parietal cell and gastric motility.

questions.q: Which ion does the colon secrete into the lumen rather than absorb?
options: Cl-
K+
HCO3- is neither secreted nor absorbed
Na+
questions.why: The colon absorbs Na+ and Cl- and secretes K+ and HCO3-, which is why prolonged diarrhea causes both potassium loss and a fall in blood bicarbonate. Na+ and Cl- are the ions being recovered. Bicarbonate is very much secreted here, exchanged for the Cl- being absorbed, so calling it neither is incorrect.

questions.q: What do colonic bacteria produce when they ferment undigested carbohydrate and fiber?
options: Free glucose and galactose released from fiber
Amino acids and urea made from the dietary nitrogen
Short chain fatty acids such as butyrate and acetate
Bile salts and cholesterol newly synthesized
questions.why: Fermentation of material the small intestine could not digest yields short chain fatty acids plus gas, and those acids are absorbed and used as fuel, so fiber contributes some energy indirectly. Urea is made by the liver, not by colonic bacteria. Bacteria deconjugate and modify bile salts but do not synthesize them. Free glucose is not a fermentation end product; it is the substrate that is consumed.
questions.answerText: Short chain fatty acids such as butyrate and acetate

questions.q: Which vitamin made by colonic bacteria contributes meaningfully to the body's supply?
options: Vitamin D
Vitamin C
Vitamin K
Vitamin A
questions.why: Colonic bacteria synthesize vitamin K and several B vitamins, and the vitamin K contribution matters enough that wiping out the flora can lengthen clotting time. Vitamin C must come from the diet in humans. Vitamin A comes from diet and is stored in the liver. Vitamin D is made in skin from a cholesterol derivative under ultraviolet light.

questions.q: What is a mass movement in the colon?
options: A strong wave that pushes a large volume a long distance at once
The fasting sweep that clears residue from the tract between meals
The reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter during filling
A slow segmenting contraction that mixes contents within a single haustrum
questions.why: Mass movements occur a few times a day, often after a meal through the gastrocolic reflex, and move colonic contents toward the rectum in a single sustained push. Mixing within a haustrum is haustral churning, a different and much weaker pattern. The fasting sweep is the migrating motor complex, which belongs to the small intestine. Internal sphincter relaxation is part of the defecation reflex, not a propulsive wave.
questions.answerText: A strong wave that pushes a large volume a long distance at once

questions.q: Which anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control?
options: Both sphincters equally
Neither, since both are smooth muscle
The internal anal sphincter
The external anal sphincter
questions.why: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle innervated by the pudendal nerve, so it can be held closed consciously, while the internal sphincter is smooth muscle that relaxes reflexly when the rectum distends. Treating both as equal misses the entire basis of continence. Saying both are smooth muscle would leave no voluntary control at all, which does not match experience.

questions.q: A person becomes volume depleted and aldosterone rises. Predict the effect on colonic function and on stool water.
options: K+ absorption increases and stool water is unchanged
Colonic motility stops and stool accumulates without changing in water content
Na+ and water absorption in the colon increase and stool becomes drier
Na+ secretion into the colon increases and stool becomes wetter
questions.why: Aldosterone increases ENaC and Na+/K+ ATPase activity in colonic epithelium, and water follows the absorbed Na+ osmotically, so the body conserves both salt and water at the expense of stool water. The hormone promotes absorption, not secretion. Aldosterone actually promotes K+ secretion rather than absorption. Motility is not the target of this hormone.
questions.answerText: Na+ and water absorption in the colon increase and stool becomes drier

questions.q: A course of broad spectrum antibiotics greatly reduces colonic bacteria. Which laboratory value is most likely to change, and in which direction?
options: Clotting time lengthens, because bacterial vitamin K synthesis falls
Serum albumin falls, because bacteria no longer supply amino acids
Blood ammonia rises, because bacteria no longer remove nitrogen
Blood glucose falls, because bacteria no longer supply glucose
questions.why: Vitamin K from colonic bacteria supports hepatic synthesis of several clotting factors, so losing the flora can measurably prolong clotting, particularly when dietary intake is also low. Bacteria do not supply blood glucose. Albumin comes from hepatic synthesis using dietary amino acids. Colonic bacteria actually generate ammonia from urea and protein, so removing them tends to lower blood ammonia rather than raise it.
questions.answerText: Clotting time lengthens, because bacterial vitamin K synthesis falls

questions.q: A person doubles dietary fiber intake. Predict the effect on colonic transit time and explain the mechanism.
options: Transit speeds up, because fiber adds bulk and water that distend the colon
Transit is unchanged, because dietary fiber is absorbed in the small intestine
Transit speeds up, because fiber is an osmotic solute that is actively secreted
Transit slows, because fiber is fermented and its products are absorbed slowly
questions.why: Fiber increases stool mass and water content, and the resulting distension is itself a stimulus for colonic contraction, so contents move through faster and less water is removed. Fermentation does occur but does not slow transit. Fiber is by definition not digested or absorbed in the small intestine. Fiber is not secreted; it arrives from the diet.
questions.answerText: Transit speeds up, because fiber adds bulk and water that distend the colon

questions.q: A drug slows colonic transit so that residue spends 60 hours in the colon instead of 30. Predict the effect on stool consistency and explain why.
options: Stool becomes softer, because the bacteria have longer to ferment and generate water
Stool consistency is unchanged, because water absorption in the colon is not time dependent
Stool becomes harder, because the colon secretes less mucus at slow transit rates
Stool becomes harder, because longer contact with the epithelium removes more water
questions.why: Colonic water absorption is a slow process running against a modest gradient, so total water recovered depends heavily on how long the residue is exposed to the mucosa. Fermentation does not generate meaningful net water. Time dependence is the entire mechanism, so calling it irrelevant contradicts the observation. Reduced mucus is a minor factor compared with the extra water removed.
questions.answerText: Stool becomes harder, because longer contact with the epithelium removes more water

questions.q: Which molecule serves as the preferred fuel for colonic epithelial cells, and where does it come from?
options: Glucose, delivered to the cell from arterial blood
Butyrate, made by bacterial fermentation of fiber
Glutamine, produced by colonic bacteria from urea
Ketone bodies, delivered from the liver in portal blood
questions.why: Colonocytes take butyrate directly from the lumen and oxidize it, which is one reason fiber intake supports colonic mucosal health. They can use glucose from blood but butyrate is the preferred substrate. Glutamine is a major fuel for small intestinal enterocytes and comes from blood, not from bacterial urea metabolism. Portal blood flows away from the gut toward the liver, so the liver does not supply the colon by that route.
questions.answerText: Butyrate, made by bacterial fermentation of fiber

questions.q: Rectal distension causes the internal anal sphincter to relax involuntarily, yet a person can still delay defecation. How?
options: By voluntarily contracting the internal anal sphincter more strongly still
By voluntarily contracting the external sphincter, which is skeletal muscle
By consciously stopping the rectal stretch receptors from firing at all
By reversing colonic peristalsis under voluntary cortical control
questions.why: The reflex relaxation of the internal sphincter is not under conscious control, so continence depends entirely on the external sphincter, which is skeletal muscle innervated by the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter cannot be contracted at will. Sensory receptors cannot be silenced by intention, though the urge does fade as the rectum accommodates. Colonic peristalsis is smooth muscle activity and is not voluntary.
questions.answerText: By voluntarily contracting the external sphincter, which is skeletal muscle

questions.q: Cholera toxin drives intestinal Cl- and water secretion at about 10 liters per day. Explain why diarrhea results even though the colon is entirely normal.
options: Secretion exceeds the colon's absorptive capacity of about 4 to 5 liters a day
The secreted fluid is hypertonic, so the colon cannot absorb against the gradient
Colonic transit stops entirely, so the fluid never reaches the absorptive surface
The toxin also blocks the colonic Na+ channels, so no water can be absorbed
questions.why: The colon has a real but finite reserve, roughly three times its normal daily load, and cholera simply outruns it, which is why the stool volume can be so large in an otherwise healthy gut. The toxin acts on small intestinal crypt cells rather than blocking colonic sodium channels. The secreted fluid is essentially isotonic, not hypertonic. Transit is if anything accelerated by the volume, not stopped.
questions.answerText: Secretion exceeds the colon's absorptive capacity of about 4 to 5 liters a day

questions.q: An osmotic laxative delivers a large load of a nonabsorbable solute to the colon. Trace the two steps that produce a loose stool.
options: The solute blocks ENaC directly, so both Na+ and water absorption stop at once
The solute stimulates aldosterone release, which increases colonic secretion of water
The solute is fermented to gas, and that gas physically pushes the stool along
The solute holds water osmotically, and the added volume distends and speeds transit
questions.why: Two effects compound: water cannot be absorbed away from a solute that will not follow it, and the resulting distension triggers motility that shortens the time available for whatever absorption remains possible. Gas produced by fermentation contributes to discomfort but is not the propulsive mechanism. Osmotic laxatives do not block ENaC. Aldosterone increases absorption rather than secretion, so raising it would oppose the effect.
questions.answerText: The solute holds water osmotically, and the added volume distends and speeds transit

questions.q: A spinal cord injury above the sacral segments leaves the sacral cord and pelvic nerves intact. Predict what happens to the defecation reflex and to voluntary continence.
options: Both the reflex and voluntary control are lost, because all defecation is under cortical control
The reflex still occurs from the sacral cord, but voluntary sphincter control is lost
The reflex is lost but voluntary control remains, because the external sphincter has its own local circuit
Both are preserved, because the enteric nervous system handles the entire reflex
questions.why: Defecation has a spinal reflex arc in the sacral cord plus a descending voluntary pathway to the external sphincter, so an injury above the sacral level severs the second while sparing the first. Cortical control governs only the external sphincter, not the whole reflex. The external sphincter is driven from the sacral cord by the pudendal nerve and has no independent circuit that survives loss of descending input. The enteric nervous system contributes but cannot supply voluntary skeletal muscle control.
questions.answerText: The reflex still occurs from the sacral cord, but voluntary sphincter control is lost

questions.q: A patient has the entire colon removed and the ileum brought to the surface. Predict the daily output volume, the main electrolyte risk, and the mechanism.
options: Output rises and the main risk is protein loss, because the colon absorbs most amino acids
Output rises above a liter a day, with sodium and water lost, since the colon is gone
Output stays near 150 mL a day, because the small intestine absorbs the extra water instead
Output rises but the main risk is calcium loss, because the colon absorbs most dietary calcium
questions.why: The ileum delivers roughly 1.5 liters of isotonic fluid a day, and with no colon that volume leaves the body directly, carrying sodium with it and threatening volume depletion. The small intestine cannot simply increase its absorption to compensate, since it is already working near its limit. Most calcium is absorbed in the small intestine, and amino acid absorption is complete long before the colon, so neither is the main loss here.
questions.answerText: Output rises above a liter a day, with sodium and water lost, since the colon is gone

questions.q: What is the approximate optimal pH for pepsin?
options: About 2
About 5
About 7
About 9
questions.why: Pepsin evolved to work in gastric juice, so its activity peaks near pH 2 and falls to nearly nothing above pH 5. A pH near 7 is where salivary amylase works best. A pH near 9 suits the pancreatic proteases in the duodenum. Matching an enzyme's optimum to a region of the tract is the whole point of the experiment.

questions.q: What is the approximate optimal pH for trypsin and pancreatic amylase?
options: About 8
About 11
About 2
About 4
questions.why: Pancreatic enzymes work in the duodenum after bicarbonate has neutralized chyme, so their optimum sits in the mildly alkaline range near pH 8. A pH near 2 is gastric and would denature them. A pH near 4 is too acidic for full activity, which is why insufficient bicarbonate impairs digestion. A pH near 11 is far outside anything the body produces and would denature the enzyme.

questions.q: In a starch digestion experiment, what does a drop of iodine solution detect?
options: Reducing sugars, by turning orange
Starch, by turning blue black
Protein, by turning purple
Fat, by turning the solution cloudy
questions.why: Iodine forms a blue black complex with the helical structure of starch, so a tube that stays dark still contains starch and a tube that turns pale has had its starch digested. Reducing sugars are detected by Benedict solution, which turns orange or red. Protein is detected by the biuret test, which turns purple. Fat is not detected by iodine.

questions.q: In a digestive enzyme experiment, what is the purpose of a tube containing substrate but no enzyme?
options: It measures the optimal temperature for the reaction in that tube
It provides the baseline pH against which the other tubes are read
It is a positive control that shows the test can detect the product
It is a negative control showing the substrate does not change alone
questions.why: A tube with substrate and no enzyme tells you whether any change you see in the other tubes needed the enzyme, which is the only way to attribute the result to enzyme activity. A positive control would be a tube known to produce the product. Temperature is set by a water bath, not by a tube composition. pH is set deliberately in each tube by buffer.
questions.answerText: It is a negative control showing the substrate does not change alone

questions.q: At what temperature do human digestive enzymes work best in a laboratory assay?
options: About 60 C
About 4 C
About 25 C
About 37 C
questions.why: Enzyme optima match the environment the enzyme evolved in, and for a human enzyme that is core body temperature near 37 C. At 4 C molecular motion is too slow and the reaction nearly stops, though the enzyme is undamaged. Room temperature at 25 C gives a slow but measurable reaction. By 60 C most human enzymes are denaturing rather than accelerating.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme that has been boiled for five minutes and then cooled back to 37 C?
options: It works only at the higher temperature and stops when cooled
It regains full activity once the temperature is back in range
It stays inactive, because denaturation of its shape is not reversible
It becomes twice as active, because heat breaks it into more active fragments
questions.why: Boiling disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the active site in shape, and for most enzymes that unfolding cannot be undone by cooling. This is the key distinction from cold inhibition, where activity returns on warming. Heat does not fragment an enzyme into more active pieces. An enzyme that had been destroyed does not work at any temperature.
questions.answerText: It stays inactive, because denaturation of its shape is not reversible

questions.q: An enzyme acts on starch but produces no change when incubated with a protein solution. What property does this demonstrate?
options: Denaturation
Substrate specificity
Temperature dependence
Competitive inhibition
questions.why: An active site has a shape and chemistry that fit one substrate or one class of bond, so amylase cleaves alpha 1,4 glycosidic bonds and simply cannot bind a polypeptide. Temperature dependence would be shown by varying heat, not substrate. Competitive inhibition requires a molecule that binds the active site and blocks it. Denaturation would abolish activity on all substrates, including starch.

questions.q: In an experiment testing amylase at pH 2, 7, and 9 at 37 C, what is the independent variable?
options: pH
The amount of starch digested
The concentration of amylase
Temperature
questions.why: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes across tubes, which here is pH, while temperature and enzyme concentration are held constant as controlled variables. The amount of starch digested is what you measure, making it the dependent variable. Naming these correctly is what lets you attribute a difference between tubes to the factor you varied.

questions.q: Amylase and starch are incubated together at pH 2 and 37 C for 30 minutes, then tested with iodine. Predict the result.
options: The tube turns orange, because acid hydrolyzes the starch itself
The tube turns pale, because amylase works at any pH given enough time
The tube stays blue black, because amylase is inactive at pH 2
The tube turns purple, because iodine detects the maltose produced
questions.why: Amylase works near neutral pH and is inactive in strong acid, so the starch remains and iodine still finds it. Time cannot compensate for a pH that has denatured or inhibited the enzyme. Iodine detects starch, not maltose, and it never turns purple. Dilute acid at 37 C for half an hour does not appreciably hydrolyze starch on its own.
questions.answerText: The tube stays blue black, because amylase is inactive at pH 2

questions.q: Pepsin and egg white protein are incubated at pH 8 and 37 C. Predict the result and explain it.
options: Digestion occurs but the products are reassembled at alkaline pH
Rapid digestion occurs, because 37 C is optimal for all human enzymes
Little or no digestion occurs, because pepsin requires an acidic environment
Rapid digestion occurs, because pH 8 matches the optimum for all proteases
questions.why: Pepsin is an acid protease and is essentially inert at pH 8, which is exactly the mechanism that ends its action when chyme reaches the duodenum. Optimal temperature cannot rescue an enzyme that is outside its pH range. Not all proteases share an optimum, since trypsin prefers alkaline conditions and pepsin does not. Hydrolysis is not reversed by raising pH.
questions.answerText: Little or no digestion occurs, because pepsin requires an acidic environment

questions.q: Two tubes contain amylase and starch. One is boiled before incubation and one is not. After 30 minutes at 37 C, what difference does iodine reveal?
options: The boiled tube turns pale and the unboiled tube stays blue black
Both tubes turn pale, because boiling only slows the enzyme temporarily
Both tubes stay blue black, because iodine inhibits amylase
The boiled tube stays blue black and the unboiled tube turns pale
questions.why: Boiling denatures amylase permanently, so the starch survives and the iodine test stays positive, while the untreated enzyme digests the starch and the color fades. Iodine is added after incubation as a detector and does not inhibit the enzyme during the reaction. Reversing the two results would imply that heat activates the enzyme. Boiling is not a temporary slowdown; that describes chilling.
questions.answerText: The boiled tube stays blue black and the unboiled tube turns pale

questions.q: An enzyme tube is kept in an ice bath instead of a 37 C water bath, and almost no product forms. It is then warmed to 37 C and product appears. What does this show?
options: Cold denatures the enzyme in exactly the same way that heat does
Cold slows the reaction without denaturing, so the effect is reversible
Cold changes the pH of the buffer, and warming it back restores it
Cold destroys the substrate, and warming allows new substrate to form
questions.why: At low temperature molecules collide less often and with less energy, so the reaction rate falls, but the enzyme's folded structure is intact and full activity returns on warming. Heat denaturation is different precisely because it is not reversible, which is why this pair of experiments is worth doing. Buffer pH shifts only slightly with temperature and would not explain the result. Substrate is not destroyed by cold and cannot regenerate.
questions.answerText: Cold slows the reaction without denaturing, so the effect is reversible

questions.q: Lipase, cream, and a pH indicator are incubated at 37 C. What change in the indicator do you predict, and why?
options: The indicator does not change, because lipase does not alter pH
The indicator shifts toward alkaline, because bicarbonate is produced instead
The indicator shifts toward acidic, because free fatty acids are released
The indicator shifts toward alkaline, because glycerol is a base
questions.why: Lipase cleaves triglyceride into a monoglyceride and two fatty acids, and those free carboxyl groups release H+, so the pH of the tube falls measurably over the incubation. Glycerol is a neutral alcohol and is not even a major product of pancreatic lipase. Something must change or the assay would not work. Nothing in the reaction generates bicarbonate.
questions.answerText: The indicator shifts toward acidic, because free fatty acids are released

questions.q: A tube containing pancreatic amylase and gelatin, a protein, shows no product after incubation at pH 8 and 37 C. What is the best conclusion?
options: The enzyme was denatured by the gelatin in the tube
The incubation was far too short for any enzyme to act
The pH of 8 was wrong for amylase, so no reaction could occur
Amylase is specific for carbohydrate and cannot act on protein
questions.why: The conditions were correct for pancreatic amylase, so the absence of product points to the substrate rather than the environment, demonstrating that active sites are selective. A pH of 8 is close to this enzyme's optimum, so the pH explanation fails. Substrates do not denature enzymes. Blaming the incubation time would require a control showing that amylase also failed on starch, which is not the case.
questions.answerText: Amylase is specific for carbohydrate and cannot act on protein

questions.q: Adding bile salts to a tube of lipase and cream increases the rate at which pH falls. Does this make bile an enzyme?
options: Yes, because bile salts speed up a chemical reaction
No, because bile salts only increase the surface area available to lipase
Yes, because bile salts are consumed during the reaction
No, because bile salts lower the pH themselves rather than aiding digestion
questions.why: An enzyme catalyzes bond breaking, and bile salts break no bonds; they disperse the fat so more of it is exposed to the enzyme already present. That is a physical effect on substrate availability, not catalysis. Bile salts are not consumed, and if anything they are recovered intact. They do not acidify the tube; the fatty acids released by lipase do that.
questions.answerText: No, because bile salts only increase the surface area available to lipase

questions.q: An unknown digestive enzyme shows high activity at pH 2, no activity at pH 7, and no activity at pH 9, and it digests protein but not starch. Identify the enzyme and the region it works in, and predict what happens to it when chyme reaches the duodenum.
options: It is salivary amylase from the mouth, and it is inactivated by gastric acid
It is pancreatic lipase, and it is denatured by the acid it encounters in the stomach
It is trypsin from the pancreas, and it becomes more active as bicarbonate raises the pH there
It is pepsin from the stomach, and it is inactivated as pancreatic bicarbonate raises the pH
questions.why: Two pieces of data pin this down: an acid optimum places it in the stomach and a protein substrate makes it a protease, which together identify pepsin. Trypsin is a protease but has an alkaline optimum, so it would show the opposite pH profile. Amylase acts on starch, which this enzyme does not touch. Lipase acts on fat and prefers a near neutral pH.
questions.answerText: It is pepsin from the stomach, and it is inactivated as pancreatic bicarbonate raises the pH

questions.q: Two amylase tubes show no starch digestion. Tube A was boiled first, and tube B was buffered to pH 2. Design a single follow up step that tells the two apart and state the expected results.
options: Cool both tubes to 4 C and then reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not
Boil both tubes again and reincubate: tube A digests the starch and tube B does not
Neutralize both tubes to pH 7 and reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not
Add iodine to both tubes again: tube A turns pale and tube B stays dark
questions.why: Low pH inhibits reversibly in this range while boiling denatures permanently, so restoring a favorable pH separates a recoverable enzyme from a destroyed one. Boiling again would only destroy whatever activity remained in tube B. Repeating the iodine test adds no new information, since both tubes already tested positive for starch. Cooling would slow both reactions and reveal nothing about the difference.
questions.answerText: Neutralize both tubes to pH 7 and reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not

questions.q: A data table shows enzyme X most active at pH 2 and enzyme Y most active at pH 8, and both act on protein. A third tube shows enzyme Y placed in a pH 2 buffer produces no product even after the pH is restored to 8. Interpret all three findings.
options: X is a pancreatic protease and Y a gastric protease, and Y simply needs more time at pH 8
Both are gastric proteases, and the third tube shows that pH has no lasting effect at all
X and Y are the same enzyme measured twice, and the third tube shows a pipetting error
X is a gastric protease and Y a pancreatic protease, and acid denatured Y for good
questions.why: The pH optima assign each enzyme to the region whose pH matches it, and the failure to recover after acid exposure shows that extreme pH can denature as permanently as heat, which is why pepsin cannot be replaced by trypsin in the stomach. Two enzymes with opposite optima cannot be the same enzyme. Reversing the assignments contradicts the measured optima. If pH had no lasting effect, the third tube would have produced product once returned to pH 8.
questions.answerText: X is a gastric protease and Y a pancreatic protease, and acid denatured Y for good

questions.q: A student runs amylase with starch at pH 7 in three water baths: 4 C, 37 C, and 90 C. The 4 C and 90 C tubes both show undigested starch. Explain why the two negative results have different causes and predict what happens if each tube is moved to 37 C for another 30 minutes.
options: Both were only slowed, so both will digest the starch at 37 C
The hot tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the cold tube was denatured and will not
Both were denatured, so neither will digest the starch at 37 C
The cold tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the hot tube was denatured and will not
questions.why: Identical results can have opposite mechanisms, which is exactly what makes the recovery test informative: low temperature reduces collision energy without unfolding the protein, while high temperature breaks the bonds that maintain the active site. Only the reversible case recovers on rewarming. Cold does not denature enzymes at these temperatures, so calling the cold tube the denatured one has the two causes exactly backward.
questions.answerText: The cold tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the hot tube was denatured and will not
